2. Add a partial pushCredit(address token, address account, uint256 amount), so heirs that are contracts and cannot start a call can also be paid in chunks. Or let the credited account authorize chunked pushes.
3. Update the NatSpec, README and index.html to name per-transfer-capped, max-wallet and cooldown tokens as unsupported, and replace the "any ERC-20" claim.
4. Optionally have the app warn when a token's transfer of the full amount fails an eth_call simulation, or keep a supported-token allowlist in the frontend.
Restricting topUp to the owner is not required once a partial exit exists. Neither is refusing withdraw to third parties.

sev.reasoning:
VERDICT: real defect, not by design and disclosed. MEDIUM stands, but the finding needs a narrower cost claim and some variants should be trimmed.

CODE CHECK (b8baf34):
- _credit (InheritanceVault.sol:338-341) merges everything into _credits[token][to].
- finalizeClaim (:682-704) credits the whole v.balance minus the fee to one claimRecipient.
- withdrawCredit (:714-722) and pushCredit (:726-733) take no amount. Each sends the entire credit in one safeTransfer through _payout (:358-366).
- topUp (:441-454) is permissionless while the vault is ACTIVE.
- withdraw (:552+) credits any `to`.
- The PoC token (PocMaxTxToken) is a fair model of a SafeMoon-fork cap that applies to every transfer. The PoC applies its limit to all non-mint transfers with an immutable cap, which is the renounced-ownership case.
- The patched copy's partial withdrawCredit is correct: it runs only for msg.sender, reduces both _credits and totalCredited, and leaves surplus() unchanged.

DISCLOSURE: this is not disclosed, and the existing wording understates the risk.
- The contract's NOT SUPPORTED list (:59-65) names only NFTs and rebasing tokens. It presents fee-on-transfer as handled (:50-51, :343-344), which implies other ERC20s are supported.
- The README (:43) lists only rebasing tokens, NFTs and multiple assets per vault.
- site/index.html:75 says "any ERC-20". The app (app.html:60-67) accepts any token address without a check.
- The only related wording is how-it-works.html:97: "unusual transfer behavior can break normal accounting assumptions". terms.html:34 has an undefined "unsupported token". Neither tells an owner that a transfer-capped token makes any estate above the cap undeliverable, or that a stranger can cause this.
- security.html says nothing about tokens.
- OQ-1..OQ-3 are unrelated. The negative-rebase note is disclosed, but it covers a different trigger.

WHY NOT HIGH:
(1) The owner must choose a non-standard token: one whose cap applies to wallet-to-wallet transfers out of the vault and can never be lifted. Many BNB anti-whale tokens cap only AMM-pair buys and sells, or call removeLimits() after launch. For those, a lifted cap unfreezes the credit.
(2) The funds are frozen, not stolen. The loss is permanent only if the cap is immutable or the token's owner is gone.
(3) The griefing cost is NOT "the gap" in general. It is C - E: the cap minus the heir's credit, plus the fee. That is cheap only when the estate is already close to the cap (the PoC's 90/100 and 98.5/100 examples). For a typical holder the cap is usually 0.5-2% of supply, so the attacker must donate almost the whole cap. The donation also lands in the frozen credit, so the attacker loses it. The finding's "griefing is cheap" should say this.

WHY NOT LOW:
(a) The no-malice path is systematic. createVault and topUp each obey the cap, so the natural way to build an estate above the cap is several deposits. The contract accepts every one of them and then can never deliver the result to the heir. A living owner can escape only by withdrawing in chunks to distinct addresses, but the product exists for the owner who is gone.
(b) An unprivileged party can deny an inheritance. topUp works any time the vault is ACTIVE. withdraw(to=recipient) works throughout the ≥7-day window in which ClaimInitiated publishes the recipient, and it can be bundled with the permissionless finalizeClaim in the same block. So the heir's defense of choosing a fresh recipient per claim (initiateClaim :639, :654) does not help against an active griefer. It does help against the no-malice merge of several under-cap vaults to the same heir, which the finding does not mention.
(c) BNB Chain is a stated target and the homepage invites "any ERC-20".
This fits "a core guarantee broken under specific conditions" and "griefing with strong cost asymmetry when the estate is near the cap".

TRIM OR CORRECT:
- Max-wallet does not freeze credits. The vault is itself a capped wallet, so no credit can exceed maxWallet, and a fresh recipient can always take it. The real effect is a pool-wide denial of service on createVault and topUp for that token (LOW, separate).
- The per-sender cooldown grief is speculative. The PoC did not show it, it is a retry race rather than a freeze, most cooldowns apply only to pair buys, and the recommended fix does not address it. Drop it or mark it unverified or LOW.
- The fee-recipient pooled credit is LOW. The admin can pull it at any time.

FIX:
The recommended withdrawCredit(token, to, amount) is correct and sufficient. It needs 0 < amount <= credit, must act only on msg.sender's credit, keep the full-amount overload, and reduce totalCredited by the amount. It breaks no guarantee: the admin still cannot reach credits, and the surplus arithmetic is unchanged. It also turns the negative-rebase "last claimant gets nothing" into "gets the remainder".
- Do not add an amount to pushCredit unless it is needed for contract recipients that cannot originate calls. It is harmless because the destination is fixed, but a permissionless partial push adds a dust-spam surface on cooldown tokens.
- Do not restrict topUp or withdraw's `to` instead. That removes legitimate features and still leaves the no-malice path.
- If a supported-token allowlist (F01) is adopted, it must gate only createVault and topUp, never withdrawCredit, pushCredit or finalizeClaim. Otherwise it becomes an admin freeze lever, which contradicts T4.
- The Base contract is immutable, so the code fix reaches only the BNB and any v2 deployment. For the live contract:
  - Replace "any ERC-20" on index.html.
  - Add transfer-capped and cooldown tokens to the NOT SUPPORTED list in the README, the NatSpec for the next deploy, and how-it-works, stated as a permanent-freeze risk.
  - Have the app warn on tokens that are not on an allowlist. Optionally, simulate a transfer of the vault's full balance from the vault address with an eth_call state override before createVault and topUp, and show the heir the same check.
  - Advise owners of capped tokens to keep each vault below the cap, and heirs to use a distinct fresh recipient per claim. This does not stop an active griefer.
sev.better_fix:
For new deployments (BNB, any v2), add withdrawCredit(address token, address to, uint256 amount) that acts only on msg.sender's credit, requires 0 < amount <= credit, reduces _credits and totalCredited by the amount, and keeps the full-amount overload. Leave pushCredit full-only unless contract recipients that cannot originate calls need partial pushes. If an allowlist (F01) is added, it must gate only createVault and topUp, never any exit, or it becomes an admin freeze lever against T4. The live Base contract is immutable, so there the fix is off-chain:

confirmed.title: Fee lock ignores the 'no fee recipient means no fee' state: the admin can set a recipient during the challenge window and charge a claim that was fee-free at initiation
confirmed.location: contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:647-652 initiateClaim (locks only the rate), :692-699 finalizeClaim (reads feeRecipient live at :698-699), :750-754 setFeeRecipient (immediate); :411 createVault (snapshot ignores the recipient); NatSpec :57-58; site/index.html:114 ('if our fee address is ever unset, no fee is taken at all'); site/how-it-works.html:58 ('locked when the claim begins and can only fall'); README.md:53
confirmed.description: The effective fee has two inputs: the rate, min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps), and the recipient switch (fee = 0 when feeRecipient == address(0)). The A-04 fix freezes only the rate, lockedFeeBps = min(global, ceiling), at initiateClaim. finalizeClaim reads feeRecipient live. A claim initiated while no recipient was set (effective fee 0 by every public statement) is therefore charged the full locked rate if a recipient is set at any point before settlement. finalizeClaim is permissionless, so the admin can bundle setFeeRecipient(X), finalizeClaim and setFeeRecipient(0), leaving public state reading 'no recipient' before and after. This is the same sandwich A-04 was meant to close, reached through the recipient instead of the rate. It can also happen without malice: re-enabling fees after a fee-free period charges every claim already in flight. The A-04 regression tests (test/Audit.ts:248-300) cover only the rate path.
confirmed.impact: The heir loses up to the vault's creation ceiling (at most 1%, currently 0.5%) on a claim that on-chain state said would be fee-free. The guarantees in index.html:114 and how-it-works.html:58 are broken. Bounded, and not reachable today because feeRecipient is set to the hardware wallet 0x883C...CdCA3. It needs a future unset, or a new deployment (e.g. BNB) that starts with no recipient.
confirmed.exploit_scenario:
1. The admin calls setFeeRecipient(address(0)) and announces a fee holiday. claimFeeBps stays 50.
2. Owner Alice (10 ETH vault, ceiling 50 bps) goes inactive. Heir Bob calls initiateClaim. lockedFeeBps = 50 is recorded silently (no getter, not in ClaimInitiated), while public state shows no recipient.
3. One block before finalizableAt, or in one bundle at it, the admin calls setFeeRecipient(admin), then finalizeClaim(alice, 0), then setFeeRecipient(0).
4. ClaimSettled shows fee = 0.05 ETH credited to the admin, and Bob receives 9.95 ETH.
confirmed.recommendation: v2: in initiateClaim set v.lockedFeeBps = feeRecipient == address(0) ? 0 : min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps). Keep finalizeClaim's min() and zero-recipient rule so the fee can still only fall. Optionally snapshot v.feeBps = 0 at createVault when no recipient is set. Add a regression test for the toggle. Live deployment: publicly commit never to unset the fee recipient (or never to re-set it once unset), and correct index.html:114 and how-it-works.html:58.

test_names: PoC F05: fee lock ignores the zero-recipient switch control: a claim that starts and settles with no recipient is fee-free
PoC F05: fee lock ignores the zero-recipient switch a claim begun with no fee recipient stays fee-free when the admin sets one mid-window
PoC F05: fee lock ignores the zero-recipient switch the admin cannot sandwich the settlement through the recipient in one block

poc.explanation:
F05 is confirmed by an executable test. I traced the path in contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:
- `initiateClaim` (lines 651-652) locks only `lockedFeeBps = min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps)`. It never reads `feeRecipient`.
- `finalizeClaim` (lines 695-699) reads `feeRecipient` live and charges `amt * lockedFeeBps / 10000` whenever it is non-zero.
- `setFeeRecipient` (lines 750-754) is `onlyOwner` and takes effect immediately. Nothing stops a call while a claim is pending.
- `createVault` (line 411) snapshots `v.feeBps = claimFeeBps` even when no recipient is set.

The test file asserts the safe, intended property: a claim begun while no fee recipient is set settles fee-free. It has four tests.

**Control (passes).** The recipient is unset before the claim and stays unset. The claim settles with fee 0. This shows the zero-recipient rule works when nobody toggles it, so the other failures come from the toggle and not from the fixture.

**Test 2 (fails, as expected).** This uses the live configuration: 50 bps and a fee sink set.
1. The admin calls `setFeeRecipient(0)`.
2. Bob, the heir, calls `initiateClaim` after the inactivity period.
3. With a day of the window left, the admin calls `setFeeRecipient(admin)`.
4. Dave, a third party, calls `finalizeClaim`.

`ClaimSettled` pays Bob 9.95 ETH instead of 10 ETH.

**Test 3 (fails, as expected).** This is the one-block sandwich. With automine off, the admin sends `setFeeRecipient(admin)`, then `finalizeClaim(alice, 0)`, then `setFeeRecipient(0)`. All three are mined in one block at `finalizableAt`. The setup checks pass:
- all three transactions succeed and share one block number;
- `feeRecipient` reads `address(0)` in the block before and in the latest block;
- the vault is SETTLED.

The failing assertion is that the admin's credit should be 0. It is 0.05 ETH.

**Test 4 (fails, as expected; quantifies the damage).** This is a fresh deployment with recipient `address(0)` and 100 bps, like a new BNB deployment. The 100 ETH vault's ceiling is still snapshotted at 100 bps. The admin sets a recipient after Bob initiates, and the settlement credits 1.0 ETH to the fee sink.

**Why the tests fail for the right reason.** Every failure is the fee or credit assertion itself. There are no reverts and no fixture errors. I also checked the other direction. I made a patched copy at `contracts/test/InheritanceVaultF05Fixed.sol`, a new file in the sandbox, with the recommended one-line change in `initiateClaim`: `v.lockedFeeBps = feeRecipient == address(0) ? 0 : min(...)`. Against that copy:
- all 4 PoC tests pass (runner: `test/poc-F05-fixcheck.ts`, contract chosen by the `F05_IMPL` environment variable);
- the existing `test/Audit.ts` and `test/InheritanceVault.ts`, re-pointed at the patched copy under `test-fixcheck/`, give 56 passing and 0 failing. That includes the A-04 rate-path regressions.

So the tests are valid regression tests for the fix. InheritanceVault.sol and NotifySubscription.sol were not edited, and nothing in the repo was touched.

**Public claims the tests contradict:**
- NatSpec, InheritanceVault.sol:58: "No fee is taken while no fee recipient is set."
- site/index.html:114: "if our fee address is ever unset, no fee is taken at all."
- site/how-it-works.html:58: "The effective settlement fee is locked when the claim begins and can only fall before settlement".
- README.md:53: "No fee recipient configured ⇒ no fee taken."

poc.severity_observation:
The impact is as the finding describes. The loss is capped by the vault's creation ceiling: 0.5% at the current 50 bps and at most 1% (the MAX cap). A few details go beyond the finding.

1. **The heir has no defence.** `setFeeRecipient` can be called at any point in the 14-day window, not only in a bundle at `finalizableAt` (test 2 shows this). Finalizing early is impossible because `finalizeClaim` reverts before `finalizableAt`. `lockedFeeBps` has no getter and is not in `ClaimInitiated`, so the heir cannot even see what rate was locked.

2. **A new deployment is fully exposed.** A deployment that starts with no recipient (test 4) still snapshots a 100 bps ceiling at `createVault`. Every vault created during the fee-free period is chargeable later. Re-enabling fees, even innocently, charges every claim already in flight.

3. **The fix only needs to touch `initiateClaim`.** The one-line fix changes no other behaviour. A fee cut, or an unset recipient after initiation, still lowers the fee because `finalizeClaim` keeps its `min()` and its zero-recipient rule. The fix passes the existing A-04 rate tests.

4. **It is not reachable on the live Base deployment today.** The recipient is set, so a malicious use first needs a publicly visible `setFeeRecipient(0)` event. For the live immutable contract, the only mitigations are an operational commitment and corrected site copy.

Low severity is appropriate. The admin can take only a bounded fee on a claim that on-chain state said would be fee-free. It is not a path to principal.

reach.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. The code path and the PoC both hold up.

Code trace (repo at b8baf34, contracts/InheritanceVault.sol):
- createVault :411 stores v.feeBps = claimFeeBps without reading feeRecipient.
- initiateClaim :651-652 sets v.lockedFeeBps = min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps). Its guards (:640-645) check the recipient, the state, that msg.sender is the beneficiary, the deadline and a non-zero balance. None of them reads feeRecipient.
- setFeeRecipient :750-754 is onlyOwner. Its only guard is newRecipient != address(this), and it takes effect immediately. Nothing checks for pending claims.
- finalizeClaim :682-710 is permissionless. Its guards are state == CLAIM_PENDING and block.timestamp >= finalizableAt. It then reads feeRecipient live at :698 and charges amt*min(lockedFeeBps, claimFeeBps)/10000 whenever that is non-zero.

So a claim initiated while feeRecipient == 0 is charged the full locked rate if any recipient is set before finalization. Every step uses only legitimate admin calls and permissionless calls. There is no path through state that cannot be reached. The heir has no defence: the heir cannot finalize before finalizableAt, and lockedFeeBps is not exposed in VaultView (:147-160, getVault :813-836) or in the ClaimInitiated event.

PoC validity:
- I diffed the sandbox's contracts/InheritanceVault.sol and TestHelpers.sol against the repo. Both are byte-identical.
- The test uses no hardhat_setStorageAt, no impersonation and no contract-as-sender. It uses only the real admin signer, the heir, a third party, evm_setAutomine and setNextBlockTimestamp.
- I ran it: 1 passing (the control, which proves the zero-recipient rule works when nobody toggles it) and 3 failing on the fee and credit assertions themselves. The failures are 9.95 vs 10 ETH, a 0.05 ETH admin credit, and a 1.0 ETH fee-sink credit. None is a revert or a fixture error.
- The one-block sandwich test checks that feeRecipient reads address(0) both at the prior block and at the latest block. That matches the A-04 threat model: "Public state read unchanged".

Why it is not merely by design: the zero-recipient rule was written as a liveness escape (:694, README:53 "An abandoned admin can never strand a claim"). The NatSpec at :58 ("No fee is taken while no fee recipient is set") is literally satisfied at settlement time. But site/how-it-works.html:58 promises "The effective settlement fee is locked when the claim begins and can only fall before settlement". When the claim began, the effective fee was 0 by the contract's own rule (:699). It then rises to the locked rate. That is exactly the sandwich AUDIT-2026-08-09 A-04 said was closed. The A-04 tests (test/Audit.ts:246+) cover only the rate path.

Mitigating factors, which keep this at Low:
(1) The heir is never charged more than min(the owner-accepted creation ceiling, the global rate at initiation). The numeric rate lock itself holds, so the owner never pays above what they agreed to at createVault. The loss is only against the fee holiday that the docs imply.
(2) It requires two deliberate admin actions, both of which emit FeeRecipientChanged: unset, then set. On Base today the recipient is set (deployments/base.json:7, 0x883C…CdCA3). scripts/deploy.ts:43-45 defaults the recipient to the deployer, so a new BNB deployment would not start with a zero recipient unless someone chose that on purpose.
(3) Impact is capped at 1% by MAX_CLAIM_FEE_BPS, and at 0.5% for vaults created at the current 50 bps. Principal is never reachable.

Severity: this is a bounded fee taken by the admin, contrary to a published guarantee and an incomplete prior fix. It has real but capped fund impact, so it goes above Informational. It is not the admin reaching principal, so HIGH does not apply. LOW fits the rubric.
reach.better_fix:
The recommended v2 change is correct and minimal: in initiateClaim, set v.lockedFeeBps = (feeRecipient == address(0)) ? 0 : min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps). Keep the live min() and the zero-recipient rule in finalizeClaim, so a fee can still only fall. The patched copy passes the existing 56 A-04 and core tests.

Also add lockedFeeBps to VaultView and to the ClaimInitiated event, so an heir can see the locked rate. The finding's other suggestion, snapshotting v.feeBps = 0 at createVault when no recipient is set, is optional. It would permanently zero the fee for vaults created during a fee holiday, which may be broader than intended.

For the immutable Base deployment, the only lever is operational: commit publicly never to call setFeeRecipient(address(0)), or never to re-set a recipient once unset. Reword how-it-works.html:58 to say that the rate, not the effective fee, is locked at initiation, and that a fee is taken if a fee address is set at settlement. Reword index.html:114 the same way.

sev.reasoning:
I checked the code at b8baf34, and the behaviour is real.
- initiateClaim (contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:651-652) locks only the rate, `lockedFeeBps = min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps)`, and never reads feeRecipient.
- finalizeClaim reads feeRecipient live (:698) and charges `amt * min(lockedFeeBps, claimFeeBps) / 10000` whenever the recipient is non-zero (:699).
- setFeeRecipient (:750-754) is onlyOwner and takes effect immediately. Nothing checks for pending claims.
- lockedFeeBps is not in VaultView/getVault (:809-833) or in ClaimInitiated (:212), so the heir cannot see what was locked.
- The A-04 tests (test/Audit.ts:248-300) cover only the rate path.

**Is it intended and disclosed? No on both counts.**
- The zero-recipient rule was not designed as a pricing input. The code (:694, :272) and README.md:53 describe it only as a liveness guard for an abandoned admin.
- The prior audit never considered how this rule interacts with the A-04 lock. OQ-1 to OQ-3 do not cover it. OQ-3 is about the ceiling slipping at creation, which is a different moment.
- security.html:53-55 and the how-it-works.html:86-90 table disclose "change the fee recipient" as an admin power. They do not say it can switch a fee on for claims already in flight.
- how-it-works.html:58 says the effective fee "is locked when the claim begins and can only fall". That is flatly contradicted: the effective fee is 0 at initiation and rises to lockedFeeBps.
- AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:50-53 says A-04 was fixed to stop a sandwich that takes "a fee the heir had every public reason to believe was lower" while public state reads unchanged. That same sandwich still works through the recipient.
- README.md:53 and NatSpec :58 ("while no fee recipient is set") are only literally true if read as the state at settlement.
- index.html:114 is stated under "We disappear". It holds for an admin who is truly gone, since that admin cannot re-set the recipient, but it is worded absolutely.
So the behaviour is undisclosed, and one public guarantee is false. Not refuted.

**Severity: LOW is right under the rubric, and not higher.**
1. Only the privileged admin can trigger it. A third party, the heir or an MEV searcher cannot.
2. It needs an unusual precondition that the admin must create deliberately and in public: feeRecipient == 0 when the claim is initiated.
   - The live Base deployment has the recipient set to the hardware wallet (deployments/base.json).
   - scripts/deploy.ts:43-45 defaults the recipient to the deployer, never to zero. A BNB deployment through the standard script would therefore not start in the exposed state unless FEE_RECIPIENT were explicitly set to the zero address.
   - The natural way to run a fee holiday is setClaimFee(0), and that path is correctly locked. Unsetting the recipient is an odd operation.
   - The FeeRecipientChanged events are emitted on-chain, so a sandwich is detectable afterwards but cannot be prevented.
3. The loss is bounded by the vault's own creation-time ceiling: 0.5% today, 1% hard cap. The owner accepted that fee at creation. No principal and no credited payout can be reached, so this is not "admin able to reach user funds" in the HIGH sense.
4. It is the same class as A-04, which was rated LOW, and harder to reach than A-04 was.

It is not INFORMATIONAL because value really moves from the heir to the admin, against a published guarantee. The PoC engineer's observation that the heir has no defence is correct: finalizeClaim reverts before finalizableAt, and the locked rate is invisible. That does not raise the ceiling on the loss.

**On the recommended fix**
The v2 one-liner is correct and minimal: `v.lockedFeeBps = feeRecipient == address(0) ? 0 : min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps)` in initiateClaim, keeping finalizeClaim's min() and zero-recipient check.
- It keeps the property that the fee can only fall.
- It does not affect the rule's stranding purpose.
- The PoC engineer reports that the existing A-04 and full test suites pass against the patched copy.
- An admin rotating the recipient through zero only forgoes the operator's own revenue, which is user-favourable. The heir cannot influence feeRecipient, so the fix cannot be abused.

I do not recommend the optional createVault change (v.feeBps = 0 when no recipient is set). It permanently zeroes a vault's ceiling, which turns a liveness switch into a lifetime pricing decision. It also goes beyond what any public statement promises: index.html:131-134 promises the claimFeeBps rate as the ceiling, and the claim-time lock already honours the "unset means no fee" claim. If it is adopted, it should be treated as a business decision, not a security fix.
sev.better_fix:
**v2 contract**
- Keep the one-line fix in initiateClaim: `v.lockedFeeBps = feeRecipient == address(0) ? 0 : min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps)`.
- Leave finalizeClaim's min() and its zero-recipient rule unchanged.
- Expose lockedFeeBps in VaultView/getVault, and add the locked fee (recipient-adjusted) to the ClaimInitiated event. This lets the heir and watchers verify the locked fee, which is the missing piece that makes both the rate sandwich and the recipient sandwich silent today.
- Add regression tests for three cases:
  - a claim begun with a zero recipient, with a recipient set mid-window, settles fee-free;
  - the same with a one-block sandwich;
  - a recipient unset after initiation still gives a fee of 0.
- Do not snapshot v.feeBps = 0 at createVault. It is unnecessary to fix this finding and changes pricing semantics permanently.

**Live Base contract (immutable)**
- Correct how-it-works.html:58 to say the rate is locked at claim start and a fee is charged only if a fee recipient is configured at settlement.
- Reword index.html:114 as "if our fee address is unset at the moment a claim settles, no fee is taken".
- Publish an operational commitment never to set feeRecipient to address(0) on the live contract. With the current design there is no legitimate reason to do so, because fees accrue as credits and cannot strand a claim.

**Future deployments (BNB)**
- Deploy with a non-zero recipient (the deploy.ts default already does this).
- Record in the deployment record that the zero-recipient state is never used as a fee holiday. setClaimFee(0) is the locked, safe mechanism for that.

confirmed.description: createVault snapshots claimFeeBps at mining time as the vault's permanent ceiling and has no maxFeeBps argument. A wrapper cannot do the check atomically for an EOA, because msg.sender becomes the vault owner. Only smart-account batching (Safe MultiSend, EIP-7702) lets a user bound it. initiateClaim likewise locks min(global, ceiling) at mining time with no heir-supplied maximum. A-04 was meant to stop a settlement sandwich. It now takes two sandwiches instead of one: raise the rate around the heir's initiateClaim, lower it, then raise it again around finalizeClaim, which the admin can call itself. The heir pays the ceiling while claimFeeBps read lower in almost every block. Verified: no bound parameter exists and setClaimFee applies immediately.
confirmed.impact: Up to the 1% bytecode cap per vault through a creation front-run, and up to the vault's ceiling per claim through the two-point sandwich, while the advertised rate is lower. Bounded, and visible after the fact in ClaimFeeChanged and VaultCreated.feeBps. An owner can escape a bad ceiling for free with a full withdraw and re-create. An heir can avoid only the finalize leg, by finalizing before the admin raises the rate. Practical on BNB Chain's public mempool. On Base it needs sequencer access or predictable timing; deadlines are on chain, so timing is predictable.
confirmed.exploit_scenario:
Creation leg: 1. Owner Alice submits createVault while the site advertises 0.5%. 2. The admin, watching the BNB mempool, front-runs with setClaimFee(100) and back-runs with setClaimFee(50). Alice's vault has a permanent 1% ceiling.
Claim leg: 3. The admin runs a public promotion, setClaimFee(10). 4. Heir Bob submits initiateClaim; the admin front-runs with setClaimFee(ceiling) and back-runs with setClaimFee(10), so lockedFeeBps = ceiling. 5. At finalizableAt the admin sends setClaimFee(ceiling), finalizeClaim(alice, 0), setClaimFee(10) with consecutive nonces (atomically with EIP-7702 batching). ClaimSettled.fee is 1% while claimFeeBps() reads 10 before and after.
confirmed.recommendation: v2: add uint16 maxFeeBps to createVault and to initiateClaim, reverting when the rate to be snapshotted or locked exceeds it. Alternatively, timelock fee increases (e.g. effective no sooner than MAX_CHALLENGE plus a delay; decreases stay immediate), so min() only ever sees pre-announced rates. App: show the current rate before signing, compare VaultCreated.feeBps with the quoted rate after mining, and offer withdraw-and-recreate on a mismatch. Heir guides: call finalizeClaim yourself at finalizableAt. Live deployment: publish a 'rates only go down' operating commitment.

poc.explanation:
F06 is reproduced: all four tests fail on the assertion that states the defect, and every setup check passes first.

**How the tests work**
- Automine is off. Each sandwich puts three transactions in one block: the admin's front-run with a 100 gwei tip, the user's transaction with a 2 gwei tip, and the admin's back-run with a 1 gwei tip on the next nonce. Hardhat's default priority ordering mines the front-run first.
- Before any fee assertion runs, each test checks that `block.transactions` is exactly [front, victim, back] and that both admin transactions succeeded. This makes the ordering real, not assumed.
- Each test then asserts the intended property: nobody pays more than `claimFeeBps()` showed at the last mined block when they signed.

**Test 1 (creation leg, OQ-3)**
- Alice is quoted 50 bps. In one block: `setClaimFee(100)`, then Alice's `createVault`, then `setClaimFee(50)`.
- `claimFeeBps()` reads 50 before and after that block.
- `getVault(alice,0).feeBps` is 100, against a quote of 50. The cause is `InheritanceVault.sol:411` (`v.feeBps = claimFeeBps`). The `createVault` signature at :370-377 has no bound parameter.

**Test 2 (two-point claim sandwich)**
- Alice creates her vault honestly with a 50 bps ceiling. The admin then runs a promotion at 10 bps. Bob is quoted 10.
- Leg 1: `setClaimFee(50)`, Bob's `initiateClaim`, `setClaimFee(10)`. The lock at :651-652 captures `min(50, 50) = 50`.
- Leg 2: at `finalizableAt`, the admin sends `setClaimFee(50)`, then calls `finalizeClaim` itself, then `setClaimFee(10)`, all in one block. The min() at :695-697 gives 50.
- `ClaimSettled.fee` is 0.05 ETH, against 0.01 ETH at the quoted rate. `claimFeeBps()` read 10 at every block boundary.

**Test 3 (heir finalizes himself)**
- Same setup as test 2, but this time Bob sends `finalizeClaim` himself, and the admin sandwiches Bob's transaction.
- The fee is still 0.05 ETH.

**Test 4 (full scenario, quantified)**
- `claimFeeBps()` at every block boundary over the whole life of the vault: [50, 50, 10, 10, 10, 10], so the maximum was 50.
- Vault ceiling is 100 and the locked rate is 100.
- Fee taken is 0.1 ETH (the 1% cap). At the 10 bps rate public when Bob claimed it would have been 0.01 ETH, so the excess is 0.09 ETH on a 10 ETH vault. The fee recipient is credited 0.1 ETH and the heir 9.9 ETH.

**Why the failure is the defect and not the setup**
- The failing lines are the `lte` assertions at poc-F06.ts:143, 187, 213 and 274. The ordering, status and public-rate assertions before them all pass.
- I generated two patched copies of the vault as new files, so `InheritanceVault.sol` was not edited. The first, `contracts/test/F06FixBound.sol`, adds `uint16 maxFeeBps` to `createVault` and `initiateClaim`. The second, `contracts/test/F06FixTimelock.sol`, delays fee increases and applies decreases at once. The script that makes them is `make-fixed-copies.js` in the sandbox.
- With `F06_VAULT=F06FixBound` or `F06_VAULT=F06FixTimelock`, the same 4 tests pass without changes. With the bound, the victim's transaction reverts on it. With the timelock, the fee is 0.01 ETH. So the tests can serve as regression tests for either fix.
- The full sandbox suite is 63 original tests passing plus these 4 failing. One early full run reported 62 passing and 5 failing. That did not recur in 7 reruns, and I could not tell which test failed.

poc.severity_observation:
The finding is confirmed, with the loss bounded as it says: at most the 1% bytecode cap per settlement (0.09 ETH above the advertised rate on a 10 ETH vault in the PoC). The PoC shows two points where the finding understates the impact.

1. **The heir cannot escape the finalize leg on a public mempool.** The finding says the heir can avoid that leg by finalizing himself before the admin raises the rate. Test 3 shows the admin can sandwich the heir's own `finalizeClaim`, and the same 50 bps is taken. On Base the admin can instead raise the rate in the block before `finalizableAt`, which is predictable because it is on chain. So finalizing at `finalizableAt` helps only if the admin is not watching.

2. **The locked rate cannot be seen through any view function.** `lockedFeeBps` is not in `VaultView`, so `getVault()` does not return it. `getVault().feeBps` returns the creation ceiling (100 in the PoC), and `claimFeeBps()` returns the current global rate (10). The rate actually locked against the heir (100) could only be read from raw storage; the test had to compute the storage slot from the compiler's storage layout. The ClaimFeeChanged events show the raise and the lowering, but the heir has to work out their order inside the block to know which rate was locked. So "visible after the fact" is weaker than the finding states.

**On severity:** LOW is defensible because the loss is bounded by a disclosed cap and needs the admin key. Under the rubric it arguably reaches MEDIUM, as a core guarantee broken under specific conditions. A-04 and the T4 trust-model NatSpec both say the rate can only move down once a claim is in flight, and an heir who saw 10 bps at every block boundary is charged 100 bps.

**Preconditions:**
- The finalize leg needs no mempool access at all: the admin calls `finalizeClaim` itself, in one block, on consecutive nonces.
- Only the creation and `initiateClaim` legs need front-running: a public mempool (BNB) or sequencer access (Base).

reach.reasoning:
Not refuted. I checked every step against the code at b8baf34, and the sandbox copy of InheritanceVault.sol is byte-identical to the repo.

**Code path**
- `createVault` (InheritanceVault.sol:370-377) takes no bound argument. At :411 it sets `v.feeBps = claimFeeBps` at mining time. The owner is `msg.sender`, so an EOA cannot use a checking wrapper.
- `initiateClaim` (:639) locks `min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps)` at :651-652, also with no bound argument.
- `finalizeClaim` (:695-697) takes `min(lockedFeeBps, claimFeeBps)`, and anyone can call it.
- `setClaimFee` (:742-746) checks only `onlyOwner` and the cap of 100. There is no timelock and no same-block guard.
- The heir cannot abort or re-lock a claim; only owner actions can displace it. Once the lock is taken at the front-run rate, it stays.
- `getVault` does not expose `lockedFeeBps`.

**PoC**
- I read and ran poc-F06.ts: 0 passing, 4 failing, each on the `lte` assertion that states the defect.
- It uses no `setStorageAt` and no impersonation. `getStorage` is used only to read `lockedFeeBps` for the report.
- Ordering is real: automine is off, the admin's front-run pays a higher priority fee, and the back-run is the admin's next nonce. The test asserts that the block holds exactly [front, victim, back] and that both admin transactions succeeded.
- The patched copies show the tests are not self-confirming.
- The two-point sandwich is valid. A-04 only moved the attack point from `finalizeClaim`, which the admin can call itself, to the heir's `initiateClaim`, which needs a front-run.

**Corrections that bound the finding**
1. **The live Base deployment is effectively not exposed.** Base has no public mempool, so both front-run legs need collusion with the sequencer. The finding says timing is predictable because deadlines are on chain. That is true only for `finalizableAt`. The heir chooses when to call `initiateClaim`. The finalize leg does nothing unless the initiate leg succeeded, because the lock caps it. So the finding is practical mainly on the planned BNB deployment.
2. **The heir mitigation is misstated.** "Finalize before the admin raises the rate" fails on a public mempool (PoC test 3), and the finalize leg is irrelevant on its own anyway. The mitigation that works is the one the finding gives only for `createVault`: a smart account or EIP-7702 EOA can bound `initiateClaim` atomically with `require(claimFeeBps() <= quote); initiateClaim()`. That defeats the whole claim leg.
3. **The Ledger precondition is weaker than stated.** A keyless bot can hold pre-signed setClaimFee pairs on consecutive nonces and broadcast them around a victim's transaction. Each pair works once.
4. **Ordering is readable after the fact.** A heir can recover the order from `transactionIndex` in the receipts. The real observability gap is only that `lockedFeeBps` is absent from `getVault`, which is informational.

**Disclosure**
- The creation leg is disclosed: OQ-3 in AUDIT-2026-08-09.md, and AUDIT_SCOPE.md lists "create-time fee-ceiling slippage" as a known unresolved design question.
- The claim leg is not disclosed. A-04 is presented as fixed, and how-it-works.html advertises the lock at claim start. That page's statement stays literally true, since the locked value never rises afterwards, but the purpose of A-04 is defeated.
- index.html promises "0.5%... your rate is locked when you create the vault", and the creation front-run defeats that quote. Because the claim leg is undisclosed, `by_design_and_disclosed` is false overall.

**Severity: LOW, not MEDIUM**
- The actor is the privileged admin.
- The fee is capped by each vault's own ceiling, which is at most the 1% bytecode cap. The admin could always charge the ceiling openly. On the claim leg the sandwich only hides the rate from someone relying on a voluntary lower rate; it adds no entitlement.
- An owner escapes the creation leg at no fee cost by withdrawing everything and re-creating.
- The attack is impractical on the only live chain.
- Smart-account users can bound both calls.
- It does not meet HIGH's "admin reaches user funds": nothing beyond the fee ceiling is taken, and no locked or credited balance can be reached.
reach.better_fix: For v2, timelock fee increases and keep decreases immediate. An increase should take effect no sooner than MAX_INACTIVITY... in practice, no sooner than a fixed public delay of at least MIN_CHALLENGE, with a pendingFeeBps/effectiveAt pair and an event. Then every value that createVault snapshots or initiateClaim locks will have been announced in advance. This protects plain EOAs with no ABI change. Also add optional maxFeeBps overloads to createVault and initiateClaim for integrators, and expose lockedFeeBps in VaultView. For the live immutable deployment, publish a "rates only go down" operating commitment. The app should also read VaultCreated.feeBps after mining and offer to withdraw and re-create on a mismatch; that costs no fee. Heir tooling should wrap initiateClaim in an atomic claimFeeBps() check where the wallet supports EIP-7702 or smart-account batching.

sev.reasoning:
**Verdict: the finding is real, and LOW is the right severity. It is not by design and disclosed.** Only the creation leg is disclosed, in repo documents, and the public pages say the opposite. The claim-leg sandwich is disclosed nowhere, and the prior audit lists A-04 as fixed.

**Code check** (contracts/InheritanceVault.sol, commit b8baf34):
- `createVault` (:370-377) has no bound parameter. It snapshots `v.feeBps = claimFeeBps` (:411).
- `initiateClaim` (:639) has no bound either. It locks `min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps)` into `lockedFeeBps` (:651-652).
- `finalizeClaim` (:695-697) takes `min(lockedFeeBps, claimFeeBps)`.
- `setClaimFee` (:742-746) applies at once, checks only `<= MAX_CLAIM_FEE_BPS`, and has no cooldown. `claimFeeBps` is written nowhere else (:271, :745).
- Anyone can call `finalizeClaim`, so the admin can call it too.
- The A-04 tests (test/Audit.ts:248-300) only cover a rate that is visible on chain when `initiateClaim` runs. They never front-run `initiateClaim`.
- So the two-point sandwich works: raise, `initiateClaim`, lower; then later raise, `finalizeClaim`, lower. The lock is only as good as the rate in force when the heir's transaction was mined. The PoC confirms this.

**Disclosure check:**
- OQ-3 (AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:192) and AUDIT_SCOPE.md:80-83 disclose only create-time ceiling slippage, and only in repo documents.
- The user-facing pages say the opposite:
  - site/index.html:117 ("We turn evil ... cannot ... raise your fee") and :133-134 ("Your rate is locked when you create the vault").
  - site/how-it-works.html:58-59 ("locked when the claim begins and can only fall").
- The app never reads `claimFeeBps()` before `createVault`. The site hard-codes "0.5%".
- The NatSpec T4 line (:42-43, "lower (never raise above ...)") misstates the power: the global rate can be raised to 1%.
- So at minimum this is a code-versus-claims defect.

**Why LOW and not MEDIUM (strict rubric):**
1. Only the admin can do it. It is a privileged actor, currently a Ledger hardware wallet that must sign each transaction by hand. Moving to a bot means a two-step ownership transfer or signing by hand under time pressure.
2. The loss is strictly bounded:
   - Creation leg: at most (1% − advertised rate) of the estate.
   - Claim leg: at most (vault ceiling − promotional rate).
   - Nothing ever exceeds the per-vault ceiling or the 1% bytecode cap. The site advertises that cap as the absolute worst case ("No admin ... can ever take more"), and that promise holds.
3. No core guarantee breaks. Locked and credited balances stay unreachable, the 1% cap holds, and a vault's ceiling cannot be raised after creation.
4. The claim leg gains nothing an honest admin could not get openly by never running a promotion. What it adds is deception: advertising a promotion and denying it to chosen heirs. The heir never pays more than the ceiling the owner accepted.
5. The creation leg can be seen and undone:
   - The app shows the vault's `feeBps` right after creation (site/assets/app.js:286), and so does `VaultCreated.feeBps`.
   - Owner withdrawals carry no fee, so a full withdraw and re-create costs only gas.
6. On the live Base deployment it is largely impractical. The sequencer mempool is private.
   - The heir chooses when to call `initiateClaim` (any time after the deadline), and without sequencer collusion the admin cannot front-run it.
   - Without that front-run, A-04 does work: the promotional rate gets locked and the finalize leg can only lower it.
   - So the finding's claim that "deadlines are on chain, so timing is predictable" is overstated for the claim leg. The deadline is predictable; the heir's `initiateClaim` is not.
   - It is practical only on the planned BNB deployment, which has a public mempool, and even there wallets that submit through private RPCs are protected.
7. The Base contract holds no user funds today.

It stays above INFORMATIONAL because it takes users' money above the advertised rate (at most 1% of an estate) and defeats the stated purpose of a fix the prior audit marked done.

**Adjustments to the PoC engineer's points:**
- (a) Agreed: on a public mempool the heir cannot escape the finalize leg. But that leg only matters if the initiate leg succeeded.
- (b) `lockedFeeBps` is missing from `VaultView` and from the `ClaimInitiated` event. That is a real observability gap (LOW or INFO in its own right: return values that mislead integrators; the app shows the ceiling, not the effective rate). It is not strictly invisible, though. The locked rate can be rebuilt from log order in the block (the logIndex of `ClaimFeeChanged` versus `ClaimInitiated`), so raw storage reads are not required.
- Arguing MEDIUM on "a core guarantee broken" stretches "core": the broken promise is a fee-transparency promise, not fund safety or inheritance delivery.
sev.better_fix:
**1. Live, immutable Base deployment.** Make the rule "rates only go down" enforced by code, not just a written commitment.
- Use `Ownable2Step` to transfer ownership of the vault to a small FeeGovernor contract that the Ledger controls. The governor exposes:
  - `lowerClaimFee(bps)`, which requires `bps <= claimFeeBps()` and applies at once.
  - `proposeRaise(bps)`, applied with `executeRaise()` only after a public delay (7 days or more), with the pending value readable on chain.
  - Plain pass-throughs for `setFeeRecipient`, `setCreationPaused` and `sweepSurplus`.
  - A `transferOwnership` pass-through only behind the same delay. Without that, the admin can take direct control back and sandwich again.
- This closes both the creation sandwich and the claim sandwich on the existing contract, with no redeploy. No raise can happen inside a block.

**2. v2 contract.**
- Add `uint16 maxFeeBps` to `createVault` and `initiateClaim`, reverting when the rate to be snapshotted or locked exceeds it.
- A bound on `initiateClaim` alone closes the whole claim leg, because `finalizeClaim` can only lower the rate. `finalizeClaim` needs no parameter.
- The heir must always be able to pass `maxFeeBps >= ceiling`. Then an admin who front-runs to force reverts can only waste the heir's gas and can never block the inheritance.
- Add `lockedFeeBps` (or the effective rate) to `VaultView` and to the `ClaimInitiated` event.
- If a timelock is used instead:
  - There is no need to delay increases by `MAX_CHALLENGE` (365 days). The lock at `initiateClaim` already protects claims in flight, so any public delay long enough for users to react is enough, and a promotion can end without a one-year wait.
  - Compute the effective rate lazily and read it at both snapshot points.
  - Expose the pending rate and the time it takes effect.

**3. App and documentation.**
- Read `claimFeeBps()` and show it before signing. After mining, compare `VaultCreated.feeBps` with the quoted rate, and offer a fee-free withdraw and re-create when they differ.
- Show heirs the rate actually locked, rebuilt from log order.
- Fix site/index.html:117 and :133-134, and the NatSpec T4 wording at :42-43.
- Re-open A-04 in the prior audit as "partially fixed: defeats a one-point sandwich only".

poc.explanation:
The test asserts the property the site promises: a vault's rate "can go down if we lower fees later; it can never go up" (site/index.html:133-134). Both tests fail on that assertion, not on setup.

How the code produces it: createVault stores only a ceiling, v.feeBps = claimFeeBps (InheritanceVault.sol:411). initiateClaim sets lockedFeeBps = min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps) at the moment the claim starts (:651-652). finalizeClaim takes min(lockedFeeBps, claimFeeBps) (:695-697). No function records the lowest global rate a vault has seen. checkIn and the other owner actions do not touch the fee. setClaimFee (:742-746) only checks the 100 bps hard cap. So a vault's effective rate follows the global rate back up to its creation ceiling.

Test 1, 'an heir never pays more than the lowest rate the vault was lowered to':
- Alice creates a 10 ETH vault at 50 bps.
- The admin calls setClaimFee(0).
- Alice checks in twice during a 50-day promotion, so even a v2 fix that ratchets the rate on owner actions would capture 0 bps.
- The admin calls setClaimFee(50).
- Alice goes silent. Bob initiates, then anyone finalizes.
- Expected ClaimSettled fee 0. Actual fee 0.05 ETH, i.e. 50 bps.

Test 2, 'quantifies it: the vault's effective rate is not monotone non-increasing', uses takeSnapshot to measure what the heir would pay at three points: at creation, during the cut, and after the restore. Its two controls pass: 0.05 ETH at creation and 0 during the cut, so the cut really did reach this vault. The mechanics hold, but the finding overstates how false the copy is. I rate it Informational, not Low.

What I verified:
- A vault's effective rate is min(v.feeBps, global rate at initiateClaim, global rate at finalizeClaim):
  - createVault stores only the creation snapshot, v.feeBps = claimFeeBps (InheritanceVault.sol:411).
  - initiateClaim locks min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps) into v.lockedFeeBps (:651-652).
  - finalizeClaim re-takes the minimum with the current global rate (:695-697).
- setClaimFee (:742-746) is onlyOwner and checks only the 100 bps hard cap. No function records the lowest rate a vault has seen; checkIn and abortClaim never touch the fee.
- Every step in the scenario is reachable under all guards: admin setClaimFee(0), then setClaimFee(50) while no claim is in flight, then a normal initiate and finalize.
- I ran the PoC (test/poc-F07.ts). The sandbox InheritanceVault.sol is byte-identical to the repo copy. The test uses only public calls, time.increase and takeSnapshot/restore to probe hypothetical settlements. No setStorageAt and no impersonation. Its controls pass: 0.05 ETH at creation, 0 during the cut. Its final assertions fail with fee 0.05 ETH after the rate is restored.
- The behaviour is intentional. test/Audit.ts:270, "a rate locked during a promotion does not survive an aborted claim", asserts it.

Why the severity drops:
1. The PoC's "safe property" (a vault's rate never rises once it has fallen) is the finder's own reading of site/index.html:133-134. The copy says "Your rate is locked when you create the vault. It can go down if we lower fees later; it can never go up." The rate being locked is the creation rate, so the more natural reading is "never above what was locked at creation", and the code honours that exactly. The one-way-ratchet reading is plausible but not the only one. The PoC therefore demonstrates the code's behaviour correctly, but whether that behaviour contradicts the copy is a matter of wording, not a code defect.
2. The same reading explains index.html:117, "We cannot ... raise your fee": "your fee" is the vault's creation rate, which the admin cannot exceed.
3. Every detailed public page describes the ceiling model correctly:
   - how-it-works.html:79-81 ("records the global rate at creation as its personal ceiling; an administrator cannot later raise that vault above the ceiling")
   - how-it-works.html:88 (the admin-powers table lists "Change the global fee within the 1% hard cap" as a power, and "Raise an existing vault above its creation ceiling" as something the admin cannot do)
   - how-it-works.html:58-59
   - security.html:55
   - terms.html:41
   - guides/dead-mans-switch-crypto.html:148-150 ("the effective rate can fall, but cannot rise above that ceiling")
4. The app shows only the ceiling ("fee X%" from vault.feeBps, site/assets/app.js:286). No page or on-chain value ever tells an owner their vault's rate has fallen to a lower figure. The impact claim ("more than the rate the site told the owner their vault had fallen to") therefore rests on a statement the site never makes.
5. The heir never pays more than the rate the owner accepted and saw at creation, which index.html:129 advertises as the fee. There is no loss beyond the agreed rate, no unprivileged actor, and nothing an integrator reads from events or return values misleads them.

Under the rubric this is a code-vs-documentation clarity mismatch with no fund impact beyond the disclosed ceiling: Informational. The copy fix is still worthwhile because the index bullet is the only place the wording is ambiguous. Suggested wording: "Your vault's fee can never exceed the rate in force when you created it; fee cuts apply while they are in force."

sev.reasoning:
This is not refuted. The code works as designed, but the homepage misstates the design.

**How the code works**
- createVault stores the global rate as v.feeBps (InheritanceVault.sol:411). This is a ceiling and never changes.
- initiateClaim locks min(claimFeeBps, v.feeBps) into lockedFeeBps (:651-652).
- finalizeClaim takes min(lockedFeeBps, claimFeeBps) (:695-697).
- Nothing keeps a vault at the lowest rate it has seen.

**The behaviour is intended**
The B-05 fix (AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:127-131) called it a defect that "a rate locked during a promotion survived an aborted claim permanently." The test Audit.ts:270-286 asserts that the promotion rate is lost once the promotion ends.

**Where it is disclosed accurately**
- README.md:51-52: a creation ceiling; "a lower global rate at settlement time wins".
- how-it-works.html:58-59 and :79-81, :88: the fee "can only fall before settlement, never rise above the vault's creation-time ceiling"; the admin "can change the global fee within the 1% hard cap"; the admin cannot "raise an existing vault above its creation ceiling".
- security.html:53-55: existing vaults keep their creation-time ceiling.

**Where it is misstated**
The homepage, the most-read page, says otherwise in two places:
1. index.html:133-134 says "Your rate is locked when you create the vault. It can go down if we lower fees later; it can never go up." You can read "your rate" as the creation rate, which is never exceeded. But "can go down ... never go up" plainly promises a one-way ratchet. The code has none.
2. index.html:116-117, the "We turn evil" trust row, says the admin cannot "raise your fee" and calls this an arithmetic fact of the bytecode. That is false in plain terms. After setClaimFee(0), the call setClaimFee(50) raises every pre-existing vault's settlement fee from 0 back to 0.5%.

The line "locked when you create the vault" also contradicts how-it-works.html, which says the rate is locked when the claim begins. The prior audit's open questions OQ-1..OQ-3 do not cover this. OQ-3 is about the ceiling being set at mining time.

Result: the behaviour is intended and disclosed on three pages, but the homepage understates the admin's power. That makes it a documentation/disclosure finding, not a code defect.

**Severity, applying the rubric strictly**
- Only the admin can trigger it. The most likely trigger is harmless: a promotion ending, not malice.
- It costs the admin nothing.
- The heir never pays more than the rate the owner accepted when creating the vault (0.5% today, bytecode cap 1%). There is no theft, no freezing, and no denied or hijacked inheritance.
- What the heir "loses" is a discount the contract never guaranteed.
- Timing is ordinary: the fee only has to be restored before the heir initiates.

That puts it between LOW and INFORMATIONAL. I keep LOW, not INFORMATIONAL, because:
- The false statement is in the trust-model table, about exactly this admin power, and is framed as bytecode fact.
- It has a real money effect, up to the ceiling. On a 10 ETH vault that is 0.05 ETH more than the 0% the owner was told the vault had fallen to.
- An owner who loses their wallet (the designed recovery path) cannot act to protect the lower rate.

INFORMATIONAL is defensible if the reviewer treats the creation rate as the agreed price. HIGH does not apply: the admin cannot reach principal and cannot exceed the vault's ceiling.
sev.better_fix:
**1. Fix the copy now (the deployed contract is immutable)**
Rewrite both index.html spots.
- Fees bullet: "Your vault's fee can never exceed the rate in force when it was created (0.5% today; bytecode cap 1%). Lower global rates apply only while they are in force. When your heir starts a claim the rate is capped, and a cut made during the challenge window still applies."
- The finding's suggested wording, "the rate is fixed when your heir starts a claim", is itself slightly wrong: a cut during the challenge window still reaches the heir (:695-697). Say "capped", not "fixed".
- "We turn evil" row: replace "or raise your fee" with "or raise any vault's fee above the rate in force when that vault was created".
- Consider a footnote on OQ-3: the ceiling is the rate at mining time, not at signing.

**2. Frontend (today)**
Show the current effective rate as min(getVault().feeBps, claimFeeBps()). Label it as able to return to the ceiling, so the UI never implies a permanent reduction.

**3. v2: do not adopt the proposed per-vault ratchet as written**
- Ratchet on owner interaction: the fee then depends on owner activity. It gives nothing to lost-wallet owners, whom the product is designed to serve.
- Strict ratchet over global history: needs per-change checkpoints, which is gas and complexity.
- Either kind turns every temporary promotion into a permanent liability on all existing vaults. A rational admin would then never cut fees, which hurts users.
- Cheaper and more honest: add a single global permanentCeilingBps that can only decrease (O(1), one slot), with effective = min(v.feeBps, permanentCeilingBps, claimFeeBps). The admin then chooses which cuts are binding promises (permanent) and which are promotions (claimFeeBps). The site can promise a one-way ratchet only for the former.

confirmed.title: Permissionless pushCredit lets anyone override the credited account's routing choice, forcing a credit into a blocklisted address or a contract that cannot move the asset
confirmed.location: contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:724-733 pushCredit() (always pays the account itself); :714-722 withdrawCredit(); guarantee stated in NatSpec :67-72 ('withdrawCredit lets the credited account route anywhere, which covers blocklisted EOAs and any contract able to make one call'); :682-710 finalizeClaim (permissionless)
confirmed.description: The NatSpec escape for blocklisted EOAs and 'any contract able to make one call' works only if the account moves first. pushCredit is permissionless and always delivers to the credited account. (1) Some tokens check only the SENDER's blocklist status: Tether's TetherToken checks msg.sender in transfer, and the issuer can later destroyBlackFunds. A third party can push the credit INTO the blocklisted address before its owner routes it elsewhere. Because finalizeClaim is permissionless, a helper can run finalizeClaim then pushCredit in one transaction in the first block after the window, leaving the heir no block in which to route. (2) A contract recipient that can call withdrawCredit but cannot transfer the asset out (a purpose-built forwarder, or a contract with receive() and no native send) can be front-run: pushCredit delivers the asset into it, and its own pull reverts NothingCredited. pushCredit's stated purpose (:724-725, 'a contract recipient with a payable receive()') applies only to native coin. With two-sided blocklists such as USDC's FiatToken the push reverts instead, which is harmless.
confirmed.impact: An unprivileged party can turn a recoverable credit into frozen or burnable tokens, permanently freezing one heir's or withdrawer's credit. The attacker gains nothing (griefing). This breaks a documented guarantee. Rated LOW because the credited account must already be blocklisted by a sender-only-blocklist issuer, or be a narrow type of contract, though that is exactly the case the NatSpec says is covered.
confirmed.exploit_scenario:
Blocklist variant: 1. Alice's vault holds a Tether-style token and heir Bob has a claim with recipient = Bob. 2. During the window the issuer blocklists Bob. Only the beneficiary can set that address, and nobody can front-run it, because initiateClaim is gated on msg.sender == beneficiary. The binding routing choice is therefore made at claim initiation, not at withdrawal. This is not the rubric's "hijack or deny an inheritance".
(2) Variant 1 needs an independent adverse act by a privileged outside party. The token issuer must blocklist the heir's own named recipient during the challenge window of at least 7 days. The issuer must also use sender-only blocklist semantics, as Tether does. The "guarantee" being defeated is in effect a way around the issuer's blocklist. The freeze or burn is the issuer's decision and can be reversed by the issuer, so it is not a permanent loss caused by the protocol.
(3) Variant 2 needs the heir, or a withdrawing owner, to have chosen a recipient contract that can make an arbitrary call to withdrawCredit but cannot move the asset it will receive. That is contrived and self-inflicted. Safes, 4337 wallets and EOAs are unaffected.
(4) The attacker gains nothing, and the target chains may not carry a sender-only-blocklist token. I did not verify whether one circulates on Base or BNB.

The cost asymmetry is real: one transaction's gas against 100% of one credit. A well-meaning keeper that finalizes and then pushes does the same damage. So this is a bounded edge case with a real fund impact, which is LOW, not INFORMATIONAL.

The recommended fix is weak and partly harmful.
(a) "Restrict pushCredit to NATIVE" misses the native case. The PoC engineer showed that a receive()-only forwarder is still stranded.
(b) Worse, native-only would create a new class of permanently frozen funds that is much more likely than this bug. Today every ERC20 credit is deliverable, because an ERC20 transfer to any address succeeds. pushCredit is the only route for an ERC20 credit to an address that cannot originate a call. The main example is an exchange deposit address, which the dapp invites: site/assets/app.js:245 prompts for a free-form "Payout address" at initiateClaim. The same applies to an owner withdrawing to such an address. A heir who enters a CEX deposit address would lose the whole inheritance permanently under that fix.
(c) Opt-in per account fails for the same reason: an account that cannot originate a call cannot opt in.

The finding's NatSpec correction is right. The Base deployment is immutable, so documentation and UI are the only remedy there.

Recommendation: rate LOW, keep it as a disclosed-limitation and documentation finding for Base, and fix it with a delayed push, not a native-only push, in the BNB or any future deployment.
sev.better_fix:
For a new deployment (BNB, or a Base redeploy):
- Keep pushCredit for every asset, but let third parties push only after a delay.
- In _credit, record creditedSince[token][account] = block.timestamp only when the credit goes from zero to nonzero. Record the first moment the credit was owed, not the latest credit, so accounts that keep accumulating (such as the fee recipient) cannot have pushes postponed forever.
- Clear the timestamp in withdrawCredit and pushCredit.
- In pushCredit, require msg.sender == account || block.timestamp >= creditedSince + PUSH_DELAY, with PUSH_DELAY around 14-30 days.

What the delay gives:
- Recipients that cannot originate a call (exchange deposit addresses, receive-only contracts; ERC20 and native) can still be paid, just later.
- Any account able to make one call gets a window to route first that cannot be front-run. This covers the blocklisted EOA and both forwarder variants, including the native one.
- It does not change the owner or heir trust model.

Optional extra: setPushOptOut(bool) for accounts that never want to be pushed. Non-callers keep the default (push allowed), so opt-out breaks nothing. Do not use native-only or opt-in: both permanently strand ERC20 credits paid to addresses that cannot originate a call.

For the immutable Base contract (documentation and UI only):
- Correct NatSpec :67-72 in the repo source.
- Correct site/how-it-works.html:73-74.
- Add a README trust-table row saying:
  - the payout address named at initiateClaim is the binding routing choice;
  - after settlement anyone may push the credit to it;
  - so name an address that can hold and move the asset and is not exposed to a token blocklist;
  - do not rely on withdrawCredit re-routing.
- In the dapp's "Payout address" prompt (app.js:245), warn that a contract recipient must be able to transfer the asset. A pushCredit button for recipients that cannot pull would also help.

confirmed.description: initiateClaim and withdraw reject only address(0) and the vault itself as destinations. How the defect works:

- finalizeClaim credits _credits[NATIVE][WETH] = 9.95 ETH.
- pushCredit (:726-733) is permissionless. Its _payout (:358-366) does call{value}, WETH9's fallback runs deposit(), and the vault now holds 9.95 WETH that no lane tracks.

- F2c (damage): the admin does both steps alone. A control check first confirms that before the push sweepSurplus reverts with NoSurplus, so the value is only stuck, as NatSpec :67-72 says. The admin then calls pushCredit itself and sweeps 9.95 WETH. Afterwards creditOf(NATIVE, WETH) = 0, Bob's credit = 0, the vault holds 0 WETH, and only the 0.05 fee credit remains in totalCredited(NATIVE).

The scenario steps run inside a tolerant attempt() wrapper, so a fixed contract can refuse the destination, the push or a non-native sweep. poc.severity_observation:
Slightly stronger than the finding claims. No third party ("Mallory") is needed: pushCredit is permissionless, so the admin alone can run push-then-sweep (F2c). The admin takes 100% of the misdirected credit (9.95 of 9.95 ETH in the test), and after the push nothing else can move that WETH. The vault has no path to pay vault-held WETH to Bob, because Bob holds no WETH credit. Once pushed, the value is therefore reachable only by the admin, who could return it at their discretion (an undocumented trust-based rescue) or keep it.

Before the push, sweepSurplus reverts NoSurplus and the value is just stuck, as NatSpec :67-72 describes. Compared with that world the user loses nothing extra, which keeps this LOW.

Preconditions:
- The heir or owner must name a wrap-on-receive contract (WETH9 on Base, WBNB on BNB Chain) as the destination. The app's actClaim prompt (site/assets/app.js:245-248) accepts any address with no contract check.
- The owner withdraw path (F2b) lets the admin take the owner's own money under the same mistake.
- Canonical WETH9 fallback semantics are assumed. The test places them at the real Base predeploy address but does not fork Base mainnet.

reach.reasoning:
I could not refute F09. I traced every step against the code and every precondition is reachable.

1. **The claim path accepts the WETH address.** initiateClaim (InheritanceVault.sol:640) rejects only address(0) and address(this). The other guards (:642-645: state ACTIVE, caller is the beneficiary, deadline passed, balance > 0) are all met by an honest heir. The app's actClaim (site/assets/app.js:244-249) takes a free-text address and only runs ethers.getAddress() on it. There is no code or contract check, so an heir can reach this from the official UI.
2. **finalizeClaim credits the WETH address.** finalizeClaim (:682-710) is permissionless and makes no external calls. It sets _credits[NATIVE][WETH] = amt - fee.
3. **Before a push the value is stuck.** WETH9/WETH98 cannot originate a call: its only outbound call is withdraw(), which pays msg.sender. So withdrawCredit can never run for that account. This matches NatSpec :67-72, and the PoC's F2c control confirms that sweepSurplus reverts NoSurplus at this point.
4. **pushCredit turns the credit into vault-held WETH.** pushCredit (:726-733) is permissionless and has no destination check beyond _payout's to != this (:359). _payout does call{value} with all remaining gas. The receive/fallback of Base's WETH predeploy (0x4200...0006) and of BSC's WBNB both run deposit() for msg.sender, so the vault now holds WETH. The vault's own receive() revert (:786-788) plays no part, because no ETH is sent back to it.
5. **The admin can sweep it.** totalLocked[WETH] and totalCredited[WETH] do not include this WETH, so surplus(WETH) (:768-772) equals the pushed credit. sweepSurplus(WETH, admin) (:774-780) is onlyOwner, has no token restriction, and transfers it out.

**The PoC is sound.** The sandbox InheritanceVault.sol is byte-identical to the repo file (I diffed them). The test uses no hardhat_setStorageAt and no impersonation. Its only cheat is hardhat_setCode, which puts WETH9 behaviour at the real Base predeploy address, and that behaviour matches mainnet. The test asserts the safe property: the admin gains nothing. It fails on exactly that assertion, after its setup checks pass: the credit equals DEPOSIT minus the fee, and surplus is 0 before the push. I ran it and got 3 failing, with the admin gaining 9.95, 4 and 9.95 WETH.

**Two scope notes.**
- **F2b needs a direct contract call.** The owner-withdraw path is not reachable from the app, because actWithdraw (app.js:214-223) always passes S.account. F2b therefore needs a direct call, for example from a block explorer.
- **There is a third entry point.** withdrawCredit(NATIVE, WETH) (:714-722) checks only to != 0. If a credited account routes its own credit to WETH, the vault gets WETH that the admin can sweep, with no push at all. The finding does not list this path. It is reachable only by a direct call, because the app's withdrawCredit also uses S.account.

**Severity: LOW, and arguably INFORMATIONAL.**
- **No extra loss.** The heir's value is already lost to the heir by their own choice of destination. Without the push it is burned forever; with it, only the admin can reach it. Either way the heir loses the same amount. The admin's reach is actually the only possible recovery, so this is not "the admin able to reach user funds" in the HIGH sense.
- **Still a real defect.** It requires user error and is bounded to the misdirected amount. But the code contradicts a stated guarantee: NatSpec :44-46, index.html:116 ("We cannot touch a wei of any vault") and the "No admin rescue exists on purpose" claim at :71-72. It also creates an undocumented, trust-based custody path.
- **Not by design.** The disclosure at :67-72 says this value is stuck, which is wrong for wrap-on-receive recipients. So the behaviour is not by design and disclosed.
reach.better_fix:
**Base (live and immutable):** code cannot change here.
- In actClaim, refuse known wrapped-native and token addresses, and warn when the address has contract code.
- Correct NatSpec :67-72 and the site's admin-powers text. They should say that a native payout sent to a wrap-on-receive contract (WETH/WBNB) comes back as vault-held surplus that only the admin can move, and that returning it is a discretionary, trust-based rescue.

**BNB (or any redeploy):** check the destination inside _payout, not only at the entry points.
- When token == NATIVE, revert if `to == wrappedNative`, where wrappedNative is an immutable constructor argument.
- Because it sits in _payout, this also covers withdrawCredit's `to`, which the proposed initiateClaim/withdraw checks miss, as well as pushCredit.
- Keep the early checks in initiateClaim and withdraw so the error surfaces at claim time rather than at payout.
- Do not restrict sweepSurplus to NATIVE only. That would permanently strand genuinely force-fed ERC20s, and it removes the only recovery for this mistake rather than preventing the mistake.

sev.reasoning:
I checked this against commit b8baf34. The mechanics are as described. The behaviour is not intended, and no document discloses it. The right severity is LOW.

What the code does:
- initiateClaim (InheritanceVault.sol:640) rejects only address(0) and address(this) as the recipient. withdraw (:552-554) does the same for `to`, and _payout (:358-366) adds only a self check.
- pushCredit (:726-733) is permissionless and does a plain call{value}. WETH9 and WBNB wrap incoming coin for msg.sender, which here is the vault.
- The vault then holds WETH that neither totalLocked[WETH] nor totalCredited[WETH] tracks. surplus (:768-772) therefore returns all of it, and sweepSurplus (:774-780), which is onlyOwner, pays it out.
- The admin needs nobody else. It can call pushCredit and then sweepSurplus itself, as the PoC's F2c shows.

A path the finding missed: withdrawCredit (:713-721) checks only `to != 0`. An heir who calls withdrawCredit(NATIVE, WETH) sends the coin to WETH, and the vault receives WETH straight away, with no push needed. That is the most direct way for a user to make this mistake, so any fix has to cover withdrawCredit's `to` as well.

Is it disclosed? No, and what is published says the opposite:
- NatSpec :67-72 and the prior audit (AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:71-72) cover only addresses that "can neither originate a call nor receive native value". They say such value is stuck, with "no admin rescue ... on purpose".
- WETH can receive native value, so it falls outside that disclosure, and the outcome is the reverse: the admin can reach the value.
- The following statements are all false in this case: NatSpec :44-46 ("cannot reach a wei of ... any credited payout"), the README.md:41 trust-model row, site/security.html:55-56 ("cannot withdraw a user's ... payout credit") and site/index.html:116.
- OQ-1..OQ-3 are unrelated.
- Compare the positive-rebase case: there the design team did disclose that value becomes admin-sweepable surplus. This case has no such disclosure.

Why LOW and not MEDIUM or HIGH:
- The rubric's HIGH item "the admin able to reach user funds" does not fit in substance. The heir or owner has already lost the value by their own mistake before the admin can do anything.
- The Base WETH predeploy is not proxied and WBNB is immutable. Only WETH could call withdrawCredit on its own credit, and it cannot. Without this path the value is permanently stuck, so admin reach adds no loss compared with that.
- No unprivileged party gains anything, and nobody can push someone else into the mistake. The trigger is always the victim's own choice of address.
- The official app lowers the likelihood. actWithdraw and the credit withdrawal hard-code S.account, so those two paths need a direct contract call. Only actClaim (site/assets/app.js:244-249) takes a free-text payout address, and it defaults to the connected wallet.
- A MEDIUM case can be made under "core guarantee broken under specific conditions", because the no-admin-reach claim is literally false. But that guarantee exists to protect users from the admin, and here the admin's reach only turns permanent loss into loss that a trustworthy admin could undo.
- What remains is: public guarantees that are false in a concrete case, an unintended and undocumented rescue path that depends on trusting the admin (and contradicts the stated "no admin rescue on purpose" design), and a UI with no check on the payout address. That is LOW, with a documentation component.
sev.better_fix:
1. The Base deployment is immutable and cannot be fixed on-chain, so the recommended constructor parameter only helps a new deployment (BNB or a redeploy). For the live contract, remediate off-chain:
   (a) In actClaim, call provider.getCode on the payout address. Hard-refuse the chain's wrapped-native address and any address that responds to ERC20 totalSupply(). Warn on any other address with code.
   (b) Correct README.md:41, site/security.html, site/index.html:116 and :161 to state the exception: coin sent to a wrap-on-receive contract becomes admin-sweepable surplus.
   (c) Either publish a written admin policy to return any such WETH surplus to the vault's beneficiary (identified from the ClaimInitiated/ClaimSettled and CreditPaid(NATIVE, x, WETH) events), clearly labelled as depending on trust in the admin, or state that it will never be swept.

2. For new deployments, pass wrappedNative as an immutable and reject it everywhere coin can be routed:
   - initiateClaim recipient
   - withdraw `to`
   - withdrawCredit `to`, which the finding's fix omits and which is the one-call path
   - pushCredit's account when token == NATIVE

   Also reject the vault's own ERC20 address as a recipient (that is the stuck-forever case).

3. Structural option for a redeploy: credit the claim to the beneficiary itself, which has just proved it can originate calls, rather than to an arbitrary recipient. The heir then routes it with withdrawCredit(to). This removes the whole class of credits stuck at an address that can never call, and keeps the fresh-address routing through withdrawCredit. The heir pays for one extra transaction.

4. On making sweeps NATIVE-only (the F01 fix): it does remove the admin-reach half. But it also removes the documented ability to rescue accidentally sent ERC20s ("sweeping accidental transfers", index.html:161), and it turns this value into permanently stuck WETH. If adopted, both consequences must be disclosed.

confirmed.title: Tokens that debit the vault by more than the recorded amount (fee on top, issuer wipe, negative rebase) make the shared pool insolvent, and the whole loss falls on whoever withdraws last
confirmed.location: contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:358-366 _payout() (no balance measurement), :714-722 withdrawCredit(), :726-733 pushCredit(), :774-780 sweepSurplus(); inbound-only measurement in :345-356 _pull(); exclusions at :60-65; site/index.html:75 ('any ERC-20')
confirmed.description: Deposits are measured (_pull records the balance difference). Payouts are not: each assumes the vault's balance falls by exactly 'amount'. Tokens that charge the sender value + fee, issuers that can wipe or burn a holder's balance (TetherToken.destroyBlackFunds, Paxos wipeFrozenAddress), and negative-rebase tokens all push the pool below totalLocked + totalCredited. All vaults of a token share one balance and every withdrawal is full-amount, first come first served. Early withdrawers are paid in full, and later ones, including owners and heirs of unrelated vaults who did nothing, get nothing, not a pro-rata share. surplus() floors at 0, so no view shows the shortfall. A sweepSurplus of a fee-on-top token also overdraws into the locked lane. The NatSpec documents only the rebasing case; fee-on-top and issuer-wipe tokens are mentioned nowhere.
confirmed.impact: Value moves between unrelated vaults using the same token and lands on whoever withdraws last. Confined to one token's lane: other tokens and native coin are unaffected. Rated LOW because every affected user chose a token outside the supported class, but the public copy does not warn about it.
