poc.severity_observation:
LOW is right; one could also argue for INFORMATIONAL. No funds move wrongly: the owner is entitled to withdraw, and storage is consistent. The damage is limited to integrators that track claims through the ClaimInitiated/Aborted/Superseded/Settled lifecycle and ignore the closed flag on Withdrawn. They show the heir a phantom claim that never clears, and at the announced finalizableAt the heir's finalizeClaim reverts NoClaimPending with no event explaining why. An integrator that reads Withdrawn(closed=true), or re-reads getVault, avoids the problem.

The past-horizon case makes this more than cosmetic. There, abortClaim is closed and a partial withdraw deliberately leaves the claim running, so a full withdraw and extendHorizon are the only owner actions that can stop a claim. extendHorizon emits ClaimSuperseded(ACT_EXTEND_HORIZON); the full withdraw emits nothing claim-shaped. Heir-protection tooling watching for claims being displaced past the horizon misses exactly this case.

The Base deployment (0xC821...fE2f) is immutable, so the code fix only helps a new or BNB deployment. For the live contract, the only remedy is documentation for integrators that Withdrawn(closed=true) ends any pending claim.

The one-line fix, emitting ClaimSuperseded before state is set to CLOSED when the prior state was CLAIM_PENDING, was checked only against this PoC suite, not against the full existing 63-test suite.

reach.reasoning:
I could not refute F14. The code, the reachability analysis and the PoC all hold up.

Code path (contracts/InheritanceVault.sol, identical to the sandbox copy per diff):
- withdraw (:552-580) runs _requireLive (:282-285). That check reverts only for NONE, SETTLED and CLOSED, so a CLAIM_PENDING vault gets through.
- Nothing else in withdraw stops an owner from withdrawing the full balance mid-claim, before or after the horizon.
- When the balance reaches 0, the closing branch (:566-573) writes state=CLOSED and zeroes claimInitiatedAt and claimRecipient directly. It never calls _clearPending (:312-322), the only place ClaimSuperseded is emitted (:320).
- _credit (:338-341) and _removeFromOpen (:324-336) emit nothing. The only log is Withdrawn(..., closed=true) at :579.
- The partial-withdraw branch before the horizon (:574-577) does go through _clearPending(ACT_WITHDRAW). So the same user action, withdraw, emits the claim-lifecycle event on one path and not on the other. This contradicts the stated purpose of the ACT_* tags at :89: "so an indexer can tell WHICH owner action displaced a claim".

Past-horizon claim: with a claim pending and block.timestamp >= absoluteDeadline, I checked what each owner action does:
- abortClaim reverts HorizonReached (:670).
- setBeneficiary and setInactivityPeriod revert inside _clearPending (:314).
- setCheckInChain reverts at :509.
- checkIn reverts ClaimPendingUseAbort (:460).
- topUp needs ACTIVE.
- A partial withdraw skips _clearPending (:574), so the claim keeps running.

Only extendHorizon, which emits ClaimSuperseded(ACT_EXTEND_HORIZON), and a full withdraw can end the claim. The finding's "one of only two" statement is correct.

After closing, every entry point reverts on a CLOSED vault, so no later closing event can ever be emitted. Disclosure: code comments (:310, :568) say a full withdraw ends the claim, but nothing in the README, the prior audit or the docs says it does so without a lifecycle event. The ACT_WITHDRAW comment implies the opposite.

PoC: I ran it myself: 1 passing (CONTROL), 4 failing, with exactly the failure messages reported.
- It uses only public entry points and time.increase. There is no setStorageAt, impersonation, setCode or balance manipulation, and the sandbox InheritanceVault.sol is byte-identical to the repo's.
- The patched copy differs by one line, which emits before state is set to CLOSED. That isolates the defect.
- The CONTROL test shows the event-sourced tracker is correct whenever the contract does emit ClaimSuperseded, so the failures are not an artefact of the model.
- The asserted property is a design expectation, but a reasonable one, because the contract itself defines the ACT_WITHDRAW vocabulary.

Mitigating factors, which are why this stays LOW and does not go higher:
- No funds move wrongly: the owner is entitled to withdraw everything, and storage stays consistent.
- The information is on-chain, since the same tx carries Withdrawn(closed=true). An indexer that treats closed=true as terminal, or re-reads getVault, is unaffected. The project's own notify/watcher.js (:296-299) and site/assets/app.js (:205, :216) re-read getVault.
- Minor overstatement in the finding: "reverts NoClaimPending with no event explaining why". A revert can never emit events. The explanation exists as the earlier Withdrawn(closed=true), just outside the claim vocabulary.

Severity: this matches the rubric's LOW class ("events/return values that mislead integrators"). There is a real inconsistency on the one claim-ending path an heir-protection monitor most needs to see past the horizon. INFORMATIONAL would be defensible only if one holds that Withdrawn(closed) is enough.
reach.better_fix: In the closing branch, emit ClaimSuperseded(v.owner, vaultId, ACT_CLOSE) before state is set to CLOSED, and only when the prior state was CLAIM_PENDING. ACT_CLOSE is a new tag (6), not a reuse of ACT_WITHDRAW. Every other ClaimSuperseded tag means the vault went back to ACTIVE, so an indexer seeing ACT_WITHDRAW would conclude the vault is ACTIVE unless it also reads Withdrawn.closed; a separate tag makes the terminal outcome clear from the claim event alone. Alternatively, add a general VaultClosed(owner, vaultId, hadPendingClaim) event. Run the patch against the full existing suite: tests that assert exact event lists on a full withdraw will need updating. The Base deployment is immutable, so for it the only remedy is integrator documentation: Withdrawn(closed=true) is terminal and ends any pending claim, and claim trackers must consume it (or re-read getVault) as well as ClaimAborted, ClaimSuperseded and ClaimSettled.

sev.reasoning:
Confirmed against the code. withdraw() (InheritanceVault.sol:552-580) passes _requireLive (:282-285) for a CLAIM_PENDING vault. When the balance reaches 0, the closing branch (:567-573) writes STATE_CLOSED and zeroes claimInitiatedAt and claimRecipient directly, and emits only Withdrawn(..., closed=true) at :579. I listed every path that clears a claim (grep for claimInitiatedAt = 0, _clearPending and STATE_CLOSED): setCheckInChain :513, a partial withdraw before the horizon :577, setBeneficiary :592, setInactivityPeriod :602 and extendHorizon :629 all go through _clearPending, which emits ClaimSuperseded (:320). abortClaim emits ClaimAborted (:676) and finalizeClaim emits ClaimSettled (:709). The full-withdraw close is the only path that ends a claim without a claim-lifecycle event. Past the horizon it is one of only two actions that can stop a claim at all. The comment on the ACT_* tags (:89) says they exist so an indexer can tell which owner action displaced a claim. The code does not do that for this action.

Intended and disclosed? The behaviour itself, a full withdraw ending a pending claim, is intended and disclosed: code comments at :307-308 and :567, prior audit B-01 (AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:103-106), and site/how-it-works.html §5 (:63-64, "close the vault by withdrawing everything"). The missing event is NOT disclosed anywhere I found: README, security.html, how-it-works.html or the OQ list. No integrator note says that Withdrawn(closed=true) ends a pending claim. The README state diagram (README.md:13-17) also draws CLOSED as reachable only from ACTIVE and leaves out the CLAIM_PENDING -> CLOSED edge. So this is not by-design-and-disclosed, but a documentation and event-completeness defect.

Severity, applying the rubric strictly: the only party who can trigger it is the vault owner, spending their own funds, which they are entitled to do. Nothing is stolen, frozen or misaccounted, and storage stays consistent. The victim is an event-driven third-party indexer, explorer or heir dashboard that models only the claim lifecycle. It shows a phantom pending claim that never clears, because CLOSED is terminal and no later call can emit anything. At finalizableAt the heir's finalizeClaim reverts NoClaimPending. In practice this is usually caught at eth_estimateGas, so the heir loses gas at most, plus confusion. Two points argue for INFORMATIONAL. The information is not lost: Withdrawn carries closed=true, so an indexer that models vault state rather than only claims derives the right answer. And the project's own tooling is unaffected: notify/watcher.js re-reads getVault (:254, :299-306) and has a vault-closed path (:239-273). But the rubric names "events/return values that mislead integrators" as LOW, and this is an internal inconsistency with the contract's own stated event contract: a partial withdraw emits ClaimSuperseded(ACT_WITHDRAW), a full withdraw does not. So LOW stands, not higher. The Base deployment at 0xC821...fE2f is immutable, so for that address the only remedy is documentation.

The recommended fix is sound in spirit but has one trap to name. Do NOT fix this by calling _clearPending(v, vaultId, ACT_WITHDRAW) in the closing branch. Past the horizon, _clearPending reverts HorizonReached for any action other than ACT_EXTEND_HORIZON (:314-316). Every full withdrawal past the horizon while a claim is pending would then revert. That removes the documented "close the vault by withdrawing everything" exit (how-it-works §5) and changes the trust model. Emit the event directly instead, as the PoC patch does, and capture the prior state before it is overwritten.
sev.better_fix: For a new deployment (BNB, or a Base redeploy), in withdraw()'s closing branch, capture `bool wasPending = v.state == STATE_CLAIM_PENDING;` before writing STATE_CLOSED. Then `if (wasPending) emit ClaimSuperseded(msg.sender, vaultId, ACT_CLOSE);`, where ACT_CLOSE = 6 is a NEW tag, not ACT_WITHDRAW. A dedicated tag keeps the documented rule unambiguous for indexers: a partial withdraw past the horizon never supersedes a claim, and only closing the vault does. Do not route this through _clearPending: its HorizonReached revert (:314-316) would block full withdrawals past the horizon and break the documented exit. Run the full 63-test suite in addition to the PoC, because tests that assert exact log lists (for example Audit.ts A-02 "a full withdrawal ... still closes the vault") may need updating. For the immutable Base deployment, add an integrator note to the contract docs, README and security page: Withdrawn(closed=true) is a terminal transition that ends any pending claim, and claim status should be derived from getVault or from a full vault-state machine, not from the ClaimInitiated/Aborted/Superseded/Settled family alone. Also fix the README state diagram to show the CLAIM_PENDING -> CLOSED edge (owner withdraws everything).

reach.reasoning:
I read the code and ran the PoC. The sandbox contract is byte-identical to the repo at b8baf34, and the run gives 0 passing, 4 failing, as reported.

**What holds up.** `checkInMany` (InheritanceVault.sol:481-498) skips ids with `continue` at :490 (unknown id) and :492 (not ACTIVE or horizon reached). Neither skip emits anything. `refreshed += 1` (:494) counts array entries, so `[0,0,1]` returns 2. Both preconditions are reachable with no special state:
- **Claim pending:** `initiateClaim` (:639-659) only needs ACTIVE, the beneficiary as caller, `block.timestamp >= deadline` and a nonzero balance.
- **Horizon reached:** this only needs time to pass.

The PoC does not use `setStorageAt` or impersonation. Every setup step is asserted before the failing check, so the failures come from the missing event, not from the fixture.

**What does not hold up.**

1. **The count can be read from the receipt, and so can the skipped ids.**
   - Every `refreshed += 1` (:494) is paired with exactly one `emit CheckedIn(msg.sender, vaultIds[i], ...)` (:495), and `vaultId` is indexed. So `refreshed` equals the number of CheckedIn logs in the transaction.
   - The skipped ids are the submitted ids minus the logged ids. A keeper always knows what it submitted.
   - The PoC's own output shows this: input `[0,1]` gives `vaultIds mentioned: [0n]`, so vault 1's absence is visible.
   - Duplicates show up as two CheckedIn logs for the same id, so de-duplicating from the receipt is trivial.
   - The only thing missing from the receipt is the reason for a skip. That is one `getVault` view call away (`state`, `horizonReached`).
   - So the headline claims "the only signal is the return value" and "the count is unreadable from a mined receipt" are false.

2. **The recommended fix does not help the keeper type the scenario is about.**
   - The exploit rests on a keeper that only checks `receipt.status`. That keeper would ignore a `CheckInSkipped` log just as it ignores a missing CheckedIn log.
   - A keeper that parses logs can already detect skips.
   - The event would add convenience and a reason code. It would not add detection.

3. **The fund-loss path in PoC test 4 is caused by something else.** The keeper stayed down past the deadline, which makes the claim legitimate under the contract's rules. Then nobody called `abortClaim` during the 14-day window. Other signals were available the whole time:
   - `ClaimInitiated` (:212/:658), indexed by owner and vaultId.
   - The vault state from `getVault`.
   - The app, which calls `refreshMine` after "Check in all" (app.js:337-340, :102-117) and redraws the card as "Claim pending" (app.js:27).

   The PoC engineer agrees the root cause is the F03 area.

4. **The horizon case has no fund impact.** `absoluteDeadline` is fixed in advance and public. `_resetClock` (:287-291) caps the deadline at the horizon, so a check-in past the horizon could never have helped. The skip is correct, deterministic and predictable.

5. **All of this is by design and disclosed.**
   - The skip-not-revert behaviour is the deliberate A-03/B-03 fix, documented in NatSpec at :471-479.
   - The missing skip event is open question OQ-2 in AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:189-191.
   - AUDIT_SCOPE.md:80-83 lists "invisible skips in `checkInMany`" as "disclosed, not represented as fixed".
   - Duplicate counting is disclosed inline at :488-489.

**Why not fully refuted.** There is a small code-vs-documentation mismatch. The NatSpec `@return` says "how many vaults were actually checked in" (:472), but the code counts array entries. In the app, "Check-in (all vaults)" shows a plain "confirmed" even when a claim-pending vault was skipped. Both are real but carry no fund impact.

**Severity: INFORMATIONAL.** It is a missing convenience event plus a documentation mismatch, both disclosed. It does not meet LOW's "events/return values that mislead integrators", because the receipt already encodes which vaults were refreshed and which were skipped.
reach.better_fix:
The Base deployment is immutable, so the practical fix there is off-chain.

Off-chain fixes, for Base now:
- Keepers compare the distinct submitted ids with the vaultIds of CheckedIn logs in the receipt. Any missing id triggers an alert and a `getVault` lookup for the reason.
- Keepers subscribe to `ClaimInitiated` filtered on the indexed owner. A CLAIM_PENDING vault should prompt `abortClaim`, not a retry of the check-in.
- The app's "Check in all" handler does the same log diff. For each skipped vault it shows a warning naming the vault and whether a claim is pending (with an Abort button) or the horizon has been reached, instead of a plain "confirmed".

For the BNB deployment or any redeploy:
- Add `CheckInSkipped(owner indexed, vaultId indexed, uint8 reason)` as a reason-code convenience.
- Change the `@return` NatSpec to "number of check-ins performed (duplicates counted)", or revert on duplicate ids.
- A skip event only helps keepers that parse logs. It does not help one that checks status alone, so keeper documentation must still require alerting on `ClaimInitiated`.

sev.reasoning:
Verdict: real, LOW, intended but not disclosed to users. Two overstatements in the finding need correcting.

Code verified at contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:481-498 checkInMany.
- :490 skips an out-of-range id.
- :492 skips when `state != STATE_ACTIVE || block.timestamp >= absoluteDeadline`.
- Neither skip path emits an event. CheckedIn (:495) is emitted only for refreshed vaults.
- `refreshed += 1` runs once per array entry, so duplicate ids are counted again. The comment at :488-489 admits this.
- The only revert is NothingCheckedIn when nothing at all was refreshed (:497).

The contrast with the single-vault path is the real point. checkIn (:458-468) reverts loudly with ClaimPendingUseAbort and HorizonReached. Its own comment at :462-463 says a no-op green toast "is a lie to the owner". checkInMany does exactly that for batch callers. The A-03/B-03 fixes turned a loud, estate-wide failure into a silent, per-vault one. That trade was correct, since the brick was worse, but it left the observability gap that OQ-2 describes.

Intended and disclosed?
- The skip is intended (A-03, NatSpec :474-479).
- The invisibility is known internally: OQ-2 in AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:189-191 ("adding one is cheap and probably right"), and AUDIT_SCOPE.md:80-83.
- Nothing aimed at users discloses it:
  - README.md:20-21 says "One call refreshes a whole split estate".
  - site/how-it-works.html:47 says "One batch transaction can refresh several owned vaults".
  - The contract header :74-75 recommends checkInMany for split estates.
  - site/security.html:64 only says generically that "unresolved design questions" exist.
- OQ-2 also understates the issue by calling it a design question rather than a defect. So this is not refuted.

Overstatements in the finding:
1. "Skipped vaults produce no log. The only signal is the return value" is wrong about the information. The skip set is fully recoverable from the mined receipt: the ids that were sent minus the vaultIds of the emitted CheckedIn events. Both owner and vaultId are indexed. Deduplicated CheckedIn vaultIds also give the true distinct count, which neutralises the duplicate problem for any log-reading caller. What is missing is an explicit marker and a reason. The PoC's assertion requires the skipped vaultId to be named in a log. That is a design preference, not proof that the information is lost.
2. A keeper that checks only receipt.status gains nothing from the recommended CheckInSkipped event either. Only log parsing helps, and log parsing already works today by absence. The event makes the skip easier to catch and gives the reason. It does not close the gap for status-only automation.

Severity under the rubric: LOW, near the floor.
- Who triggers it: the legitimate heir, only after the owner's own deadline has lapsed. Or the passage of time to a horizon the owner chose.
- Cost to them: nothing. There is no griefing asymmetry and no theft.
- What the victim loses: the owner's own chosen heir receives the vault early.
- Preconditions for that loss, all required:
  - the owner is alive but relies on a scripted batch keeper;
  - the keeper misses the deadline (the primary failure, which is the dead-man switch working as designed);
  - the keeper ignores logs;
  - the owner ignores the app for the whole challenge window of at least 7 days.
- The official app mitigates this. After "Check in all" (site/assets/app.js:337-341), runTx calls refreshMine. That redraws the card with the "a claim is pending" warning (app.js:188) and a "Veto claim" button (app.js:301). Only the toast ("confirmed") is misleading.
- No keeper exists in the repo. ClaimInitiated (:212) is indexed by owner and vaultId, so any competent monitor sees the claim.
- The duplicate-count part is INFORMATIONAL on its own. It needs a malformed id list, is visible only by pre-simulation, and is already acknowledged in the code comment.
- Net: an event or return value that misleads integrators, which is LOW. It is not MEDIUM, because no core guarantee breaks: a pending claim is surfaced by ClaimInitiated, getVault().warnings and the app.

Better fix. The contract is immutable, so the recommended event cannot help the live Base deployment.
- Now, off-chain:
  - The app's "Check in all" should diff the requested ids against the CheckedIn vaultIds in the receipt. For each skipped id it should read getVault and name the reason, with the remedy inline: "claim pending -> Veto", "horizon reached -> extend horizon".
  - Better still, pre-filter openVaultIds and warn before sending.
  - Publish keeper guidance: diff CheckedIn logs against the sent ids, subscribe to ClaimInitiated(owner), and alert on either. Do not rely on receipt.status or the return value.
  - Add a line to README and how-it-works saying batch check-ins silently skip claim-pending and horizon-reached vaults.
- For the BNB and any future deployment:
  - Emit CheckInSkipped(owner, vaultId, reason).
  - Enforce strictly ascending ids, either by skipping any id <= the previous one or by reverting deterministically. A deterministic revert shows up on the first run, unlike A-03's time-dependent trap. This removes duplicates in O(n) with no set.
- What not to do:
  - Do not add a "revert on any skip" strict mode as the default. That reintroduces A-03's estate-wide brick.
  - Never let checkInMany abort a pending claim, whether to "fix" visibility or for any other reason. That would give automation veto power and break T3 and the ClaimPendingUseAbort design of checkIn.

confirmed.title: OQ-1 re-evaluated: the heir can permanently kill a keyless owner's chain recovery path whenever a chain check-in lands at or after the deadline; the 'unfixable without veto authority' rationale is overstated
confirmed.location: contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:535-548 checkInByChain (:537 reverts unless ACTIVE), :639-659 initiateClaim (:644), :663-677 abortClaim, NatSpec :529-533; AUDIT-2026-08-09.md OQ-1
confirmed.description: Once block.timestamp >= deadline, initiateClaim and checkInByChain are both valid and only ordering decides. If the heir is first, even in the same block, checkInByChain reverts VaultNotActive, only the owner key can return the vault to ACTIVE, and every remaining preimage is dead. No mempool is needed: on Base (private sequencer mempool) the heir simply submits initiateClaim in the deadline second with a higher priority fee; on BNB the relayer's transaction is also visible. A reverted relayer transaction still publishes its preimage, which feeds F02. The 'same-block guard' remedy cannot work: the EVM cannot see a later-ordered transaction, and if the chain transaction is ordered first the heir already reverts. An exclusive post-deadline grace for chain check-ins is equivalent to a longer inactivity period. The stated reason for not fixing ('grants the paper seed veto authority') is overstated. A seed holder can already hold the heir off until the horizon by checking in before each deadline. A chain cancel refused at or after absoluteDeadline, consuming a preimage and calling _resetClock reaches no new end state, and adds at most one challenge window of slack per cycle.
confirmed.impact: A keyless but living owner whose chain check-in lands seconds late loses the whole recovery chain, and the vault settles to the heir after the window. The recipient is the owner's chosen heir, the case is disclosed in NatSpec, and the heir is the claim authority, so LOW.
confirmed.exploit_scenario:
1. Keyless Alice's relayer submits checkInByChain at T = deadline.
2. Heir Bob's bot submits initiateClaim at T with a higher tip (BNB), or the sequencer happens to order it first.
3. Both land in one block. Bob's claim succeeds and the chain transaction reverts VaultNotActive.
4. Alice has no key for abortClaim, her remaining preimages are useless, and after the window anyone finalizes.
confirmed.recommendation: v2: let checkInByChain supersede a pending claim (emit ClaimSuperseded with a new ACT_CHECKIN_CHAIN) only when block.timestamp < absoluteDeadline, consuming a preimage and calling _resetClock. Optionally restrict it to within CHAIN_RACE_GRACE of claimInitiatedAt. Alternatively, for vaults with hbAnchor != 0, require initiateClaim at deadline + GRACE (e.g. 72 h). Update the OQ-1 rationale and public docs. Relayer guidance: submit at least a day early; use private or bundled submission on BNB; allow at least 24 h margin on Base because OP-stack forced inclusion can take about 12 h.

poc.explanation:
I reproduced F16 with a Hardhat test at C:/Users/Vinoth/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-Vinoth-OneDrive-Claude-claude-code/005aaa32-3c49-4f96-8428-bacda0a96f78/scratchpad/poc/F16/test/poc-F16.ts. I did not edit the repo or the contracts.

Setup: alice creates a 10 ETH native vault (PERIOD 30 d, WINDOW 14 d, horizon 730 d) with bob as heir, then installs a 10-link S/KEY chain. After that the tests never sign as alice, so she is treated as having lost her key. dave is her relayer, bob is the heir running a claim bot, and carol is an arbitrary finalizer.

Two tests assert the safe property and fail on the current code because of the defect itself. Every setup precondition passes before the failing assertion.

1. Same-block race. Automine is off. bob sends initiateClaim with a 50 gwei tip and dave sends checkInByChain with a valid preimage at a 1 gwei tip. Both are mined in one block with timestamp exactly equal to the deadline, about 700 days before the horizon. The test confirms both transactions are in the same block, bob is ordered first, the timestamp equals the deadline and is below the horizon, and the preimage hashes to the anchor. The assertion that fails is: the chain check-in must succeed and leave the vault ACTIVE. Result: the chain transaction has status 0 and the vault is state 2 (CLAIM_PENDING). Resubmitting the same valid preimage reverts VaultNotActive(0, 2).

The code path behind this:
- initiateClaim (InheritanceVault.sol:639-659) passes :644 because block.timestamp is not below the deadline, and sets CLAIM_PENDING.
- checkInByChain (:535) then fails :537 (state != ACTIVE → VaultNotActive).
- The only way back to ACTIVE is abortClaim (:663), which is keyed by msg.sender (_vault(msg.sender, ...)). A keyless owner cannot call it.

2. Damage. bob claims in the deadline second. The relayer lands 2 s later (one Base block) and retries at +4 s; both attempts revert VaultNotActive(0, 2). After WINDOW + 1, carol calls finalizeClaim. The assertion that the vault is still ACTIVE with 10 ETH and nothing credited to bob fails. Actual result: state 3 (SETTLED), balance 0, bob credited 9.95 ETH (0.5% fee), 10 of 10 preimages unused and now worthless, horizon still 700 days away.

Both failing tests are written to pass under either remedy F16 proposes: (a) checkInByChain supersedes a pending claim before the horizon, or (b) a grace period before initiateClaim on vaults with a chain. So they can serve as regression tests.

Two control tests pass on the current code and should also pass after a fix:
- The same two transactions with the tips reversed leave the vault ACTIVE: the deadline resets to deadline+PERIOD, hbLeft becomes 9, and bob's claim reverts NotYetExpired. Ordering alone decides the outcome, not validity or timing.
- Using only seed check-ins made a day before each deadline, bob gets NotYetExpired at every point before the horizon. The deadline clamps to the horizon after 4 periods. At the horizon, checkInByChain reverts HorizonReached and bob can claim. This supports the claim that the "grants the paper seed veto authority" rationale (AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:185-188) is overstated: the seed can already delay the heir all the way to the horizon, and a supersede-only-before-horizon fix reaches no new end state.

The race is disclosed in NatSpec at InheritanceVault.sol:529-533 ("front-run a chain check-in ... lands STRICTLY BEFORE the deadline"). The PoC confirms the disclosed behaviour, and shows that it needs no mempool snooping (same-block ordering is enough) and that even a 2-second-late landing loses the whole chain.

poc.severity_observation:
The impact matches LOW, and on one axis it is sharper than the finding states.

Sharper: the loss is total and irreversible even with the horizon about 700 days away. The whole balance settles (9.95 of 10 ETH to the heir, 0.05 ETH fee), all 10 of 10 preimages are left unused and worthless, and a 2-second-late relayer loses the race outright, with no mempool monitoring needed. A pure same-block ordering by priority fee is enough.

Why it stays LOW:
- The money goes to the owner's own chosen heir, not an outside party.
- It needs three things together: the owner is keyless, the chain check-in lands at or after the deadline, and the heir acts first.
- The behaviour is disclosed in the NatSpec (InheritanceVault.sol:529-533). It is not surfaced on the public site pages I grepped.

The passing seed-only control confirms the finding's argument against the OQ-1 rationale: the seed can already keep the heir from claiming right up to the horizon. So letting a chain check-in supersede a claim before the horizon adds delay, at most one challenge window per cycle, but no new outcome.

Side observation (not asserted): the reverted relayer transaction is still mined with the valid preimage in its calldata, so the preimage becomes public. This is relevant to F02.

reach.reasoning:
I could not refute the mechanics. Every step in the finding matches the code, and the PoC is a real demonstration, not a self-confirming one. The finding does, however, re-raise a design decision that is already disclosed, and it overstates the impact. I would rate it INFORMATIONAL (acknowledged design question), not LOW.

**Code path, checked end to end (contracts/InheritanceVault.sol)**
- `initiateClaim` (:639-659) needs four things: state is ACTIVE (:642), the caller is the beneficiary (:643), `block.timestamp >= deadline` (:644) and a balance above zero (:645). It then sets `CLAIM_PENDING` (:656).
- `checkInByChain` (:535-548) has no deadline check. It is valid for any `timestamp < absoluteDeadline` (:540) while the vault is ACTIVE (:537). So when `timestamp == deadline < horizon`, both calls are valid and only their order in the block decides the outcome.
- Once the claim lands, `checkInByChain` reverts at :537, and nothing a keyless owner can do returns the vault to ACTIVE:
  - `abortClaim` (:663) looks the vault up by `msg.sender`.
  - `_clearPending` is reached only through owner-keyed setters (:513, :577, :592, :602, :629).
  - `topUp` needs ACTIVE (:444).
  - `setCheckInChain` is owner-keyed.
  - The heir has no function to withdraw their own claim.
  - `finalizeClaim` (:682) is permissionless after the window.

  The "permanently kills the chain" claim is therefore correct.

**The PoC**
- I ran it in the sandbox. The sandbox `InheritanceVault.sol` is byte-identical to the repo file, and `hardhat.config.ts` matches apart from comments.
- It uses no `setStorageAt` and no impersonation. It turns automine off, sends two real signed transactions with different tips, and mines one block at the deadline timestamp.
- Result: 2 failing and 2 passing, as reported. The claim succeeds, the chain transaction reverts with `VaultNotActive(0,2)`, and after the window the vault is SETTLED with 9.95 ETH credited to the heir and 10 of 10 preimages unused.
- The tips-reversed control shows that ordering alone decides the outcome. The seed-only control is sound.
- On Base, no mempool monitoring is needed: the heir simply claims in the first block whose timestamp is at or after the deadline.

**Why it is by design, disclosed, and not a vulnerability**
1. **The precondition is the owner missing their own deadline.** From `deadline` onward the heir is entitled to claim under the contract's core rule (:644), so the heir is exercising a documented right, not attacking. The "race" exists only when the owner's liveness proof is already late.
2. **The exact rule is disclosed.** The NatSpec at :529-533 states it: "The chain survives only if every check-in lands STRICTLY BEFORE the deadline". The "watching the mempool" wording there is narrower than the reality, but the stated condition is complete and correct. The same issue is disclosed as OQ-1 in AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:185-188, and AUDIT_SCOPE.md:72 lists "the known post-deadline chain-sniping race".
3. **For a permanently keyless owner, the end state is the same in every branch.** The chain grants liveness only, never authority. A keyless owner can never withdraw or change the heir, so the funds reach the chosen heir either way. The NatSpec at :527 calls this "claim and hand back" and says it is the real endgame. Losing the chain changes when the heir is paid, not who is paid.
4. **The only real loss is narrow.** A temporarily keyless owner who would have recovered their key before the horizon loses the vault to their own heir. That is bounded, needs a late check-in, and pays the owner's chosen heir. No third party or admin gains anything.

**Minor corrections to the finding's argument (they do not change the verdict)**
- "A seed holder can already hold the heir off until the horizon" is true only while `hbLeft * period` covers the time left to the horizon. The chain is otherwise capped at `hbLeft` periods (`MAX_HB_COUNT` = 100k).
- The "rationale overstated" point is a sound design critique. A supersede-before-horizon remedy that consumes a preimage reaches no new end state and adds at most one challenge window per link. It would still weaken the heir's expectation stated at :609-610, and whether to accept that is a product decision, not a defect.
- The preimage published by the reverted transaction is harmless for this vault once it settles. Its relevance to F02 would need to be argued in F02.

**Documentation gap (supports INFORMATIONAL)**
The public pages never state the strictly-before-deadline caveat. index.html:104-105 says only "An optional paper-seed check-in chain can keep the vault alive while you coordinate", and README.md:28-29 says the same. A code-vs-documentation clarity gap with no fund impact to an unintended party fits INFORMATIONAL. LOW is defensible only if one weights the missing public caveat for temporarily keyless owners.

**Recommended outcome**
Keep the finding as INFORMATIONAL / Acknowledged. Add the relayer-margin caveat to the public site, and optionally revisit the OQ-1 rationale in a v2. Files checked: the in-scope contract, AUDIT-2026-08-09.md, AUDIT_SCOPE.md, README.md, site/index.html, site/how-it-works.html, and the PoC at C:/Users/Vinoth/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-Vinoth-OneDrive-Claude-claude-code/005aaa32-3c49-4f96-8428-bacda0a96f78/scratchpad/poc/F16/test/poc-F16.ts.
reach.better_fix: The cheapest remedy needs no contract change: state the strictly-before-deadline rule on index.html and in the README, and have the relayer or watcher submit chain check-ins with a margin of at least one full day. On BNB, submit privately or bundled. On Base, remember that OP-stack forced inclusion can take about 12 h. If a v2 is built, prefer the finding's option (b): on vaults with an installed chain (`hbAnchor != 0`), `initiateClaim` would wait until `deadline + CHAIN_GRACE`. That leaves the heir's rule, that only the owner key can stop a pending claim, unchanged, whereas letting the seed supersede a claim changes that guarantee. Note that (b) is equivalent to asking the user for a longer inactivity period. A UI default of period plus grace for chain users achieves the same thing without any bytecode change.

sev.reasoning:
The behavior is real and the PoC matches the code. It is not a contract defect: it is the designed outcome. What remains is a gap in the user-facing documentation, so I downgrade it from LOW to INFORMATIONAL. It is not refuted, because the user-facing disclosure understates the rule.

Code path, verified:
- initiateClaim (InheritanceVault.sol:639-659) passes once block.timestamp >= v.deadline (:644) and sets CLAIM_PENDING.
- checkInByChain (:535-548) requires STATE_ACTIVE (:537).
- The only ways back to ACTIVE are keyed by msg.sender: abortClaim (:663) via _vault(msg.sender), and the owner actions that call _clearPending (:312-322).
- At timestamp == deadline both calls are valid, so ordering decides. The PoC's same-block and 2-second-late cases are both 'late' by the contract's own definition, since the deadline is the first expired second.

Why it is by design and harmless relative to the documented model:
- The function's NatSpec (:518-533) says the chain 'proves liveness, not authority. It cannot veto a claim that is already pending'. It also says 'A keyless owner's real endgame is for the NAMED heir to claim and hand back', and that the chain 'survives only if every check-in lands STRICTLY BEFORE the deadline'. That rule is exact, and it already covers the same-block case the finding presents as new.
- README:37 and index.html:103-105 state the model: 'Owner key lost -> vault expires, heir inherits. This is the designed recovery.'
- AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:69-70 and :185-188 (OQ-1), and AUDIT_SCOPE.md:72-73, record it as a known, deliberately unchanged race.
- In the loss scenario, the owner's own chosen heir receives the funds after the owner's deadline has already lapsed. That is exactly the documented keyless endgame.
- No outside party gains, no guarantee is broken, and the hard date absoluteDeadline + challengeWindow is unaffected.
- The trigger is the designated claim authority exercising a right that has already matured. Sequencer ordering alone can also cause it, with no malice needed.
- The rubric's HIGH/MEDIUM language about 'an unprivileged party able to deny or hijack an inheritance' does not apply. The heir is privileged, and nothing is denied or hijacked.
- The same result follows from any post-deadline claim, not only a race: if the heir claims a day after the deadline, a chain check-in two days late is equally dead. So the 'race' framing overstates novelty.

Likelihood is low as well:
- site/assets/app.js has no setCheckInChain or checkInByChain UI. It only reads warning bit 8.
- The repo has no official relayer.
- So only users who install a chain by calling the contract directly are exposed, and they can see the verified source and its NatSpec.
- The mainnet deployment currently holds no user funds and is immutable.

Why it is not refuted (the documentation gap):
- The pages users actually read market the chain with no timing caveat. index.html:104-105 says it 'can keep the vault alive while you coordinate'. README:28-29 says 'keep the vault alive ... even after losing your wallet'.
- Neither page, nor how-it-works.html or security.html, says that one landing at or after the deadline forfeits the whole remaining chain irreversibly.
- The NatSpec framing, 'an heir watching the mempool can front-run', is narrower than reality. No mempool watching is needed: a higher tip, or the sequencer's ordering, is enough.
- Two related mismatches in the watcher mislead a keyless owner:
  - notify/watcher.js:154 tells the owner during a pending claim that 'Any action from your wallet cancels the claim — a check-in is enough'. A keyless owner may read that as including a chain check-in, which reverts.
  - notify/watcher.js:169 says 'Install a fresh one from the app', but the app has no chain UI.

On the re-evaluation of OQ-1:
- The finding is right on end states. A chain supersede allowed only while block.timestamp < absoluteDeadline, consuming a preimage and calling _resetClock, reaches no new end state. The deadline clamps to the horizon (:287-291), so the hard date holds. The PoC's seed-only control confirms the seed can already hold the heir off to the horizon.
- The prior rationale is still not overstated. It is a legitimate trust-model choice, and literally accurate: a supersede is a veto, and README:29 publicly promises 'liveness only, never authority'.
- The change would also have real costs:
  - A leaked paper seed, or a zombie relayer (the T3 threat the horizon exists for), could cancel claims that are already initiated, not merely pre-empt them.
  - Each cancel stretches a cycle by up to one challenge window and forces the heir to spend gas and attention again. This is bounded by the horizon and by hbLeft.
  - The heir loses the property that an initiated claim yields only to the owner key.
- The finding's alternatives are weak:
  - 'Within CHAIN_RACE_GRACE of claimInitiatedAt' just moves the race to the edge of the grace window. The heir's best response is to wait out the grace, which makes it equivalent to a longer inactivity period.
  - 'initiateClaim at deadline + GRACE for chain vaults' is also just a longer inactivity period, which the owner can already choose with setInactivityPeriod.
- There is no on-chain fix that is not either a seed veto or a longer period, and v1 is immutable.

Severity under the rubric:
- Who triggers it: only the named heir (or incidental ordering), after the deadline has lapsed.
- Cost to them: gas only.
- What the victim loses: control of a vault that goes to their own chosen heir, which is the documented keyless endgame.
- How likely: it needs three things together: the owner is keyless, the owner has hand-installed a chain outside the app, and the check-in lands late.
- Fund impact beyond the designed outcome: none. That makes it INFORMATIONAL: documentation mismatch, no fund impact.
sev.better_fix:
Keep the v1 contract as is: it is immutable, and any on-chain change either gives the seed a veto or amounts to a longer inactivity period. Fix it operationally and in the documentation.

(1) State the rule on the pages users read: README 'Lost wallet insurance', the index.html:103-105 trust table, and how-it-works.html failure modes. Suggested wording: 'A chain check-in counts only if it is mined strictly before the deadline. Once your heir has claimed, the chain cannot stop the claim and every remaining code is void. Only your wallet key can abort.'

(2) Reword the NatSpec and OQ-1 from 'an heir watching the mempool can front-run' to 'any claim ordered first at or after the deadline, even in the same block, wins'.

(3) Fix the watcher:
- Make the pending-claim alert (notify/watcher.js:154) say explicitly that a chain check-in cannot cancel a claim.
- Remove 'Install a fresh one from the app' (:169) until the app actually has a chain UI.
- Add a 'chain vault within margin of deadline and no check-in seen' alert.

(4) Relayer guidance:
- Submit when about half the period has elapsed, not near the deadline.
- Keep at least 24-72 h of margin. On OP-stack chains, allow for forced-inclusion latency of about 12 h.
- Use private or bundled submission on BNB.

(5) If v2 wants to close the gap without giving the seed a general veto: offer an owner-opt-in flag, set with the key when the chain is installed, that makes initiateClaim require deadline + chainGrace for that vault. It is equivalent to a longer period, but it is explicit, and the owner consents with the key. Do not add a before-horizon chain supersede unless README:29 ('liveness only, never authority') is formally changed. Such a supersede lets a leaked seed or a zombie relayer cancel claims the heir has already initiated.

confirmed.title: Chain values are bearer credentials that can delay the heir up to the horizon: 'liveness only, never authority' is overstated, and a leaked but unmined preimage stays spendable indefinitely
confirmed.location: contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:535-548 checkInByChain (permissionless, no freshness), NatSpec :521-527; README.md:28-29 ('Lost wallet insurance ... liveness only, never authority'); site/index.html:103-105; app default horizon 20 years (site/assets/app.js:437-439)
confirmed.description: checkInByChain is permissionless and each valid preimage resets the deadline to min(now + inactivityPeriod, horizon). (1) Whoever holds the paper seed (a relayer, a non-heir relative, someone who finds it after the owner dies) can keep postponing the heir's claim eligibility for up to hbLeft x inactivityPeriod, capped only by the horizon, which the app defaults to 20 years. That is authority over timing, the thing an heir cares about most. (2) A single preimage is not bound to msg.sender or to any time window. A value that was broadcast but never mined (evicted from BNB's mempool, or handed to a relayer) can be submitted by whoever kept it at a time of their choosing, pushing the deadline a full period past the owner's real last action. The accurate statement is 'cannot veto, withdraw or change the heir, but can delay the inheritance up to the horizon'.
confirmed.impact: Owners may guard a paper seed less carefully than a key, believing it has no power. If it leaks, the heir can be kept out until the horizon, possibly decades. A leaked single value costs the heir up to one extra period. Bounded by the horizon, so LOW. The domain-separation flaw (F02) is a separate root cause that multiplies the exposure.
confirmed.exploit_scenario:
1. Alice installs a chain (count 1000, period 90 days) and keeps the seed in a desk drawer. Her horizon is 20 years out (the app default).
2. Alice dies. Mallory, a relative who is not the heir, finds the seed and calls checkInByChain every 80 days.
3. Bob's initiateClaim reverts NotYetExpired each time, and he can claim only at the horizon.
Freshness variant: keyless Alice broadcasts checkInByChain(H^9) on BNB with too low a gas price. It is evicted, she dies before rebroadcasting, and mempool observer Dave submits H^9 one minute before the deadline, adding a full period.
confirmed.recommendation: Replace 'liveness only, never authority' with 'cannot move funds or change the heir, but whoever holds the seed or any unused chain value can postpone your heir's claim until the horizon. Guard it like a key.' Document that a chain value is live until mined: rebroadcast the same value until it lands, use private submission, and hand relayers one value at a time. If stronger guarantees are wanted, a time-slotted chain (value i valid only in slot i) removes banking at a UX cost.

test_names: F17 chain values are bearer credentials over timing [F17-a freshness] a broadcast-but-unmined chain value cannot push the deadline past the owner's last real action + one period
F17 chain values are bearer credentials over timing [F17-b 'never authority'] a non-owner who holds the paper seed cannot keep the heir out once the owner is silent
F17 chain values are bearer credentials over timing [F17-quant] damage: a seed holder alone postpones the heir from t0+PERIOD to the horizon (20-year app default)
poc.explanation:
I reproduced both halves of F17 on the unmodified InheritanceVault.sol. The fixture is a 10-ETH native vault with Alice as owner and Bob as heir, a 90-day period, a 14-day window, and a horizon 20 years out, which is the app's pre-filled default (site/assets/app.js:436-439). Chains follow the S/KEY rule H^k(seed) = keccak256(H^(k-1)), which is the check at InheritanceVault.sol:542.

The code path: checkInByChain (InheritanceVault.sol:535-548) does not check msg.sender, and the preimage carries no time binding. Whenever a valid preimage is mined, the function consumes it and calls _resetClock (:287-291), which sets deadline = min(now + inactivityPeriod, absoluteDeadline). initiateClaim then reverts NotYetExpired while block.timestamp < deadline (:644). Only the horizon caps this: checkInByChain reverts once the horizon is reached (:540).

F17-a (freshness) fails for the intended reason. Alice calls setCheckInChain(H^10, 10) at t0, her last real action, which sets the deadline to t0+90d. The H^9 check-in she broadcast is never mined. Dave submits H^9 at t0+90d-60s, and the deadline moves to t0+179.9993d. The assertion deadline <= t0+PERIOD fails with 1805768206 against 1797992265, so Dave added 89.9993 days that Alice never earned.

F17-b ("never authority") fails for the intended reason. Alice installs a 1000-value chain and dies. Mallory, who is neither the owner nor the heir, submits H^999 on day 80. On day 91 Alice has been silent for a full period, but Bob's initiateClaim reverts with the decoded error NotYetExpired(1804904266), because Mallory moved the deadline to t0+170d. The test asserts that Bob is not blocked, and that assertion fails. No setup call reverts. The only failing lines are the property assertions.

F17-quant passes and measures the damage. Mallory checks in every 80 days using 91 of the 1000 values. Bob is rejected with NotYetExpired 91 times. The last check-in clamps the deadline to exactly the horizon, and Bob can claim only then: 19.75 years later than t0+90d.

Citations:
- README.md:28-29: "keep the vault alive from a 32-byte paper seed even after losing your wallet — liveness only, never authority."
- InheritanceVault.sol NatSpec :525: "it proves liveness, not authority."
- site/index.html:104-105: "An optional paper-seed check-in chain can keep the vault alive while you coordinate."

The fix for part (b) is a wording change. The contract is immutable on Base, and binding values to time slots would not stop a seed holder either, because they can compute every value and submit each in its slot. So F17-b is a spec-vs-code witness that will stay red until the claim is reworded, not a code regression test. F17-a would turn green only under a time-slotted chain.

poc.severity_observation:
The delay is as large as the finding says: with the 20-year app default it is 19.75 years, from 91 cheap transactions and no owner key. MAX_HORIZON is 36500 days, so a directly configured vault could be held back for up to about 100 years. The chain length is not a real limit: a 1000-value chain with a 90-day period covers about 246 years.

Two things keep this at LOW:
1. The web app never calls setCheckInChain or checkInByChain; outside abi.js they appear nowhere in site/*.html or site/assets/*.js. Only users who call the contract directly can install a chain today.
2. The seed holder cannot withdraw, change the heir, or veto a pending claim. Once a claim is pending, checkInByChain reverts VaultNotActive (:537), and the funds still reach the heir at the horizon.

The single-value freshness variant is capped at one extra period per leaked value (89.99 days here). An observer holding several banked values could stack them.

The public wording still needs fixing. README.md:28-29 and NatSpec :525 tell owners the seed carries no authority, but it controls when the heir can claim. index.html:104-105 does not repeat the "never authority" line, but it also does not say who else can use the seed.

reach.reasoning:
The mechanics are real, but F17 is not a vulnerability. It describes the feature's intended behavior, and the only real gap is in the documentation. I recommend dropping it from LOW to INFORMATIONAL as a wording fix.

What I verified:
- The sandbox copy of contracts/InheritanceVault.sol is byte-identical to the repo copy (diff -q printed nothing).
- The PoC does not change storage, impersonate accounts or use impossible state. I ran it and got the same result: F17-quant passes, and F17-a and F17-b fail only on their property assertions.
- The code path is as described. checkInByChain (:535-548) never checks msg.sender. It checks the state is ACTIVE, the anchor is set, hbLeft > 0, the horizon is not reached, and keccak(preimage) == anchor. It then calls _resetClock (:287-291), which sets deadline = min(now + period, absoluteDeadline). initiateClaim (:644) reverts NotYetExpired while now < deadline. So a seed holder can keep the heir out until the horizon, and every precondition is reachable.

Why it is not a LOW vulnerability:
1. **The behavior is the feature, and the code says so.** setCheckInChain's NatSpec (:500-501) says installing a chain "extends liveness and therefore delays inheritance, so it carries the same authority as checkIn itself." checkInByChain's NatSpec (:520-522) says "possession of the preimage is the authentication, so msg.sender is irrelevant and the transaction is relayable." Keeping the vault alive is the same thing as postponing the heir's claim.
2. **"Liveness only, never authority" is not false.** README.md:28-29 says the seed can "keep the vault alive". In the README, "authority" means the owner key's powers: withdraw, change the heir, veto a pending claim. The seed has none of them. Once a claim is pending, checkInByChain reverts VaultNotActive (:537).
3. **The precondition is a compromised owner credential.** The seed is generated by the owner and installed only by the owner (setCheckInChain is owner-gated through _vault(msg.sender, ...)). Mallory is not an unprivileged party. She holds a leaked credential, which the README trust model treats as compromise ("defends against absence, not compromise"). Her power is strictly less than a leaked owner key: she cannot move funds, change the heir or veto a claim.
4. **The damage has a disclosed backstop.** The horizon exists for "runaway check-in automation" (README:24-26). checkInByChain reverts at the horizon (:540), and the heir then gets 100% of the funds. PoC F17-quant confirms this. The owner can also revoke a leaked seed while alive by installing a new chain.
5. **The freshness half is not specific to hash chains.** A signed ordinary checkIn transaction that was broadcast but not mined also stays valid indefinitely, as long as the owner's nonce is unused. If the owner is dead it stays unused, so any observer who kept the raw transaction can rebroadcast it just before the deadline. The effect is identical: the deadline becomes now + period. The only difference is that a preimage can be resubmitted with the submitter's own gas. Each leaked value is worth at most one period, and values must be spent in order.
6. **F17-a tests a property no one promised.** Its assertion, "a check-in the owner produced at t0 buys at most t0 + PERIOD", appears in no code comment, README line or site page. F17-b likewise tests the finding's reading of "authority", not a stated guarantee.
7. **Site users cannot reach the feature.** The web app never calls setCheckInChain or checkInByChain; outside abi.js they appear in no site file. The PoC engineer found the same. site/index.html:104-105 says only "can keep the vault alive while you coordinate", which is accurate.

What survives:
- The public text never tells owners that anyone holding the seed, or any unused chain value, can postpone the heir up to the horizon. So it never tells them to guard the seed like a key.
- The 20-year horizon the app pre-fills makes that delay long. The app itself does not install chains.

That gap is a documentation clarity item with no fund impact, which is INFORMATIONAL under the rubric. The finding's recommended rewording is a good fix. A time-slotted chain would not stop someone who holds the seed, as the PoC engineer also noted.
reach.better_fix:
Change only the documentation; the contract is immutable and the behavior is intended.
- **README.md:28-29:** keep "cannot withdraw, change the heir or veto a claim", then add: "Whoever holds the seed, or any unused chain value, can postpone your heir's claim up to your horizon. Guard it like a key; if it leaks, install a new chain from a fresh seed while you still can."
- **checkInByChain NatSpec (:525):** replace "proves liveness, not authority" with "proves liveness, which is itself authority over timing".
- **If the app ever exposes chains:** it should cap how far out the pre-filled horizon goes when a chain is present. It should also tell relayed users to rebroadcast the same value until it is mined.

sev.reasoning:
I checked the code path myself. checkInByChain (InheritanceVault.sol:535-548) never looks at msg.sender. It checks only that keccak256(preimage) equals hbAnchor, that hbLeft > 0, that the vault is ACTIVE and that the horizon has not passed. It then calls _resetClock (:287-291), which sets deadline = min(now + inactivityPeriod, absoluteDeadline). initiateClaim reverts NotYetExpired while now < deadline (:644). Anyone who holds the seed can therefore push the deadline back by up to hbLeft x inactivityPeriod, never past the horizon. MAX_HB_COUNT is 100,000, so in practice only the horizon limits it. The app pre-fills a horizon 20 years out (site/assets/app.js:436-439). The behavior is real, as the PoC shows.

Intended? Yes. The NatSpec says possession of the preimage is the authentication and the call is relayable (:518-519), and header T3 (:34-41) makes the horizon the backstop against runaway check-ins, naming checkInByChain. So the upper bound on the damage is designed and disclosed.

Disclosed? No, and the public wording understates the risk:
- README.md:28-29 says "liveness only, never authority", and the checkInByChain NatSpec (:525) says "proves liveness, not authority".
- The contract's own setCheckInChain @dev (:500-501) contradicts both. It says installing a chain "extends liveness and therefore delays inheritance, so it carries the same authority as checkIn itself". The code author knew that liveness controls when the heir can claim, but the text owners read says the seed carries no authority.
- The README trust table, site/index.html:104-105, how-it-works.html and security.html never say that someone other than the owner who holds the seed can hold the heir off.
- OQ-1 covers the opposite race (the heir sniping a late chain check-in), not this one.
- The guide dead-mans-switch-crypto.html:135 says "no secret is ever shared", which could encourage casual storage of the seed.
So this is a documentation defect at minimum. It is not refuted.

Severity, applying the rubric strictly: this is not the HIGH tier "unprivileged party able to deny an inheritance".
1. The attacker must hold a credential the owner created and was responsible for keeping safe. That is a compromise of a secondary credential, and it is strictly weaker than a stolen owner key, which T1 already places outside the model.
2. The heir is delayed, not denied. The seed holder cannot withdraw, change the heir or veto a pending claim (checkInByChain reverts VaultNotActive once a claim is pending), and funds reach the heir at guaranteedInheritanceAt.
3. It is reachable only by users who call the contract directly. The web app never calls setCheckInChain or checkInByChain; it only shows the "chain exhausted" warning bit (app.js:189). The Base deployment holds no user funds.
Against that, the delay can be decades, and the motive is plausible: spite, or extortion ("pay me or wait 20 years"), for a few cents of gas per period. A public claim that leads owners to guard the seed loosely is worth fixing. LOW is right. It is not MEDIUM, because the documented core guarantee (the hard horizon date) holds.

The freshness half (F17-a) is weaker than presented and should be INFORMATIONAL inside this finding. It is not specific to the chain. A signed ECDSA checkIn transaction that was broadcast and evicted also has no expiry: if the owner dies and the nonce is never used, anyone who kept the raw transaction can mine it later with the same effect. In both designs the value, or the transaction, is invalidated only when it is mined. The owner also meant to check in with that value, so the extra time is at most one period beyond an intended action.

Recommended fix: the proposed wording should be more precise. "Until the horizon" overstates the typical bound and gives no mitigation. Suggested text: "Anyone holding the seed, or any unused chain value, cannot move funds, change the heir or veto a claim, but can postpone your heir's claim by up to (remaining count x inactivity period), never past the horizon. Guard it like a key."
sev.better_fix:
1. Mitigation available now on the immutable Base contract, with no code change: the count parameter already bounds the damage, because the most a seed holder can add is count x inactivityPeriod. Tell owners in the docs, and in any future chain UI, to size count to the coordination span they actually need, not to decades. For example, count 4 with a 90-day period allows about one year of keyless survival, and a leaked seed then costs the heir at most about one year.
2. Revocation while the owner still has the key: setCheckInChain with a fresh random anchor and count 1, with the preimage never recorded, disables a leaked chain. anchor = 0 reverts, so this is the only way to disable a chain. Document it.
3. Revocation after the key is gone: there is none, and the docs should say so.
4. Wording: correct README:28-29 and the checkInByChain NatSpec so they match the setCheckInChain @dev (:500-501). State the delay bound, the "guard it like a key" rule, and that a broadcast value stays usable until mined: rebroadcast the same value, use private submission, and give relayers one value at a time.
5. For the planned BNB deployment, where code can still change: add an owner-chosen chainSpanEnd, fixed when setCheckInChain is called with the owner key. Chain check-ins would clamp the deadline to min(now + period, chainSpanEnd, horizon), while ECDSA check-ins keep clamping at the horizon only. This bounds a leaked seed's delay to the span the owner chose, matches the stated purpose ("keep the vault alive while you coordinate"), and gives the seed no new powers, so the OQ-1 trust model is unchanged.
6. Do not adopt the time-slotted chain the finding suggests. As the PoC engineer notes, the seed holder can compute every slot's value, so it does not stop the main attack. It would only address the minor freshness variant, and it would make legitimate keyless use harder.

confirmed.title: In the last inactivity period before the horizon, check-ins succeed but extend nothing, and each chain check-in still uses up a link
confirmed.location: contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:287-291 _resetClock (clamps to absoluteDeadline), :458-468 checkIn (refuses only at >= absoluteDeadline; comment :462-463), :481-498 checkInMany (no-op refreshes counted), :535-548 checkInByChain (decrements hbLeft), :502-515 setCheckInChain, :388 createVault (accepts absoluteDeadline == now + inactivityPeriod), :800-807 warningsOf (no bit for 'deadline stuck at horizon'); site/index.html ('must wait out your full inactivity period')
confirmed.description: Once now + inactivityPeriod >= absoluteDeadline, deadline is pinned at absoluteDeadline. checkIn, checkInMany and checkInByChain refuse only when block.timestamp >= absoluteDeadline. For the whole final period they succeed and emit CheckedIn with an unchanged newDeadline, count toward checkInMany's 'refreshed' (so NothingCheckedIn never fires), and checkInByChain decrements hbLeft while extending nothing. warningsOf has no bit for this state; bit 1 is set only after the horizon passes. This is the 'no-op that shows a green toast' that the comment at :462-463 says checkIn refuses to be. createVault accepts absoluteDeadline == now + period (:388 uses <), so such a vault is pinned from creation. The index claim that the heir 'must wait out your full inactivity period' is false in this period: the heir can claim at the horizon even if the owner checked in the day before.
confirmed.impact: No direct loss; the horizon is by design and the owner can still extendHorizon. But an owner who keeps checking in during the final period gets success receipts and no warning. When the heir claims at the horizon, 'Veto claim' reverts HorizonReached, and the owner has one challenge window (as short as 7 days) to realise that extendHorizon or a full withdraw is the only remedy. A relayer wastes chain links for nothing.
confirmed.exploit_scenario:
1. Alice creates a vault with a 30-day period and a horizon 40 days away (or reaches the last 30 days of a 20-year horizon).
2. From day 11 every checkIn and checkInMany succeeds, and each event shows deadline == horizon, unchanged. Her keeper logs refreshed = 1, and her chain relayer spends one link per run.
3. At the horizon, Bob calls initiateClaim (deadline == absoluteDeadline <= now).
4. Alice presses 'Veto claim', which reverts HorizonReached. Unless she finds extendHorizon or withdraws everything within the window, Bob inherits.
confirmed.recommendation: Add a warning bit (e.g. bit 4: deadline == absoluteDeadline && now < absoluteDeadline, 'check-ins can no longer extend'). Make checkIn and checkInByChain revert, or emit a distinct event, when the new deadline equals the old one. Do not count no-op refreshes in checkInMany, and do not consume a chain link when nothing moves. Require absoluteDeadline > now + inactivityPeriod (or a margin) at creation. State in the UI and site that check-ins cannot extend past the horizon, and qualify 'full inactivity period' with 'until the horizon approaches'.

poc.explanation:
F18 is reproduced. All 7 tests fail against the current code, and in each one the failing assertion is the defect itself. Setup checks (deadline == horizon, now < horizon, hbLeft == 3) pass first.

Setup (pinnedFixture): Alice creates a native vault with a 30-day period and horizon = t0 + 40 days. On day 11 she installs a 3-link chain. setCheckInChain calls _resetClock (InheritanceVault.sol:287-291), which clamps deadline to absoluteDeadline. From then until the horizon, no call can move the deadline.

What each test shows:
1. checkIn (:458-468) refuses only when block.timestamp >= absoluteDeadline. One day into the pinned period it succeeds and emits CheckedIn(newDeadline = 1793672316), the same value as the old deadline and the horizon. The comment at :462-463 says a no-op that shows a green toast "is a lie to the owner". checkIn does exactly that before the horizon.
2. createVault (:388) refuses only absoluteDeadline < now + period, so == is accepted. The vault is pinned from birth: deadline == horizon at creation, and a checkIn one day later succeeds and changes nothing.
3. checkInMany([0,1]), where vault 0 is pinned and vault 1 is healthy, returns refreshed = 2 (expected 1). The loop at :487-497 counts every _resetClock call whether or not the deadline moved.
4. checkInMany([0]) on the pinned vault alone does not revert. Its own NatSpec (:487-488) promises that "a total no-op still cannot masquerade as success". NothingCheckedIn never fires.
5. A stranger (carol) relays the next preimage through checkInByChain (:535-548). hbLeft goes 3 -> 2 while the deadline stays at the horizon, so a link is spent for nothing.
6. warningsOf (:800-807) returns 0 while the deadline is pinned 2,505,599 seconds (about 29 days) before the horizon. The NatSpec for bit 1 at :795 reads "no check-in can extend this vault any further", which is already true here, but the bit is set only once now >= absoluteDeadline.
7. Quantified timeline: a weekly keeper on days 7, 14, 21, 28 and 35 gets 3 no-op CheckedIn success receipts (days 21, 28, 35), and a weekly chain relayer burns 3 links for nothing. On day 40 Bob calls initiateClaim 5.00 days after Alice's last "successful" checkIn, although her period is 30 days, and Alice's abortClaim reverts HorizonReached. The veto revert is horizon-by-design, so it is only checked on the way. The failing assertions are the no-op receipts and the wasted links.

Documentation mismatch, by citation: site/index.html:152 says "Your heir must first wait out your full inactivity period". In test 7 the heir claimed 5 days after the owner's last successful check-in, with a 30-day period.

Each test accepts either fix the finding recommends: a revert, or success without a CheckedIn event / link spend / refreshed count. They will pass as regression tests once the no-op is refused or reported honestly and a warning bit is added.

poc.severity_observation:
LOW looks right. No funds are lost and the horizon works as designed: extendHorizon or a full withdraw stays open to the owner through the challenge window.

The PoC shows a little more than the finding claims:
(a) The first clamped reset, the one that pins the deadline, is only a partial extension (in test 7, 3 days instead of 30). It emits an ordinary CheckedIn with no warning either. The pinned no-ops that follow make it worse.

reach.reasoning:
I could not refute F18. Every factual claim holds against the code, and the PoC shows the behaviour through legitimate calls only.

What I checked:
- The sandbox copy of contracts/InheritanceVault.sol is byte-identical to the repo copy (diff -q).
- I read poc-F18.ts. It uses no storage writes, no impersonation and no contract-as-sender tricks. It only calls createVault, setCheckInChain, checkIn, checkInMany, checkInByChain, initiateClaim and abortClaim with time travel. The setup assertions (deadline == horizon, now < horizon, hbLeft == 3) pass before the defect assertions.
- I ran it: 7 failing, each on the defect assertion, not on setup.

The code path:
- _resetClock (:287-291) sets deadline = min(now + period, absoluteDeadline).
- checkIn (:464), checkInMany (:492) and checkInByChain (:540) gate only on block.timestamp >= absoluteDeadline. None checks whether the deadline actually moved.
- Once deadline == absoluteDeadline and now < absoluteDeadline, every later call behaves as the finding says. checkIn emits CheckedIn with an unchanged newDeadline. checkInMany increments refreshed (:494), so NothingCheckedIn (:497) never fires. That contradicts its own NatSpec (:478-479): a total no-op "cannot masquerade as success". checkInByChain decrements hbLeft (:545).
- warningsOf (:800-807) sets bit 1 only at now >= absoluteDeadline. Yet its NatSpec for bit 1 (:795), "no check-in can extend this vault any further", is already true up to one full inactivity period earlier.
- createVault (:388) accepts absoluteDeadline == now + period (it uses <), so a vault can be pinned from birth.
- The precondition is not exotic. Any vault whose owner keeps checking in reaches the pinned state in its final inactivity period. With MAX_INACTIVITY of 3650 days, that period can be very long.

Why not by design and disclosed:
- The core consequence is designed and disclosed. The heir can claim at the horizon however recently the owner checked in: README:25-27 ("guaranteed inheritance date ... Check-ins stop working at the horizon"), how-it-works.html:47 ("subject to the absolute horizon"), app.html:81 ("guaranteed inheritance date, even if check-in bots run forever"). The app card also shows "Next deadline" and "Guaranteed inheritance by".
- What is NOT disclosed, and is contradicted by the code's own comments and docs:
  - check-ins that change nothing still emit success events;
  - no-op refreshes count in checkInMany's return value;
  - chain links are spent for nothing;
  - no on-chain warning exists for the pinned state.
- Several documents are also wrong about timing:
  - README says check-ins stop working AT the horizon, but they stop extending anything up to one period before it.
  - The notify/watcher.js alert (:172-178) fires only 30 days out, is off-chain, is email-only and repeats "after [horizon] check-ins stop working".
  - index.html:152 ("Your heir must first wait out your full inactivity period") is false in the final period.

Minor precision note: the first reset that enters the final period does extend the deadline, but only partly, up to the horizon. Only the resets after it are pure no-ops.

Why LOW:
- No funds can be lost or frozen, and no unprivileged party gains anything.
- extendHorizon and a full withdraw stay open through the challenge window, and the heir claiming at the horizon is intended.
- Wasted chain links are bounded by one period of relayer runs and are self-inflicted.
- The real defects are events and a return value that mislead owners and keeper integrators (the no-op CheckedIn events, refreshed counting no-ops, NothingCheckedIn unable to fire, no warning bit), plus doc and site text that disagrees with the code. The rubric places exactly this at LOW.
- INFORMATIONAL would be defensible only for the website-text part.
reach.better_fix:
The deployed contract is immutable. The redeploy and off-chain fixes below are ordered by cost.

1. In a redeploy:
   - In checkIn and checkInByChain, compare deadline before and after _resetClock. If it did not move, revert with a distinct error such as DeadlinePinnedAtHorizon(absoluteDeadline).
   - In checkInMany, skip the vault without incrementing refreshed, so NothingCheckedIn still fires for a batch that changes nothing.
   - Add warning bit 4, set when deadline == absoluteDeadline && now < absoluteDeadline.

2. Now, off-chain:
   - app.js: warn when deadline == absoluteDeadline, and tell the owner to extend the horizon.

sev.reasoning:
Verdict: real and LOW. The clamp is intended and disclosed. The no-op "success" contradicts the contract's own stated design, and it is not disclosed.

WHAT IS BY DESIGN AND DISCLOSED
- _resetClock clamps to absoluteDeadline (InheritanceVault.sol:287-291), so the heir can claim at the horizon whenever the owner last checked in. This is the stated purpose of the horizon.
- Header T3 calls absoluteDeadline + challengeWindow a hard date.
- README says check-ins stop working at the horizon and only the live key can extend it.
- how-it-works.html:47 says a check-in moves the deadline "subject to the absolute horizon".
- how-it-works.html:62-65 says that past the horizon a veto requires a full withdraw or extendHorizon.
- The heir claiming at the horizon, and abortClaim reverting HorizonReached, are therefore not defects. The owner loses nothing relative to the documented model: extendHorizon or a full withdraw stays available through the whole pinned period and the challenge window.

WHAT IS NOT BY DESIGN AND NOT DISCLOSED
The code states a rule against no-op success three times, and the pinned period breaks it each time:
1. The checkIn comment at :462-463 says a no-op "that shows a green toast is a lie". Prior-audit fix B-04 repeats the same rule. The code enforces it only at block.timestamp >= absoluteDeadline. Between deadline == absoluteDeadline and the horizon, checkIn succeeds and emits CheckedIn with an unchanged newDeadline. app.js runTx then shows "Check-in confirmed".
2. The checkInMany NatSpec (:487-488) promises "a total no-op still cannot masquerade as success". refreshed counts pinned vaults, so NothingCheckedIn never fires. That is exactly the keeper-detection signal the NatSpec tells integrators to rely on. This fits the rubric's LOW line: return values that mislead integrators.
3. The NatSpec for warningsOf bit 1 (:795) reads "no check-in can extend this vault any further". That condition becomes true one inactivity period before the bit is set. No on-chain signal marks the pinned state.

DOCUMENTATION MISMATCH
- index.html:152 says the heir "must first wait out your full inactivity period". That is false in the pinned period.
- The same FAQ says "any action from your wallet cancels the claim and resets the clock". That is false at or after the horizon.
- how-it-works.html discloses the horizon; the FAQ does not.

WHY SEVERITY STAYS LOW, NOT MEDIUM
- No adversary can trigger it. It is a state the owner reaches through their own horizon choice.
- The heir gains nothing beyond the documented hard date.
- The CheckedIn event carries the truthful newDeadline, so an integrator that reads it is not misled.
- The app card shows "Next deadline" equal to the horizon, and the countdown visibly fails to reset.
- The app's default horizon is 20 years out.
- Wasted chain links are bounded by one period of relayer runs, against MAX_HB_COUNT = 100,000. The chain cannot extend anything in this state anyway.
- The remaining harm is a misleading success receipt and a missing warning. Before the horizon, the owner can still fix everything with extendHorizon.

NOT INFORMATIONAL EITHER
- The watcher (notify/watcher.js:43, :172-178) warns only when the horizon is 30 days or less away. The pinned period lasts inactivityPeriod, which can be up to 3650 days. An owner with a 180-day period gets about 150 days of no-op receipts with no alert.
- The reminder service is retired, so even that alert may not run.
- The finding also misses a second route into the state. extendHorizon's floor is now + inactivityPeriod (:621-622). An owner who extends to the minimum is pinned immediately, and every check-in after that is a no-op. createVault has the same problem at :388.

BETTER FIX
1. Base the revert condition on "the deadline would not move" (v.deadline == v.absoluteDeadline before the reset), not on "next > cap". The first clamped reset is a real partial extension (the PoC shows 3 days) and should still succeed. It should emit a capped flag or a distinct CheckInCapped event.
2. Skip pinned vaults in checkInMany, which lets NothingCheckedIn fire honestly.
3. In checkInByChain, revert before spending a link when the vault is pinned.
4. Add a warningsOf bit for deadline == absoluteDeadline && now < absoluteDeadline, rather than widening bit 1. Bit 1 and HorizonReached gate the veto semantics and should keep meaning "past the horizon".
5. Apply one margin to both createVault and extendHorizon, for example requiring the horizon to be at least 2 x inactivityPeriod away. Fixing only createVault leaves the extendHorizon route open.
6. Do not make any of these reverts cancel or affect a pending claim. That would reopen the A-02/B-01 veto loop or grant the paper seed veto authority, which is the OQ-1 trust-model change.

For the immutable Base deployment, the practical fixes are off-chain:
- The app computes the pinned state and replaces the green toast with "check-ins can no longer extend this vault; extend the horizon".
- The watcher alerts when deadline == absoluteDeadline, i.e. inactivityPeriod before the horizon, rather than a fixed 30 days.
- index.html's FAQ is qualified for the horizon.
sev.better_fix: Revert or flag only when the deadline truly cannot move (v.deadline == v.absoluteDeadline before the reset). The first clamped partial extension is real and should succeed with a capped flag. In checkInMany, skip pinned vaults so NothingCheckedIn fires honestly. In checkInByChain, revert before hbLeft is decremented when pinned. Add a new warning bit for the pinned state instead of redefining bit 1, which gates the veto semantics. Apply the same horizon margin (for example at least 2 x inactivityPeriod) to both createVault and extendHorizon; extendHorizon's current floor of now + period pins the vault immediately. None of these reverts should touch a pending claim; that would reopen A-02/B-01 or turn OQ-1 into a trust-model change. For the immutable Base deployment, fix it off-chain. The app detects deadline == absoluteDeadline && now < absoluteDeadline and shows a warning in place of "Check-in confirmed". The watcher fires its horizon alert when the vault becomes pinned (inactivityPeriod before the horizon), not at a fixed 30 days. index.html:152 is corrected: the "full inactivity period" and "any action cancels the claim" statements do not hold near or past the horizon.
