poc.explanation:
The PoC reproduces F19 as reported. The contract behaves as designed; the defect is in the web app.

How the test works: it loads the real site/assets/abi.js and site/assets/app.js, read-only from the repo, into a node:vm context with a small fake DOM. The page clock is set to follow the chain clock. The app's own S.contract points at a locally deployed InheritanceVault with Alice's (the owner's) signer, and a Proxy records every contract call the app makes. The test builds the owner card with the app's own vaultCard() and clicks the buttons the way a user would. Setup: Alice has a 10 ETH vault with a 90-day period and a 7-day window; the horizon passes and heir Bob initiates a claim.

1. Ground truth (passes). This test covers the contract only:
   - The claim is initiated at H-2. At H-1, abortClaim still succeeds.
   - From H on, abortClaim and setBeneficiary both revert with HorizonReached(H) (InheritanceVault.sol:670 and _clearPending :314). checkIn reverts with ClaimPendingUseAbort.
   - extendHorizon(now+7d) reverts with HorizonTooSoon (:622-623).
   - extendHorizon(now+PERIOD+100) emits ClaimSuperseded(ACT_EXTEND_HORIZON) and returns the vault to state 1.
   - This confirms the window-straddling flip: the veto method changes one second into the window and stays changed for the remaining 7 days.

2. Owner card buttons (fails). Past the horizon the card still offers "Veto claim" (app.js:300-302) and "Change heir" (:298). Clicking them logs "Veto failed: ...HorizonReached" and "Change heir failed: ...HorizonReached", and the claim stays pending. The test assertion is that every stop control the card offers actually stops the claim.

3. Minimum horizon (fails). Neither the card text nor the Extend-horizon prompt ("New horizon date (YYYY-MM-DD): ", no default, app.js:234) shows the minimum accepted horizon, now + inactivityPeriod. The only related warning is app.js:187: "horizon reached - check-ins no longer work; extend the horizon to continue". It does not say that extending cancels the claim.

4. Date validation (fails). The app passes whatever date the owner types straight to extendHorizon (app.js:241) with no client-side floor check. It submitted 1798675200 against a floor of about 1805855001, and the contract rejected it with HorizonTooSoon.

5. Damage (fails). On day 1 of the window Alice clicks every stop-like control the app offers: Change heir, then Extend horizon with next week's date, then Veto. All three revert. After the window Bob finalizes: the vault ends in state 3 (Settled) and Bob is credited 9.95 ETH of 10 ETH (10 ETH minus the 0.5% fee), although the living owner objected through the app.

Every failure is the defect itself, not a setup problem: the fixture reverts are the contract's intended HorizonReached / HorizonTooSoon errors, and the failing assertions are on the app's controls, the text it shows and the calls it submits.

Check that the tests can pass: pointing the same file at a patched copy of app.js (via env F19_ASSETS_DIR, copy kept in scratchpad/poc/F19-fixcheck) makes all 5 pass. The patch hides Veto and Change heir when horizonReached && state==2, adds a "Stop this claim" button whose prompt is pre-filled with now+period+1 day, shows that minimum date on the card, and checks the date client-side. So the regression tests can be satisfied by a real fix.

The repo was not modified. git status shows only changes that were already there: site/guides/*.html, output/, tmp/.

poc.severity_observation:
LOW is the right rating. No third party gets funds; the vault goes to the heir the owner named, along the documented horizon rules. Four points refine the finding:

1. The precondition is broader than "owner inactive". _resetClock clamps the deadline to absoluteDeadline, so any vault that reaches its horizon without being extended beforehand can be claimed at H, even by a living owner who has been checking in regularly. The app gives no warning before the horizon: bit 1 is only set at or after H.

2. The owner is not entirely in the dark. The revert text the app logs includes HorizonTooSoon(minimum, given), so the floor does appear, but only as a raw unix timestamp.

3. A trap for the recommended fix: actHorizon turns the typed date into midnight UTC (app.js:236). Typing the calendar date of the floor still reverts whenever now's time of day is after 00:00 UTC. The pre-filled minimum must be rounded up by one day, as the fix-check patch does.

4. how-it-works.html section 5 (lines 61-65) does state the rule in general terms: past the horizon the owner must withdraw everything or extend the horizon "far enough". It gives neither the exact floor (now + inactivityPeriod) nor the case where a window straddles the horizon.

Withdrawing the full balance remains a working exit in the app, but nothing on the card points the owner to it.

reach.reasoning:
I could not refute F19. Each factual claim holds against the code at b8baf34, and the PoC ran the real app.js against a real deployment with nothing faked.

Contract side (correct, as designed):
- abortClaim (InheritanceVault.sol:670) reverts HorizonReached once block.timestamp >= absoluteDeadline.
- setBeneficiary (:582-593) runs _resetClock and then _clearPending (:312-322). _clearPending reverts HorizonReached for any action other than ACT_EXTEND_HORIZON, which rolls back the whole "Change heir" transaction.
- checkIn reverts ClaimPendingUseAbort while a claim is pending.
- extendHorizon (:611-631) sets floor = now + inactivityPeriod (:622-623) and reverts HorizonTooSoon below it. It is the only action that clears a claim past the horizon.
- A full withdraw (:569-575) closes the vault, which ends the claim. A partial withdraw past the horizon deliberately leaves the claim running (:576-578).

Reachability needs only time passing. _resetClock (:287-291) clamps deadline to absoluteDeadline, so an owner who checks in on schedule still reaches deadline == H, and the heir can call initiateClaim at H (:643-647). The window-straddle case (initiate at H-1s) needs an owner who lapsed before H; that is also ordinary.

App side (site/assets/app.js):
- vaultCard shows "Veto claim" whenever state == 2 (:300-302) and ignores the horizonReached field, which getVault already returns (:824). "Change heir" (:298) and "Check in" are always shown.
- actHorizon (:233-242) shows the prompt "New horizon date (YYYY-MM-DD):" with no default, gives no floor, and sends the typed date straight to extendHorizon with no client-side check.
- warningLines (:187) says "extend the horizon to continue" and never says that extending is what cancels the pending claim.

The PoC is not self-confirming. It loads the real abi.js and app.js into a vm context, and the contract is byte-identical to the repo's (diff is empty). It uses only time.increase and setNextBlockTimestamp: no setStorageAt, no impersonation. It asserts on what the app renders and what it submits. I ran it: 1 passing (the contract ground truth), 4 failing exactly as reported.

Corrections and qualifications:
1. The "damage" test models a pessimistic user. Alice tries each control once on day 1, picks "next week" as her new horizon, never retries in the remaining 6+ days of the minimum 7-day window (MIN_CHALLENGE, :101), and never uses Withdraw, which does work. The loss therefore needs the owner to give up after the first reverts. That keeps this LOW at most.
2. PoC severity note 2 says the floor "does appear as a raw unix timestamp". That wording comes from Hardhat's node ("reverted with custom error 'HorizonTooSoon(a,b)'"). On a real RPC, runTx (:113) prints error.reason or error.shortMessage from ethers v6. There it is likely to be just the error signature, or "execution reverted (unknown custom error)", with no floor value. I did not verify this against the vendored ethers build. If it holds, the owner is told even less than the finding assumes.
3. "Check in" also reverts past the horizon while a claim is pending (ClaimPendingUseAbort). It belongs to the same defect class, and the finding does not list it.
4. site/assets/app.js is not among the listed in-scope or context files. The contract behaviour is by design and disclosed: the NatSpec at :293-311 and :666-669, and how-it-works.html section 5, which tells owners to "withdraw everything or extend the horizon far enough". The card also shows "Guaranteed inheritance by <H + window>". The defect is only that the app does not follow those documented rules. No third party gains anything, and funds go to the heir the owner named on the documented schedule.

Severity: LOW. It is a bounded edge case in which the official UI works against the owner's only remaining veto. It is close to INFORMATIONAL: there is no fund impact from an unprivileged party, the contract is correct, the file is outside the listed scope, and two working exits (a valid Extend horizon, a full Withdraw) stay on the card. LOW is defensible because the rubric counts "return values that mislead integrators" as LOW, and here the product's own frontend leads a live owner into reverts during a time-limited window.
reach.better_fix:
Branch the owner card on vault.horizonReached, which getVault already returns.

When horizonReached is true:
- Hide Check in, Veto claim and Change heir.
- If state == 2, show a primary "Stop this claim" button that calls extendHorizon. Pre-fill it with the next UTC-midnight date at or after now + inactivityPeriod, plus 1 day of margin, because actHorizon rounds typed dates down to 00:00Z.
- Next to it, show "Withdraw everything" pre-filled with the full balance, and say in words that a partial withdraw does not stop the claim.

In actHorizon, check the date client-side against both limits:
- floor: now + inactivityPeriod;
- maximum: now + MAX_HORIZON.
Show the floor as a calendar date.

Before the horizon: once deadline == absoluteDeadline (that is, now + period >= H), show an advance warning. It should say that at H the heir can claim, and that the only way to stop that claim will be to extend the horizon by at least one full check-in period.

In runTx, decode custom errors with S.contract.interface.parseError(error.data) and show plain messages. HorizonReached and HorizonTooSoon should each say what to do next. This also covers the likely real-chain case where ethers gives only the error signature or "unknown custom error".

On how-it-works.html section 5:
- state the exact floor (now + check-in period);
- document the case where a challenge window straddles the horizon, where the ordinary veto stops working partway through the window.

sev.reasoning:
The contract side is intended and disclosed. The app side is neither, so the finding is not refuted. LOW is the right severity, at the top of the LOW band.

1. What is intended and disclosed. InheritanceVault.sol:670 makes abortClaim revert HorizonReached at or after absoluteDeadline. _clearPending (:314) refuses to displace a claim past the horizon except via ACT_EXTEND_HORIZON. extendHorizon (:622-623) requires newAbsoluteDeadline >= now + inactivityPeriod. The code comments give the reason: this closes the A-02/B-02 unbounded zero-cooldown veto loop. how-it-works.html section 5 (lines 61-65) says it in general terms: past the horizon the owner must withdraw everything or extend "far enough". The window-straddling flip follows from this design (a claim initiated at H-1 can be aborted for one second, then only extendHorizon or a full withdraw works). It is not a contract defect, and the contract must NOT be changed to accept post-horizon vetoes. That would reopen A-02, and the contract is immutable anyway.

2. What is not intended and not disclosed. The web app still offers "Veto claim" (app.js:300-302) and "Change heir" (:298) past the horizon, and both always revert. The warning at app.js:187 never says that extending the horizon cancels the claim. actHorizon (:233-242) has no default, no floor hint and no client-side check against now + inactivityPeriod. The prior audit's own B-06 treats this exact mismatch as a defect: it rated the watcher email saying "any action from your wallet cancels the claim" CRITICAL (off-chain) and fixed only the email (notify/watcher.js:150-154). The same false claim is still in:
   - README.md:23 ("any action from your key cancels the claim") and README.md:16 ("owner veto / any owner action")
   - site/index.html:153-154, the hospital FAQ ("any action from your wallet cancels the claim and resets the clock")

   The disclosure therefore understates the risk in the very places a user is most likely to read. None of OQ-1..OQ-3 covers this. The retired NotifySubscription means many owners may never receive the corrected email, which leaves the app and the FAQ as their only guide.

3. Severity under the rubric.
   - Who can trigger it: only the owner's own named beneficiary, and only after the owner-chosen horizon has passed without an extension.
   - What it costs the heir: gas.
   - What the victim loses: the whole balance, minus the locked fee (0.5% in the PoC), goes early to the heir the owner named, against a living owner's wishes.
   - Why it is not MEDIUM or higher: no third party can take funds, and nothing is frozen. The contract keeps two working exits for at least 7 days: extendHorizon with a valid date, and a full withdraw through the app's working "Withdraw" button. The app log shows the revert names; HorizonTooSoon carries the minimum as a raw unix timestamp, and HorizonReached is self-describing. The card also shows "Guaranteed inheritance by <date>". The frontend is mutable and can be fixed without touching the contract.
   - Why it is at the top of LOW: the PoC shows a live, objecting owner who uses only the app's controls loses the vault. An adversarial heir claiming against a living owner is exactly the threat the veto window exists for. And a regularly checking-in owner who forgets to extend is exposed at H, because _resetClock clamps the deadline to absoluteDeadline and the app gives no warning before H.

   It is not "a core guarantee broken" on-chain: the guarantee holds, and the app misroutes the owner. LOW, with the README/index.html mismatch as an INFORMATIONAL documentation item that is part of the same fix.

4. On the recommended fix. It is sound and does not change the trust model, since it is frontend-only and needs no contract change. Strengthen it as follows:
   - (a) Round the pre-filled minimum UP to the next UTC midnight. actHorizon turns the typed date into 00:00Z (app.js:236), so the floor's own calendar date usually still reverts. Or accept a full datetime.
   - (b) Simulate every owner action with staticCall before sending, and decode the custom errors into plain language. For example, turn HorizonTooSoon(min, given) into "choose a date on or after <min rounded up>", and turn HorizonReached into "the normal veto has closed; extend the horizon or withdraw everything".
   - (c) Add a pre-horizon warning, for instance when absoluteDeadline - now < inactivityPeriod + challengeWindow, with a one-click "extend horizon by N years" button. This covers the living, checking-in owner who is exposed at H.
   - (d) Past the horizon with a claim pending, also hide or relabel "Check in", which reverts ClaimPendingUseAbort in state 2. Warn in the Withdraw prompt that a partial withdraw does NOT stop the claim; only withdrawing the full balance closes the vault.
   - (e) Fix README.md:16/23 and index.html:153-154 to say "before the horizon", mirroring the B-06 email text.
   - (f) For a claim that straddles H, re-evaluate horizonReached on every card render and alert tier. The watcher already does this at send time, but a pre-H email that says "any action cancels" goes stale at H. Consider sending one extra alert when H passes during an open window.

   Do NOT "fix" this by letting abortClaim or checkInByChain veto past the horizon. That reintroduces the A-02 veto loop, and granting the paper seed veto power is the OQ-1 trust-model change.
sev.better_fix:
Frontend-only. The contract stays as is: making abortClaim or checkInByChain work past the horizon would reopen the A-02 veto loop, and the OQ-1 paper-seed veto would change the trust model.

When horizonReached && state==2:

- Show a primary "Stop this claim: extend horizon" button. Pre-fill it with ceil_to_next_UTC_midnight(now + inactivityPeriod) + 1 day, and show that date on the card next to "Withdraw everything (closes the vault)".

For every owner action:

- Decode HorizonReached, HorizonTooSoon, HorizonTooFar and ClaimPendingUseAbort into plain-language guidance with human-readable dates.

Also:
- Add a pre-horizon warning with a one-click extend once absoluteDeadline - now < inactivityPeriod + challengeWindow, so a living, checking-in owner is not exposed at H by surprise.

confirmed.description: initiateClaim fixes claimRecipient for the life of the claim. Only the owner can end a pending claim. poc.explanation:
Reproduced. I traced the code first, then confirmed it with a test.

Code trace (sandbox copy of contracts/InheritanceVault.sol, same as commit b8baf34):
- initiateClaim (:639-659) rejects only a zero recipient or the vault's own address. It then writes v.claimRecipient and sets STATE_CLAIM_PENDING.
- The only ways out of CLAIM_PENDING are:
  - _clearPending (:312), reached from setBeneficiary, setInactivityPeriod, extendHorizon, setCheckInChain and withdraw;
  - abortClaim (:663);
  - withdraw closing the vault (:566-572);
  - finalizeClaim (:682).
- Every one of these except finalizeClaim finds the vault with _vault(msg.sender, vaultId). They are owner-only by construction: when the heir calls them, they look up the heir's own vaults.
- checkInByChain requires STATE_ACTIVE. A second initiateClaim reverts at :642 with VaultNotActive.
- finalizeClaim credits v.claimRecipient (:689, :701). pushCredit (:726) is permissionless and pays whatever address holds the credit. withdrawCredit can only be called by the credited address.
- sweepSurplus cannot recover a stranded credit, because surplus() (:768) subtracts totalCredited.

The heir therefore has no path at all to cancel or re-point a claim.

The test (sandbox test/poc-F20.ts) has 4 cases. Each asserts the SAFE property: while the claim is pending and the owner is absent, the heir can fix the recipient and the net estate reaches the heir. The heir's correction helper tries three things:
1. beneficiaryCancelClaim, if the ABI has it. This is the recommended fix, so the file doubles as a regression test for it, or for a fix that lets the heir re-issue initiateClaim.
2. abortClaim, called by the heir.
3. initiateClaim with the correct address.

Results:
- **Test 1:** The heir sends initiateClaim(alice, 0, 0x...dEaD), then tries all three correction paths. The final assertion getVault().claimRecipient == bob fails because it is still dEaD. The log shows the causes: beneficiaryCancelClaim is not in the ABI, abortClaim reverts NoSuchVault(bob, 0), and initiateClaim reverts VaultNotActive(0, 2).
- **Test 2:** After WINDOW + 1, Dave (a third party) calls finalizeClaim and then pushCredit. dEaD receives 9.95 ETH and the heir receives 0.
- **Test 3:** The heir pastes a contract address (a MintableToken with no receive()). After settlement, 9.95 ETH is credited to that contract, pushCredit reverts NativeTransferFailed, and the contract has no way to call withdrawCredit. The credit is frozen for good.
- **Test 4 (control):** passes. The owner's abortClaim still works, so the gap exists only when the owner is absent.

Each failure is the defect itself, reached on the final state or balance assertion. No fixture or setup step reverted: the sanity checks for CLAIM_PENDING and claimRecipient == dEaD passed before the failing assertion.

Mismatch between the site and the code: site/how-it-works.html section 6 (around lines 70-74) says the heir "withdraws that credit to an address they choose". In the code, the credit belongs to claimRecipient, which was fixed at initiateClaim. The address is chosen at claim start, cannot be changed, and is not chosen at withdrawal.

poc.severity_observation:
The contract behaves as claimed, and the impact is the entire net estate: 9.95 of 10 ETH in the PoC.

Worse than claimed: Test 3 shows a second outcome besides "sent to the wrong address". If the recipient is a contract with no receive() and no way to call withdrawCredit, the credit is frozen permanently. It inflates totalCredited, so sweepSurplus cannot touch it, and no party can ever recover it.

Mitigating factors that support keeping this LOW (user error by the authorised party, not an attack):
- site/assets/app.js:245 pre-fills the prompt with the connected wallet (S.account).
- It passes the input through ethers.getAddress, which rejects a mixed-case address with a bad checksum.
- So random typing errors in a checksummed address are mostly caught in the official UI.

What still gets through: an all-lowercase typo, a valid but wrong pasted address, an exchange deposit address, a contract address, or an address that is meaningful only on another chain. Anyone calling the contract directly gets no protection at all.

While the owner is alive the mistake can be undone, because abortClaim works (Test 4). The loss becomes irreversible only in the product's main case, where the owner is absent. Past the absolute horizon even a live owner can undo it only through extendHorizon.

The site copy "withdraws that credit to an address they choose" (how-it-works.html section 6) misdescribes when that choice is made. Treat it as an INFORMATIONAL documentation mismatch to fix alongside this finding.

reach.reasoning:
I could not refute F20. I checked it independently against contracts/InheritanceVault.sol, which is byte-identical to the sandbox copy (diff -q). I also re-ran the PoC.

**Code trace**
- initiateClaim (:639-659) rejects a recipient only if it is address(0) or address(this). It then writes v.claimRecipient and sets STATE_CLAIM_PENDING.
- Every exit from CLAIM_PENDING except finalizeClaim resolves the vault with _vault(msg.sender, vaultId). That covers abortClaim (:663), _clearPending (:312) via setBeneficiary, setInactivityPeriod, extendHorizon and setCheckInChain, and withdraw's close branch (:566-572). So only the owner can reach them. When the heir calls abortClaim(0), the lookup lands on the heir's own vaults and reverts NoSuchVault.
- A second initiateClaim reverts VaultNotActive at :642.
- checkIn (:458) and checkInByChain (:535) cannot clear a claim. checkIn reverts ClaimPendingUseAbort, and checkInByChain requires STATE_ACTIVE. topUp also requires ACTIVE.
- finalizeClaim (:682) is permissionless and credits v.claimRecipient.
- pushCredit (:726) is permissionless and pays the credited account. Only that account can call withdrawCredit (:714).
- sweepSurplus cannot recover a stranded credit, because surplus() (:768) subtracts totalCredited.

So a heir who sets a wrong recipient while the owner is absent has no path to undo it. While the owner is alive, abortClaim works before the horizon and extendHorizon works after it, but this is not the product's main case.

**PoC**
test/poc-F20.ts is sound. It uses no hardhat_setStorageAt and no impersonation, and it relies on no impossible state. The fixture is a normal createVault followed by time.increase past the deadline. Setup sanity assertions pass before each failing assertion, and the assertions check final contract state and balances, not the log.

Re-run result: 3 failing, 1 passing, as the PoC engineer reported.
- The heir's abortClaim reverts NoSuchVault(bob, 0).
- The heir's re-initiateClaim reverts VaultNotActive(0, 2).
- A third party finalizes and pushes 9.95 ETH to 0x...dEaD.
- With a no-receive() contract as recipient, 9.95 ETH stays credited forever: pushCredit reverts NativeTransferFailed and withdrawCredit can never be called.

**Why LOW and not higher**
- No unprivileged party can cause the loss. It needs an input error by the authorised beneficiary in their own transaction.
- The official UI reduces the risk. site/assets/app.js:245 pre-fills the connected wallet, and ethers.getAddress rejects mixed-case bad checksums. All-lowercase typos, wrong pasted addresses, exchange deposit addresses, contract addresses and addresses that only work on another chain still get through, as does any direct contract call.
- A wrong recipient loses funds in any transfer system. What makes this worth reporting is that the claim is one-shot, the loss is the whole estate, and a trivial beneficiary-side undo would remove it. That puts it at LOW, the bounded user-error edge case in the rubric, not MEDIUM. It could fairly be argued down to INFORMATIONAL.

**Small correction to the documentation claim**
how-it-works.html:72-74 ("The heir then withdraws that credit to an address they choose") is accurate in the default case. There the recipient is the heir's own wallet, and withdrawCredit(token, to) lets the heir choose `to` at withdrawal. The copy misdescribes the flow only when a different recipient was entered at initiateClaim, so it is an informational mismatch, not a false claim.

sev.reasoning:
The behaviour is real, and I confirmed it against the code. initiateClaim (contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:639-659) rejects only a zero recipient or the vault's own address. It then writes v.claimRecipient and sets STATE_CLAIM_PENDING. Every way out of CLAIM_PENDING goes through the caller's own vaults, except finalizeClaim: abortClaim at :663 uses _vault(msg.sender, …), and _clearPending at :312 is reached only from owner functions. A second initiateClaim reverts VaultNotActive. So the heir has no way to cancel or re-point the recipient. finalizeClaim credits to = v.claimRecipient (:689, :701). After that, anyone may call pushCredit (:726), and sweepSurplus cannot reach the stranded credit because surplus() subtracts totalCredited.

Is it intended and disclosed? Partly intended, not disclosed. The NatSpec at :636-638 shows that choosing the recipient at claim time is deliberate ("the recipient is their choice … route the payout to a fresh address"). Nothing tells users the choice is irreversible:
- The README trust-model table does not mention it.
- The contract header does not.
- OQ-1..OQ-3 do not.
- security.html does not.
- how-it-works.html section 6 contradicts the code. It says the heir "withdraws that credit to an address they choose", which implies the choice comes at withdrawal. In fact the credit belongs to the address frozen at initiateClaim.
- index.html says "your heir claims with their own wallet … the funds are theirs".
So this is not refuted, and at minimum there is a documentation mismatch.

Severity under the rubric: LOW, not higher. Reasons:
- Only the authorised party (the heir) can trigger it, and only through their own input error. No unprivileged attacker, admin, token contract or MEV searcher can cause or exploit the mistake. A third party calling pushCredit only carries out the heir's own instruction.
- The official app lowers the likelihood. site/assets/app.js:245 pre-fills the prompt with the connected wallet, so the heir has to actively replace it. ethers.getAddress also rejects a mixed-case address with a bad checksum.
- What still gets through: all-lowercase typos, a valid but wrong pasted address, an exchange deposit address, a contract address, or an address meaningful only on another chain.
- While the owner is alive and before the horizon, abortClaim undoes it.
- The loss can be total and the ≥7-day window makes a correction natural, so this is above INFORMATIONAL. It is still user error with no attacker.

Test 3 (a native-coin credit frozen on a contract with no receive()) does not raise the severity. It is the same heir error. For an ERC20 vault, pushCredit to a contract succeeds, so the tokens land in that contract rather than freezing in the vault.

The recommended fix is weaker than stated and gives up a real property. The claim that "an attacker holding the heir key gains nothing from" beneficiaryCancelClaim is wrong. Freezing the recipient is what protects an heir who, as the NatSpec suggests, routes the payout to a separate cold address. If the heir's hot identity key is stolen after initiateClaim, the thief today has no power over the payout. With beneficiaryCancelClaim, the thief can cancel and re-initiate to their own address. The real heir can cancel back, which becomes an endless cancel war: denial at best, and at worst a race to whichever claim survives its window. Cancel and re-initiate also re-snapshots lockedFeeBps, so the heir gives up the fee lock. That cost is bounded by the vault's ≤1% ceiling.
sev.better_fix:
Contract (v2 only; the Base deployment is immutable):
- Do not add an unrestricted beneficiary cancel. Instead, make any recipient other than the heir prove it is live. If recipient != msg.sender, the recipient must call acceptClaimRecipient(vaultOwner, vaultId) before finalization.
- In finalizeClaim, if the recipient never accepted, credit the beneficiary instead. The beneficiary has already shown it can send transactions by calling initiateClaim, so it can always call withdrawCredit(token, to), which already takes a destination.
- This catches every case in the PoC: typos, exchange deposit addresses, contracts with no receive() or no way to call withdrawCredit, and wrong-chain addresses. None of them can accept.
- It also keeps the frozen-recipient protection: a thief who steals the heir key after initiation still cannot redirect the payout.
- A simpler variant: credit the beneficiary always and let the destination be chosen at withdrawCredit time, which would make the current site copy true. This loses the cold-routing protection.
- If a re-point is still wanted, limit it to a short grace period after initiateClaim (e.g. 24h). It should restart claimInitiatedAt and keep the existing lockedFeeBps (take the minimum), so the fee lock is not given up.

App and site (these matter most, because v1 stays live):
- Keep the connected wallet as the default.
- For any other address: require a checksummed or re-typed confirmation, run eth_getCode and warn loudly if the address is a contract, and state that the address cannot be changed after the claim starts.
- Correct how-it-works.html section 6 so it says the payout address is fixed when the claim is initiated.

confirmed.location: site/app.html:81 ('Horizon - guaranteed inheritance date'); site/assets/app.js:285 ('Guaranteed inheritance by' shown to heirs), :187; contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:34-41 (T3), :821 guaranteedInheritanceAt, :596-604 setInactivityPeriod (allowed while ACTIVE past the horizon), :611-631 extendHorizon (floor now + inactivityPeriod, ceiling now + MAX_HORIZON), :567-573 withdraw (full withdraw closes past the horizon); README.md:25-27; site/index.html:88-89
confirmed.description: (1) The create form calls the horizon field the 'guaranteed inheritance date'. The earliest finalization after the horizon is absoluteDeadline + challengeWindow, up to 365 days later. (2) guaranteedInheritanceAt assumes the heir initiates exactly at the horizon; the real date is claimInitiatedAt + challengeWindow. (3) The app shows 'Guaranteed inheritance by <date>' to heirs, but the owner key (or anyone holding it) can still cancel until finalization: extendHorizon clears the claim, and a full withdraw closes the vault even past the horizon. T3's 'The ONLY way past the date is extendHorizon' omits the full withdrawal. (4) T3 says an override costs 'one full inactivity period' and nothing moves the date 'without bound'. But while ACTIVE past the horizon the owner may first call setInactivityPeriod(7 days), so each override can cost MIN_INACTIVITY, and a single extendHorizon may set the horizon up to now + 36500 days. T3's protection against runaway automation holds only if automation never calls extendHorizon, and a keeper following the app's own warning ('extend the horizon to continue') would defeat it. Every such call needs the live owner key, consistent with T1.
confirmed.impact: Owners may pick a horizon expecting the heir to be paid that day, and heirs may treat a date as guaranteed when it is not. The public trust-model guarantee is stated more strongly than the code enforces. A planning error, not direct theft.
confirmed.exploit_scenario:
1. Alice sets the horizon to 2030-01-01 with a 365-day window, reading the label as the payout date.
2. The owner key is lost. Bob can initiate on 2030-01-01 and finalize no earlier than 2031-01-01 (or March 2031 if he initiates in March).
3. Separately, a thief who later obtains Alice's key sees 'Guaranteed inheritance by ...' on Bob's screen and calls withdraw(full) before Bob finalizes. The vault closes.
T3 variant: a vault with P = 365d past its horizon; owner automation calls setInactivityPeriod(0, 7 days) and extendHorizon(0, now + 7d + 1). The heir's cooldown per override is 7 days, not 365, and a keeper can repeat it on every horizonReached flag.
confirmed.recommendation: Rename the form field to 'Horizon (long-stop date; the heir can finalize no earlier than horizon + challenge window)'. On the card, label the date 'earliest finalization if the heir claims at the horizon and the owner key does not act'. In T3, README and site: list the full withdrawal, and say 'at least MIN_INACTIVITY per override, up to 100 years per call; never give extendHorizon to automation'. Optionally (v2) floor the extendHorizon cooldown at the larger of the current period and the period in force at the old horizon.

poc.explanation:
I reproduced all four parts of F21 in the sandbox. The run gave 2 failing tests and 4 passing ones. I did not touch the repo, and git status is the same as before the run.

Test 1 fails as expected. It covers point 2, the card's "Guaranteed inheritance by" date and getVault.guaranteedInheritanceAt at InheritanceVault.sol:821. Setup: horizon H = now + 730d, check-in period 30d, challenge window 365d. A check-in bot ran until H - 1d, so the deadline is capped at H. The owner key is then lost, and the heir calls initiateClaim at H + 30d. The test moves to the instant getVault reports as guaranteedInheritanceAt (H + 365d) and checks that the claim can be finalized. It cannot: finalizableAt = claimInitiatedAt + window, which is 2,592,001 s (30d + 1s) later. The view is fixed at absoluteDeadline + challengeWindow and ignores the actual claim. So the card at app.js:285 shows a "guaranteed" date that has already passed, while the pill at app.js:308 still shows the veto window running. The precondition is the heir's own late claim. A v2 view that returns max(H + W, finalizableAt) while a claim is pending would make this test pass.

Test 2 fails as expected. It covers point 4 and T3 at :34-41 ("at a cost of one full inactivity period per override"). Setup: period 365d, horizon passed, vault still ACTIVE. setInactivityPeriod(0, 7d) succeeds past the horizon, because :596-604 has no horizon check and _clearPending does nothing in ACTIVE. The heir then initiates, and the owner calls extendHorizon(ts + 7d + 1). That passes the floor check at :622, which uses the current period. The claim is displaced, and the heir's cooldown is 604,800 s (7 days) against an expected 31,536,000 s (365 days). The test also accepts either v2 fix: refusing setInactivityPeriod past the horizon, or basing the extendHorizon floor on the period in force at the horizon. With either fix, the test checks that the claim still stands and that an honest full-period extension still succeeds.

Tests 3 to 6 pass. They measure the parts where the fix is documentation or UI:
- **Point 1 (form label).** The create form at site/app.html:81 calls the horizon field the "guaranteed inheritance date". With bots running until H and the heir claiming at H exactly, finalizeClaim at H + 364d reverts with ChallengeWindowOpen(H + 365d). It only succeeds at H + 365d. The view's guaranteedInheritanceAt is correct; the form label is wrong.
- **Point 3 (full withdrawal).** At H + 396d the claim is finalizable but not yet finalized, and withdraw(0, DEPOSIT) from the owner key still succeeds. The vault closes, finalizeClaim reverts with NoClaimPending, and the heir's credit is 0. The transaction emits Withdrawn(closed=true) but neither HorizonExtended nor ClaimSuperseded. This contradicts T3's "The ONLY way past the date is extendHorizon". However, the code comments at :306-310 and :568 describe this behaviour as intended, and so does how-it-works.html:62-64. The existing test Audit.ts:138 already locks it in. Test 5 shows that calling extendHorizon and then a full withdraw reaches the same result, so blocking the full withdrawal would achieve nothing. The fix is to correct T3 and README.md:25-27.
- **Point 4 (magnitude).** Three past-horizon overrides in a row cost the heir about 14-21 days in total, not three years. A single extendHorizon(ts + 36500 days) from a past-horizon, claim-pending state succeeds and displaces the claim.

poc.severity_observation:
LOW is confirmed, and no higher. Every behaviour that goes beyond the published claims needs the live owner key, which T1 already makes the ultimate authority. No unprivileged party can move the date. The protection against a lost key holds exactly: with no owner action, the heir was paid at H + W, as test 3 shows.

The real risks are to planning and to heirs:
- **Up to a year later than the label says.** Owners may read the form's horizon as the payout date, but payout comes up to 365 days after it.
- **The window ending does not settle anything.** Even after the challenge window has elapsed, a full withdrawal from the owner key (or a thief holding it) takes everything until someone calls finalizeClaim. Heirs should finalize promptly.

Four additional details the PoC surfaced:
- **Closing the vault emits no ClaimSuperseded.** When a full withdrawal closes a vault with a pending claim, only Withdrawn(closed=true) is emitted. An indexer that tracks claims through ClaimInitiated, ClaimAborted, ClaimSuperseded and ClaimSettled never sees that claim end.
- **setInactivityPeriod past the horizon is a silent no-op.** It cannot move the deadline, which stays capped at the horizon, so the "green-toast lie" reasoning that made setCheckInChain revert past the horizon applies here too. Its only real effect is to lower the extendHorizon floor.
- **The v2 floor fix is narrow.** The owner can lower the period to 7 days before the horizon, which is a legitimate action. So the optional v2 floor fix only closes the path after the horizon. The accurate remedy is documentation: "at least MIN_INACTIVITY (7 days) per override, up to 100 years per call; never give extendHorizon to automation".
- **Blocking the full withdrawal would achieve nothing.** extendHorizon followed by a full withdrawal already reaches the same result, so T3 and the README should list the full withdrawal rather than the code being changed.

reach.reasoning:
Partly refuted. What survives is a code-vs-documentation mismatch with no fund impact. The PoC runs against a contract byte-identical to the repo's InheritanceVault.sol (checked with diff) and uses no storage hacks or impersonation. I re-ran it and got the same result: 4 passing, 2 failing. Every step is reachable. But the two failing tests do not show a defect.

Point 4 (the T3 variant) is refuted: the claimed harm runs in the opposite direction.
- The extendHorizon floor (line 622) is now + the current inactivityPeriod. It is only a minimum. The owner may always name any horizon up to now + MAX_HORIZON.
- The owner can also lower the period to MIN_INACTIVITY at any time before the horizon, with setInactivityPeriod (596-604). So "one full inactivity period" means the period currently in force, and the code enforces exactly that.
- A lower floor can never lengthen the heir's wait. Test 2 asserts heirCooldown >= 365 days, which demands that the heir be delayed longer. Its failure (7 days) is the heir-favourable outcome, and the proposed v2 floor would make heirs worse off.
- Automation that re-calls extendHorizon blocks the heir whatever P is. T3 already names extendHorizon as the one owner-key override and says it is logged as HorizonExtended.
- "Without bound" refers to the zero-cooldown veto loop that the floor closes: every override now costs at least 7 days. The 100-year jump is MAX_HORIZON, the same bound createVault allows.

Point 2 (test 1) is a strawman. The heir claimed 30 days after the horizon. No design can finalize a claim before claimInitiatedAt + the immutable challenge window. guaranteedInheritanceAt = absoluteDeadline + challengeWindow (line 821) is correct for its meaning: the earliest finalization for a heir who claims at the horizon while the owner key is lost. Test 3 shows it holds to the second (finalize reverts at H+W-1d and succeeds at H+W). The card showing that date next to a later "veto window until" pill is cosmetic.

Point 3 is disclosed. The full withdrawal is described publicly:
- how-it-works.html:62-64: "The owner must either close the vault by withdrawing everything or extend the horizon".
- The README.md:17 state diagram.
- T1 (lines 24-27): "It can withdraw everything ... A stolen owner key is a stolen vault".
- how-it-works.html:48-49, and the _clearPending NatSpec.

Only T3's single sentence "The ONLY way past the date is extendHorizon" leaves it out. A full withdrawal also does not move the date: it ends the vault, under T1 authority.

What survives is point 1. site/app.html:81 labels the horizon input "guaranteed inheritance date". The earliest payout is horizon + challenge window, 7 to 365 days later: the value the owner enters in the field directly above. README.md:25 and the view use the correct H+W definition. So this is a UI label error, plus the T3 NatSpec omission. No unprivileged party can move any date. Every override needs the live owner key (T1). The lost-key guarantee holds exactly.

Under the rubric this is INFORMATIONAL (code-vs-documentation mismatch, no fund impact), not LOW.

Side note, outside F21: closing a vault by full withdrawal while a claim is pending emits only Withdrawn(closed=true), never ClaimSuperseded or ClaimAborted. An indexer that tracks claims only by their start and end events never sees that claim end. That should be its own item (LOW/INFO).
reach.better_fix:
Documentation and UI only. Do not adopt the proposed v2 change that sets the extendHorizon floor to the period in force at the horizon. It can only raise the minimum delay imposed on the heir, never lower it.
- site/app.html:81: relabel the field as "Horizon (long-stop): check-ins stop here; your heir can finalize no earlier than horizon + challenge window".
- site/assets/app.js:285: while a claim is pending (state 2), show finalizableAt instead of guaranteedInheritanceAt, and word the idle-state line as "earliest inheritance if your heir claims at the horizon".
- T3 NatSpec and README.md:25-27: list the full withdrawal next to extendHorizon, and say "at least one current inactivity period (min 7 days) per override".
- Optional v2: have setInactivityPeriod revert past the horizon, for the same no-op reason checkIn and setCheckInChain revert. It changes nothing on the deadline there.

sev.reasoning:
I checked every part of F21 against the code and the public documents. The behaviour is real. Parts (3) and (4) are intended and disclosed, and part (4) does not weaken anything. Parts (1) and (2) are genuine wording errors in the UI and the view field name, and nothing discloses them. No part affects funds, and no unprivileged party can trigger any of it. The rubric puts a code-vs-documentation mismatch with no fund impact at INFORMATIONAL.

Part 1: the create-form label is wrong and not disclosed.
- site/app.html:81 reads "Horizon - guaranteed inheritance date, even if check-in bots run forever".
- The horizon is actually the latest date the heir can start a claim. `_resetClock` caps `deadline` at `absoluteDeadline`, and `createVault` requires the horizon to be at least now + inactivityPeriod (:388).
- The earliest payout is therefore H + challengeWindow, which is 7-365 days later. The owner picks that window in the field directly above (app.html:78), labelled "your veto period after a claim".
- Harm: an owner who takes the label literally gets a payout later than planned, by at most the window they chose themselves. Nothing is lost.

Part 2: the `guaranteedInheritanceAt` view field over-promises.
- getVault :821 returns absoluteDeadline + challengeWindow. It ignores `claimInitiatedAt` and still returns a date for SETTLED and CLOSED vaults.
- If the heir claims late, the heir card (app.js:285) shows a "Guaranteed inheritance by" date that has already passed.
- The same card shows the correct `finalizableAt` in the pill at app.js:308, and an early finalizeClaim just reverts. The heir cannot be harmed by acting on the wrong date.
- T3 (:34) states the exact formula and scopes it to a lost owner key and runaway check-in automation. T2 (:29-33) and how-it-works step 3 say the heir must claim, and nothing happens automatically.
- The field name alone could justify LOW under "return values that mislead integrators". But the formula is documented, and the correct date is returned alongside it.

Part 3: the full withdrawal is intended and disclosed.
- T3's sentence "The ONLY way past the date is extendHorizon" is imprecise.
- The behaviour itself is disclosed in several places:
  - T1 (:25-26): the owner key "can withdraw everything".
  - The README state diagram: "owner withdraws everything → CLOSED".
  - how-it-works.html:62-65: "must either close the vault by withdrawing everything or extend the horizon".
  - The watcher email (notify/watcher.js:150-153): "or withdrawing the balance outright".
  - The code comments at :306-310 and :568.
- The key-thief scenario is T1 ("A stolen owner key is a stolen vault"). Past the horizon, a partial withdrawal of all but 1 wei drains the vault to the same effect. So blocking the full withdrawal would achieve nothing, which the PoC's test 5 confirms.

Part 4: lowering the period to 7 days does not weaken the horizon. It is a restatement of disclosed T1 powers.
- T3's "one full inactivity period" is literally the period in force.
- The owner may legitimately set that period to 7 days before the horizon (how-it-works.html:46, "adjust permitted timing settings").
- Past the horizon, the same result can be reached without the setInactivityPeriod-past-horizon step. The owner calls extendHorizon(now + P), which leaves the vault ACTIVE with the new horizon ahead, and then calls setInactivityPeriod(7d). Every pre-horizon soft veto works again from there.
- So in every path, the heir waits at least MIN_INACTIVITY per override, and a living key holder can defer indefinitely. T3 says so explicitly ("a living owner can still override the date deliberately"), and each override emits HorizonExtended, so nothing happens silently.
- A 365-day floor would stop a runaway bot that calls extendHorizon no better than a 7-day floor does. The horizon only stops automation that never calls extendHorizon, which is exactly what T3 promises ("runaway check-in automation").
- The 100-year jump per call is bounded by MAX_HORIZON, the same bound createVault allows.
- The "keeper following the app's warning" scenario is speculative. app.js:187 and the watcher emails are text for a human. No keeper in the repo calls extendHorizon: a grep finds it only in app.js, abi.js, the tests and the contract.

Conclusion: not refuted, because the create-form label and the "Guaranteed" wording are undisclosed misstatements. It is not by design and disclosed as a whole, since parts 1 and 2 are not disclosed. Severity should drop from LOW to INFORMATIONAL: a documentation and UI finding with no fund impact.

Side observations, better tracked as separate items if they are not already:
- A full withdrawal that closes a CLAIM_PENDING vault emits only Withdrawn(closed=true), with no ClaimSuperseded or aborted event. Indexers never see the claim end.
- setInactivityPeriod past the horizon succeeds and changes nothing visible. This is the same "green-toast" pattern that B-04 fixed for setCheckInChain, though here the stored period does matter after a later extension.
sev.better_fix:
The contract is immutable, so the fixes go in the UI and the documents only.

1. **Create-form label (app.html:81):** change it to "Horizon (long-stop): the last day your heir may have to wait before starting a claim. Payout comes no earlier than this date plus the challenge window."
2. **Heir card (app.js:285):**
   - While a claim is pending, show `finalizableAt`, not `guaranteedInheritanceAt`.
   - Before any claim, show "If your heir claims by <H>, and no one uses your key, the heir can finalize by <H+W>. The heir must start the claim and then finalize it."
   - Hide the line for SETTLED and CLOSED vaults.
3. **T3 prose and README:25-27:** say "Past the horizon only two owner actions can stop a claim: extendHorizon, which gives the heir at least MIN_INACTIVITY (7 days) before a new claim and can be repeated without limit, and withdrawing the entire balance (T1). The horizon stops automation that only checks in. Never give extendHorizon to a bot."
4. **Drop the optional v2 floor fix** (the max of the current period and the period at the old horizon). An owner can get around it with extendHorizon(now+P) followed by setInactivityPeriod(7d), or by lowering the period before the horizon, so it adds complexity without a guarantee.
5. **For v2, if anything:**
   - Return `claimInitiatedAt + window` while a claim is pending, or rename the field to `latestFinalizeIfClaimedAtHorizon`.
   - Emit ClaimSuperseded (or a dedicated event) when a full withdrawal closes a vault that has a claim pending.
   - Optionally make setInactivityPeriod revert past the horizon, for UI honesty, matching B-04.

confirmed.title: A third party can front-run an owner's exact-balance 'close' with a 1-wei topUp and keep the vault open
confirmed.location: contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:441-454 topUp (permissionless while ACTIVE), :552-580 withdraw (closes only if balance == 0 after subtracting the exact amount); site/assets/app.js:215-224 actWithdraw (asks for an amount; no 'withdraw all')
confirmed.description: There is no close() and no 'withdraw everything' sentinel. An owner closes a vault by calling withdraw with the current balance. Anyone can front-run that with topUp(owner, id, 1). The owner's transaction then succeeds with Withdrawn(..., closed = false). The vault stays ACTIVE holding the attacker's dust, keeps one of the owner's 32 open slots, has its clock reset, and later becomes claimable by the heir, with the alerts and claim flows that follow.
confirmed.impact: Minor griefing: the owner's intent to close fails behind a successful receipt, and they must send another transaction, which can be front-run again. Cost is roughly symmetric (gas plus 1 wei per round). No principal at risk. Practical on BNB's public mempool.
confirmed.exploit_scenario:
1. The owner submits withdraw(0, 10 ETH, owner) on a 10 ETH vault to close it.
2. Dave sees it in the mempool and front-runs with topUp(owner, 0, 1 wei).
3. The withdraw succeeds with closed = false. The vault is ACTIVE with 1 wei and still in openVaultIds.
4. Dave repeats whenever the owner tries to close.
confirmed.recommendation: Accept amount == type(uint256).max as 'withdraw the full balance and close', or add close(vaultId, to). Have the app use it for a 'Withdraw all' action.

confirmed.preconditions: The vault is ACTIVE (topUp is refused while a claim is pending), and the attacker can see the owner's transaction before inclusion.

test_names: PoC F22: 1-wei topUp front-run defeats an exact-balance close SAFE PROPERTY: an owner's close is not defeated by a third party's 1-wei front-run topUp
PoC F22: 1-wei topUp front-run defeats an exact-balance close DAMAGE (current behaviour): green receipt, vault stays open, repeatable, heir claim flow fires on dust
poc.explanation:
Reproduced against the sandbox copy of contracts/InheritanceVault.sol. The sandbox holds copies only. The repo was not touched and no mainnet call was made.

How the code allows it: topUp (InheritanceVault.sol:441-454) is permissionless while the vault is ACTIVE and accepts 1 wei. withdraw (:552-580) closes the vault only when `v.balance == 0` after subtracting the exact `amount`. The contract has no close() function and no "withdraw everything" value. The dapp's actWithdraw (site/assets/app.js:215-224) prompts for an amount, so closing a vault means sending withdraw(id, currentBalance, to).

Test 1 (asserts the safe property, FAILS on the current code):
- The mempool is simulated with automine off. Alice broadcasts her close with a 1 gwei tip. Dave then broadcasts topUp(alice, 0, 1 wei) with a 50 gwei tip, and one block is mined.
- Both transactions get explicit gas limits, so neither is gas-estimated against the other's pending state.
- A helper picks the strongest close the contract offers: close(uint256,address) if the ABI has it, else withdraw(id, MaxUint256, to) if a static-call probe accepts it, else withdraw(observed balance). On the current code it falls through to withdraw(observed balance), which is what the dapp sends.
- These setup checks all pass: both transactions are in the same block, Dave's is ordered first, Dave's topUp succeeded, and Alice's close was mined with status 1.
- The first property assertion then fails: getVault(alice, 0).state is 1 (ACTIVE) where 4 (CLOSED) was expected. The failure is the defect itself: the owner has a successful receipt and the vault is still open.

Regression check: contracts/test/InheritanceVaultF22Fixed.sol is a new file in the sandbox. It copies the vault and adds one line to withdraw: `if (amount == type(uint256).max) amount = v.balance;`. Running with F22_IMPL=InheritanceVaultF22Fixed makes Test 1 pass: the vault is CLOSED, balance 0, openVaultIds is empty, totalLocked is 0, and Alice is credited DEPOSIT + 1 wei (the griefer's dust goes to her). So the test works as a regression test for the recommended fix.

Test 2 (measures the damage on the current code, passes):
- Round 1: withdraw(0, 10 ETH) emits Withdrawn(..., 10 ETH, closed=false) with status 1. Afterwards the state is ACTIVE, balance is 1 wei, openVaultIds is [0], totalLocked is 1, and the deadline is reset to block time + PERIOD.
- Round 2: Alice retries with withdraw(0, 1). Dave front-runs again for another wei, and the vault is still ACTIVE with balance 1.
- After PERIOD + 1 the expired warning bit is set and the heir (Bob) can call initiateClaim on the dust vault, so the claim flow starts on a vault the owner meant to close.
- The dust vault holds one of Alice's 32 open slots: after 31 more createVault calls, the 33rd reverts TooManyOpenVaults(32).

poc.severity_observation:
LOW is confirmed. No principal is at risk: Alice's full 10 ETH is credited to her. Only 1 wei, supplied by the griefer, is left behind, and Alice can close the vault with any later withdraw that is not front-run.

Cost to the griefer is about the same as the owner's, or slightly lower: about 44.4k gas plus 1 wei per round, against 95.6k gas for the owner's first withdraw and 61.3k for each retry. So the owner pays more gas per round than the attacker.

The side effects are real but bounded:
- The owner gets a misleading successful receipt (Withdrawn closed=false).
- The inactivity clock resets.
- One of the 32 open slots stays held. This only blocks new vaults for an owner who is already at 31 or more.
- About one PERIOD later the vault shows as expired and the heir can start a claim on 1 wei. That generates the alert and claim traffic the finding describes.

Front-running is realistic on BNB's public mempool and hard on Base, where the sequencer has no public mempool. The owner can also sidestep it with a private-relay RPC.

The fix is cheap and was verified: treating amount == type(uint256).max as "withdraw everything and close" (one added line) makes the regression test pass. The dapp would also need a "Withdraw all" action that sends that value.

reach.reasoning:
I could not refute F22. I traced every guard on the path and it holds.

**Why the path is reachable** (contracts/InheritanceVault.sol)
- `topUp` (:441-454) is permissionless. Its only checks are:
  - `amount != 0` (:442);
  - `vaultId < vaultCount` via `_vault` (:278);
  - `state == STATE_ACTIVE` before and after `_pull` (:444, :450);
  - `_pull` (:345-356) requires `msg.value == amount` for the native coin and `received != 0`.
- So any third party can add 1 wei to any ACTIVE vault. There is no horizon check and no owner check.
- `withdraw` (:552-580) checks `to`, `amount != 0`, `_requireLive` (:282, not SETTLED, CLOSED or NONE) and `amount <= balance` (:559).
- After a 1-wei top-up, `amount = old balance` still passes :559. The subtraction leaves `balance = 1`, `closed = false` (:566), the vault is not removed from `_openIds`, and the event reports `Withdrawn(..., closed=false)`.
- There is no `close()` function and no sentinel for "withdraw everything". The contract has no other way to close a vault atomically.
- The dapp's `actWithdraw` (site/assets/app.js:215-224) sends the amount the owner types, so exact-balance withdrawal is how a vault is closed in practice.

**Consequences, checked in the code**
- The inactivity clock resets (`_resetClock` at :564 runs on every withdraw).
- The vault keeps its slot, which counts toward `MAX_OPEN_VAULTS` at :399.
- After the reset deadline passes, the heir can `initiateClaim` on the dust (:639-659). The balance is 1, so :645 passes.
- Past the horizon, the vault is claimable at once, because the deadline is clamped to the horizon.

**The PoC is sound and not self-confirming**
- The sandbox `contracts/InheritanceVault.sol` is byte-identical to the repo file (checked with `diff`).
- The PoC uses only ordinary signed transactions. Automine is off to model mempool ordering, explicit gas limits keep one transaction from being estimated against the other, and the priority fee sets the order.
- It does not use `setStorageAt`, impersonation or any other impossible state. Its setup checks confirm same block, griefer first, both transactions status 1.
- I ran it:
  - The safe-property test fails because the state is 1 (ACTIVE), not 4 (CLOSED).
  - The damage test passes, reproducing all of the above.
  - Gas per round: griefer 44,422; owner 95,559 on the first withdraw and 61,299 on each retry.
- The fix candidate (one line: `if (amount == type(uint256).max) amount = v.balance;`, placed before the balance check) is the only difference from the original.

**Why it is only LOW**
- No principal is at risk. The owner's full amount is credited to them, and the only value left behind is the griefer's own 1 wei.
- The griefer gains nothing, and the cost to each side is roughly the same, so this is not "strong cost asymmetry" (MEDIUM).
- It is practical on BNB's public mempool. On Base there is no public mempool, so an attacker would have to spam top-ups every block to hit the gap between the owner reading the balance and the transaction landing. That works only sometimes, and the owner can avoid it with a private RPC.

**Nuance the finding omits**
- While a claim is pending, `topUp` is refused (:444). A full withdraw, however, still closes the vault. So the grief works only on ACTIVE vaults.
- If the heir also calls `initiateClaim` in the same block, the next close attempt cannot be griefed at all.
- The `closed=false` event is truthful, not wrong, but the owner's intent fails behind a successful receipt.

**Not by design and disclosed**
- The NatSpec on `topUp` says "a gift cannot harm". F22 shows that a gift can keep a vault from closing.
- site/how-it-works.html:64 tells owners past the horizon to "close the vault by withdrawing everything", and nothing discloses that a third party's top-up can defeat that.

**Conclusion:** real, reachable, correctly scoped as minor griefing. Proposed severity: LOW.

sev.reasoning:
The behaviour is real. I traced it end to end in contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:
- topUp (:441-454) accepts 1 wei from anyone while the vault is ACTIVE.
- withdraw (:552-580) sets STATE_CLOSED only when `v.balance == 0` after subtracting the exact `amount`, and there is no close() and no "withdraw everything" value.
- The dapp's actWithdraw (site/assets/app.js:215-224) sends the amount the user typed, so a close is always withdraw(id, observedBalance, to).
- A 1-wei topUp mined first turns that close into a partial withdraw. The vault stays ACTIVE with the griefer's dust, keeps its _openIds slot, and _resetClock runs.

Intended and disclosed? It is intended but not disclosed.
- The permissionless topUp is intended ("a gift cannot harm", :438-440).
- Nothing tells users that a close can be undone by a third party. README, the contract header T1-T4, OQ-1..OQ-3, security.html and index.html are all silent.
- site/how-it-works.html:64 tells owners to "close the vault by withdrawing everything", and that is exactly the action this griefs. So this is not by-design-and-disclosed.

Severity under the rubric: LOW is right, and it should not go higher.
- Anyone can trigger it, but it needs mempool visibility. That is practical on BNB's public mempool. On Base the sequencer has no public mempool, so the griefer would have to spam topUps blindly every block.
- Cost is symmetric or slightly in the griefer's favour: about 44k gas plus 1 wei per round, against 61-96k for the owner. The griefer gains nothing.
- The victim loses no principal. The full withdrawn amount is credited, and only the griefer's own dust is left.
- The side effects are bounded:
  - The inactivity clock resets.
  - One of 32 open slots stays used, which matters only to an owner at 31 or more.
  - About one period later the heir can claim a vault holding 1 wei, which creates alert and claim noise.
- Post-horizon no worse outcome is possible. If the heir has already initiated a claim, topUp reverts, so the "close to end the claim" route in how-it-works cannot be griefed. If the vault is still ACTIVE, the griefed close leaves a dust vault the heir can claim. Nothing the owner withdrew is at risk.
- The receipt is not a lie at contract level: Withdrawn carries closed=false. runTx (app.js:102-117) shows "confirmed", then refreshMine re-renders the vault as Active with a tiny balance, so the UI corrects itself on the next render. That is minor griefing plus a mildly misleading UX, which is LOW and not MEDIUM.

The recommended fix is sound and does not change any other guarantee.
- A close with amount == type(uint256).max (amount = v.balance) grants no new capability. topUp is already refused during CLAIM_PENDING, so an exact-balance close there already ends a claim. The B-01 property (a dust withdraw does not veto a post-horizon claim) is unaffected.
- It sweeps the griefer's dust to the owner, which is harmless. The PoC verified this.
- An explicit close(vaultId, to) is equivalent and easier for integrators to read.

The Base contract is immutable, so the fix only helps a future BNB deployment or a redeploy. The dapp needs its own mitigation (see better_fix).
sev.better_fix:
For a new deployment, such as the planned BNB one, add an explicit close(vaultId, to) or accept amount == type(uint256).max in withdraw as "withdraw the full balance and close". A dedicated close() is easier for integrators to read than a magic value. Either version sweeps any dust to the owner and keeps every other rule unchanged: the post-horizon claim rule stays as it is, and a close still ends a pending claim, as it does today.

The deployed Base contract is immutable, so for it (and for the app in general):
(1) After a withdraw, read the closed flag from the Withdrawn event. If it is false and only a small remainder is left, say so plainly ("someone added X; the vault is still open") and offer a one-click "withdraw the remainder". Do not show only "confirmed".
(2) Add a "Withdraw all" button that reads the balance immediately before signing.
(3) On BNB, send owner transactions through a private-mempool RPC so the griefer cannot see them.
(4) Add one sentence to how-it-works.html next to "close the vault by withdrawing everything": third parties can top up an active vault, so a close can leave dust that needs a second withdraw.

test_names: PoC F23 [fork] SAFE PROPERTY: a direct 'top-up' to the retired billing contract is refused on chain
PoC F23 [fork] DAMAGE: the payment is kept, time is credited to nobody's benefit, and the payer cannot get it back
PoC F23 [fork] the recommended fix works on the LIVE bytecode: admin setPrice(max) makes subscribe revert
PoC F23 [local] admin sets the price to 2^256-1: every subscribe reverts, reads, withdraw and ownership still work
poc.explanation:
F23 is reproduced against the real live contract. The two fork tests fail today because of the defect itself, and they pass once the recommended admin transaction is applied.

How the test works:
- The [fork] tests fork Base mainnet at the latest block (https://mainnet.base.org, or BASE_RPC_URL if set) and mine one local block on top. That block is needed because EDR has no Base hardfork history and cannot execute calls at the fork block itself.
- They call the real NotifySubscription at 0x60749aF621180de1DC05DB4f3d158D09dE979dC6 and read its real storage.
- The heir and the parent are fresh keccak-derived addresses, impersonated and funded only inside the fork. The test asserts they have no code, because Hardhat's well-known dev accounts can carry EIP-7702 code on public chains.
- A snapshot is taken before each fork test and restored after it, so each test starts from untouched live state. Nothing is sent to mainnet.
- If the RPC is unreachable, the fork tests skip instead of failing.

Test 1 (fork, fails): it asserts the safe property, that a 0.012 ETH direct subscribe(parent, 0) reverts. It fails with "didn't revert": the live pricePerMonth is 1e15, so added = 0.012e18*2592000/1e15 = 31,104,000 s, which is non-zero. subscribe (NotifySubscription.sol:60-76) accepts the payment.

Test 2 (fork, fails): it quantifies the damage. The contract balance rises by exactly 0.012 ETH and paidUntil moves 360 days past the purchase block. The heir calling withdraw() reverts with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount, which shows there is no on-chain way back to the payer. The final assertion (stranded == 0) fails with expected 0, actual 12000000000000000.

Test 3 (fork, passes): it impersonates the hardware-wallet owner 0x883C8211...CdCA3 inside the fork and calls setPrice(MaxUint256). After that, subscribe with 1 wei, 0.012 ETH and 1000 ETH all revert ZeroAmount on the live bytecode.

Test 4 (local, passes): it deploys a fresh NotifySubscription at 0.001 ETH/month; alice buys one month, then the admin sets the price to MaxUint256. After that:
- subscribe with 1 wei, 0.012 ETH, 1000 ETH and 1.2e8 ETH (about the whole ETH supply) all revert ZeroAmount. msg.value*MONTH would only overflow above about 4.4e70 wei.
- A plain ETH send reverts, because the contract has no receive() or fallback(). subscribe is the only way to pay it.
- alice's paidUntil and isActive are unchanged.
- withdraw pays out the earlier revenue.
- Ownable2Step transfer and accept still work, and the new owner can restore the price.

I could not refute F23's technical claims. They hold against the code and the live bytecode. The severity should drop to Informational, because the value-loss half is already disclosed and needs a user to ignore explicit warnings.

What I checked:

1. **Payments still land.** In contracts/NotifySubscription.sol:60-76, subscribe() has only four guards:
   - `account != 0`
   - `msg.value != 0`
   - `added = msg.value*MONTH/pricePerMonth != 0` (line 64-65)
   - the slippage floor, and the MAX_PREPAID cap (line 71-72)

   There is no modifier, pause flag or owner check. Payment is permissionless.
2. **The kill switch works.** setPrice (line 84-88) is onlyOwner and rejects only 0. With price = 2^256-1, `msg.value*MONTH` (MONTH = 2,592,000) cannot overflow unless msg.value > about 4.47e70 wei, which is impossible. The quotient is therefore always 0, and every subscribe reverts ZeroAmount at line 65.
   - isActive, paidUntil and withdraw have no price dependency and keep working.
   - There is no receive() or fallback(), so subscribe is the only way to pay.
   - The switch is reversible by the owner.
3. **The docs overstate.**
   - README.md:85 says "immutable and cannot be paused". That is false in effect.
   - security.html:39, AUDIT_SCOPE.md:88 and the NatSpec at line 17 say "no pause switch". That is literally true, since there is no pause() function, but misleading, since an equivalent zero-code switch exists and has not been used.
4. **I ran the PoC.** The sandbox copy of NotifySubscription.sol is byte-identical to the repo copy.
   - The [local] test passes.
   - Fork tests 1 and 2 fail as described against the real contract at 0x60749aF6...dC6. Live pricePerMonth is 1e15. A 0.012 ETH subscribe(parent, 0) from a fresh code-less EOA is accepted and credits 360 days, and the heir's withdraw reverts OwnableUnauthorizedAccount.
   - Fork test 3 passes: setPrice(MaxUint256) makes subscribe revert on the live bytecode.
5. **The test is sound.**
   - No hardhat_setStorageAt is used.
   - The contract is not impersonated.
   - Heir and parent are fresh keccak-derived EOAs.
   - The owner is impersonated only in the remediation test, and that test reflects a real signable admin transaction.
   - Tests 1 and 2 fail on the defect itself, not on setup.

Why the severity drops:

- **The payment path is intended and disclosed.**
  - site/terms.html:46 says the contract "may still accept a direct contract call; such a call is not an accepted service order. Do not send funds to it".
  - README.md:85-86 and security.html:39-40 say "do not send it funds or call it directly".
  - terms.html:51-55 gives an off-chain refund route.
- **The loss needs deliberate action.** A payer must bypass the website and call a retired contract directly against published warnings.
- **The funds are not taken by an attacker.** They go to the operator, who can withdraw and refund. No unprivileged third party can take or freeze anyone's funds.
- **Exposure is bounded and currently zero.** At most about 0.1217 ETH per account per 10-year window at today's price (MAX_PREPAID). No Subscribed events have ever been emitted and the balance is 0.

  - notify/README.md:56 is a developer doc in the repo, not the public site.

sev.reasoning:
I checked the finding against contracts/NotifySubscription.sol and the documents that describe it. The behavior is real. It is only partly disclosed, and the one claim the finding says is wrong is in fact wrong.

Code path (NotifySubscription.sol):
- subscribe() (:60-76) accepts any msg.value that buys at least 1 second at the current price. At the live price of 1e15 wei, 0.012 ETH buys 360 days.
- setPrice() (:84-88) is onlyOwner and rejects only 0.
- With pricePerMonth = 2^256-1, the calculation (msg.value*MONTH)/pricePerMonth at :64 gives 0 for any msg.value below about 4.47e70 wei, so :65 reverts ZeroAmount. Any larger value overflows at :64 and panics. So every subscribe reverts.
- paidUntil, isActive, withdraw and Ownable2Step are unaffected.
- The contract has no receive() or fallback(), so subscribe() is the only voluntary way to send it ETH.
- The admin can reverse the setting by calling setPrice() again.

So the admin has a working on-chain kill switch. The following documents say the opposite:
- site/security.html:39 ("immutable and has no pause switch")
- README.md:85 ("cannot be paused")
- AUDIT_SCOPE.md:88 ("has no pause switch")
- the NatSpec at :17 ("No refunds, no pause")

What IS disclosed: that the contract still accepts direct calls and must not be paid. This appears in:
- terms.html:46 ("may still accept a direct contract call")
- README.md:85-86
- AUDIT_SCOPE.md:88-89
- SECURITY.md:14-15
- index.html:192 ("do not pay")
- app.html:35
- about.html:67

A grep of the repo, excluding build folders, finds no subscribe call in site/, so no front end still offers the purchase.

The disclosure does not understate the risk to payers; if anything it overstates how permanent the problem is. What is undisclosed and wrong is the claim about what the operator can do. That wrong claim matters: it is the stated reason the operator has not used the available mitigation. It also means the admin's ability to block renewals is an admin power missing from the trust-model text. For a retired contract that power is harmless. This is not by-design-and-disclosed, so the finding is not refuted.

Why LOW holds, applying the rubric strictly (it sits at the LOW/INFORMATIONAL boundary):
- Who can trigger it: only the payer, by calling the contract directly against warnings on every public page. No third party can cause anyone a loss, and there is no theft or freezing by an unprivileged actor.
- What the victim loses: the payment. It is bounded by MAX_PREPAID (:71-72), about 0.12 ETH per account per 10-year window at today's price. It goes to the operator, whose withdraw() works, so it can be refunded. Terms.html promises an off-chain refund, but there is no on-chain refund path.
- Likelihood: low. The PoC found no Subscribed events since deployment and a zero balance.

The case for keeping it at LOW rather than INFORMATIONAL:
- It is a live, reachable value path, not a pure wording issue.
- The verified NatSpec on Basescan cannot be changed, and it actively invites third-party "heir top-ups" (:13-14). Only an on-chain change can neutralize that invitation.
- The fix is one zero-risk admin transaction that the documentation wrongly says does not exist.

Some of the finding's supporting evidence is weaker than presented:
- The watcher.js:406-413 "renew from any wallet" text is sent only if the watcher runs with subscription config, and the watcher is off. It is dormant.
- notify/README.md:55-56 is developer documentation in the repo, not user-facing site copy.
Both are stale and should be fixed, but they are not current exposure.

Assessment of the recommended fix: setPrice(type(uint256).max) is sound and safe.
- Previously purchased time is untouched (there is none).
- withdraw() still works, so force-fed ETH (for example via selfdestruct) can still be recovered.
- A stale integrator that multiplies the price by months will only produce a transaction that fails for insufficient balance.

The optional tombstone ownership transfer in the recommendation is the weak part:
- It needs a new contract deployment and an acceptOwnership step.
- It permanently removes the ability to withdraw and refund anything force-fed.
- It buys only irreversibility, against an admin who is already trusted with this contract's revenue.
I recommend against it (see better_fix).

Side note, a separate issue outside this finding's scope: site/security.html:58 still says administration "has not yet been transferred", while README.md:81-83 says the hardware-wallet transfer happened on 2026-09-24. The trust-model page is stale in a second place.
sev.better_fix:
1. Keep the core fix. From the hardware-wallet owner (0x883C...CdCA3), send setPrice(type(uint256).max) on Base. Then check pricePerMonth with eth_call, and simulate subscribe (1 wei and a large value) with eth_call to confirm it reverts ZeroAmount before announcing anything. Publish the transaction hash.

2. Skip the tombstone ownership transfer:
   - It adds a new contract to trust.
   - It strands any force-fed ETH.
   - It removes the only on-chain refund channel (withdraw).
   Keep the hardware wallet as owner, and state publicly that the price will not be lowered again. Only if irreversibility is truly required, use a purpose-built owner contract that can call only acceptOwnership and a hard-coded withdraw to a published refund address. Do not use a contract that cannot withdraw.

3. Add a watcher or alert on NotifySubscription events (Subscribed, PriceChanged, Withdrawn, OwnershipTransferStarted), so that any payment that ever arrives, including before the price transaction lands, is refunded proactively rather than waiting for the payer to email.

4. Correct the wording in security.html:39, README.md:85-86, AUDIT_SCOPE.md:88-89, SECURITY.md:14-15 and terms.html:44-48 to: "Sales are disabled on chain: the price is set to the maximum (tx <hash>), so every subscribe reverts. Only the admin could reverse this, and we have committed not to. Any payment that reaches the contract will be refunded." Also:

   - Remove or archive the "pay from any wallet" text in notify/README.md:55-56 and the "anyone can renew for you" text in notify/watcher.js:412-413.
   - Note that the Basescan NatSpec ("no pause", heir top-ups) is superseded.

5. Do not deploy NotifySubscription on BNB Chain.

poc.explanation:
This finding is about documentation, so the "test" is a consistency check: it compares the documents against each other, not against contract behaviour. It reads the repo files without changing them: AUDIT-2026-08-09.md, AUDIT_SCOPE.md and site/index.html. It works out the expected numbers from the report's own itemised list (the "### X-NN · SEVERITY" headings and the "| W-NN |" table rows). It then checks the report's headline and the website FAQ against those numbers. Nothing is hard-coded from the claims being tested, so the test does not simply confirm itself. All 4 tests fail against the current text, and each fails on the defect itself:

1) Report headline vs its own list. AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:11 says "12 defects fixed (2 high, 5 medium, 5 low on chain; 5 critical, 6 high off chain". The itemised on-chain findings are:
- HIGH: A-02 (:32), B-01 (:97), B-02 (:108)
- MEDIUM: A-01 (:18), A-03 (:42), B-03 (:118)
- LOW: A-04 (:50), A-05 (:58), B-04 (:122), B-05 (:127)
That is 10 findings split 3/3/4, not 12 split 2/5/5.

2) Off-chain criticals. The report lists six: W-01..W-05 under the heading "five criticals" (:74-81), plus "B-06 · CRITICAL (off-chain)" at :133. The headline says 5.

3) FAQ count. site/index.html:181 says "Twelve defects were found and fixed, every one reproduced as a failing test". The FAQ describes these as passes "over the contract" (:179), yet the report itemises 10 contract findings, or 20 if the off-chain ones are included. Neither total is 12. The FAQ repeats the report's wrong headline figure.

4) "Independent". site/index.html:179 says "a documented adversarial review we ran ourselves: five independent passes over the contract". AUDIT_SCOPE.md:93-94 says the report "was produced by the same system involved in implementation and must not be described as independent". The report does the same thing at its own line 5 ("five independent reviewers"), although its line 200 admits it "was performed by the same system that wrote the code".

On "reproduced as a failing test before it was believed": the report's own verification rule (:8) allows "a failing test or an executable scenario step". Findings B-06 to B-10 list no test at all. B-01 (:99-101) records that the A-02 test was "performing exactly that sequence and asserting success". So the A-02 fix was believed on a test that asserted the exploit worked. All 10 on-chain items do list an Audit.ts test, and the FAQ says it is about the contract, so this part of the sentence is overstated rather than false.

To fix: correct the report headline to 3/3/4 on chain (10), with 6 critical off chain. Change the FAQ's number to match. Remove "independent" from the FAQ sentence, e.g. "an internal adversarial review, not independent". After that, all four tests should pass. Once copied into the repo's test/ folder, the test finds the files from its own location.
