poc.severity_observation:
Informational is the right rating. No contract code is at fault and no funds are at risk until an operator runs the script on BNB. The rehearsal adds two details the finding did not state.

(a) The script's own post-deploy verification treats the unsafe outcome as success. With defaults it prints "ok vault owner: <deployer>" and "ok sub owner: <deployer>" and writes deployments/bnb.json with no warning apart from the "(= deployer)" tag. The handover gap therefore passes every check the operator relies on.

(b) The 0.001 payment is not merely possible. subscribe() succeeds and the balance can be withdrawn by the admin (the cold admin in test 3, the hot key under defaults). So on BNB, F23 would repeat exactly, with no "do not pay" notice for the new address, because the site's retired-contract warnings list only the Base address.

transfer-admin.ts fails even in dry-run mode on a vault-only record, so applying one recommendation (drop NotifySubscription from deploy.ts) without the other leaves the admin handover tool unusable.

Note for the regression suite: this rehearsal runs on chainId 31337. If a fixed deploy.ts adds in-run BscScan verification as recommended, that step must be skipped or guarded when the chain cannot be verified, or tests 2-4 will fail for an unrelated reason.

reach.reasoning:
Every factual claim checks out against the repo at b8baf34. The PoC exercises the real scripts: the copies in the sandbox are byte-identical to the repo, per diff -q. It does not rely on impossible state (no setStorageAt, no impersonation). Its assertions are the safe properties, and they fail because of the defect, not because of the test setup.

What the code shows:

1. scripts/deploy.ts:18 puts `bnb` in MAINNETS. hardhat.config.ts:40-42 defines `bnb` as chainId 56. The only guard is ALLOW_MAINNET=yes (deploy.ts:27), which the operator supplies. So the documented launch path works on BNB.

2. When ADMIN_ADDRESS or FEE_RECIPIENT is unset, deploy.ts:39-45 falls back to deployer.address. The only signal is a "(= deployer)" suffix on the printed line (:51-52). The post-deploy checks (:81-98) compare the result against that same defaulted value, so they print "ok" for the hot-key outcome. DEPLOY.md:40-42 calls both variables "Optional overrides" and says they only "should be" a cold wallet. deployments/base.json shows this already happened on Base: the deployer 0x4306... held admin from 2026-08-09 until the adminHandover on 2026-09-24.

3. deploy.ts:68-73 always deploys NotifySubscription, at 0.001 native coin by default (:23), and records it (:112-113). The site's "do not pay" notices name only the Base address 0x60749a... (index.html:192-193, security.html:37). A BNB copy would carry no warning.

4. deploy.ts:123 and DEPLOY.md:56 tell the operator to set CHAINS[id].notify. The CHAINS entries in site/assets/app.js:5-24 have no notify field.

5. transfer-admin.ts:35 always calls getContractAt("NotifySubscription", rec.contracts.NotifySubscription). With a vault-only record that throws before the dry-run branch at :61. This bites only after deploy.ts is partly fixed, but it is real.

6. notify/README.md:4 says "This is the paid product" and :55 says "audited alongside the vault". The enforce path in notify/watcher.js:390-414 is still live, including the "Anyone can renew for you from any wallet" email. config.example.json has enforce:false, so that part needs the operator to switch it on.

Mitigations, none of which refute the finding:
- The finding needs operator action: a BNB launch run on defaults, or re-enabling enforce.
- DEPLOY.md:61-67 asks for an independent review before mainnet.
- No contract logic is at fault, and nobody unprivileged gains anything.

Severity: INFORMATIONAL. This is an operational and documentation mismatch in off-chain tooling, with no fund impact until the operator acts. It is not LOW: nothing on-chain misleads integrators, and the damage needs the project's own operator to deploy the retired contract.

by_design_and_disclosed is false. DEPLOY.md half-discloses the cold-wallet recommendation but says nothing about redeploying the retired billing contract. Its "should be" wording is exactly the weakness the finding describes.
reach.better_fix:
In deploy.ts:
- On MAINNETS, throw unless ADMIN_ADDRESS and FEE_RECIPIENT are both set and both differ from deployer.address.
- Change the post-deploy check to assert owner != deployer on mainnets, not just owner == the configured admin, so the defaulted hot-key case fails.
- Deploy NotifySubscription only behind an explicit opt-in such as DEPLOY_NOTIFY=yes, off by default and refused on mainnets. Write the record without a NotifySubscription key when it is skipped.

In transfer-admin.ts, treat rec.contracts.NotifySubscription as optional and skip steps 3 and 4 for it when it is absent. Replace the stale CHAINS[id].notify line in deploy.ts:123 and DEPLOY.md:56.

Remove the enforce branch in notify/watcher.js:390-414, or make it throw at startup if enforce is true, and mark notify/README.md as retired. Because the Base NotifySubscription is immutable, keep the site's "do not pay" list keyed per chain so any future chain gets its own warning or none is deployed there.

sev.reasoning:
The behavior is real and I confirmed it by reading the code. It is not a contract defect, and Informational is the correct rating.

What I verified in the code:
- scripts/deploy.ts:18 includes bnb in MAINNETS.
- deploy.ts:39-45 falls back to deployer.address for both admin and feeRecipient. The only signal is the "(= deployer)" tag at :51-52. The post-deploy checks at :81-98 compare against those same defaults, so they pass.
- deploy.ts:68-73 deploys NotifySubscription unconditionally, and :89-90 and :112-113 check and record it.
- deploy.ts:123 tells the operator to set CHAINS[id].notify. The CHAINS entries in site/assets/app.js:5-24, including the empty 56 entry, have no notify field.
- scripts/transfer-admin.ts:35 calls getContractAt on rec.contracts.NotifySubscription before the dry-run branch at :61, so it cannot run on a vault-only record. Its closing text at :90 and :93 also hard-codes "on Base" and "Basescan".
- notify/README.md:4 and :55-59 still call this "the paid product", "audited alongside the vault", and describe the enforce path as working. notify/watcher.js:390-414 keeps the enforce path, including the "Anyone can renew for you from any wallet" wording. config.example.json ships with enforce: false.

Is it by design and disclosed? Only partly, so it is not refuted.
- Defaulting to the deployer as admin is intentional: the comment at deploy.ts:38 says so. It is also soft-disclosed to operators: DEPLOY.md:40-42 says the admin and fee recipient "should be" a cold wallet on mainnet. It is not disclosed to users. site/security.html:57 is stale in the opposite direction: it still says the admin has not been moved off the deployer, while README.md:81-83 and deployments/base.json record the 2026-09-24 hardware-wallet handover. That is a related code-vs-docs mismatch.
- Redeploying NotifySubscription on a new chain is not intended. It contradicts the retirement stated in README.md:85, security.html:39, terms.html:44-48, AUDIT_SCOPE.md:87-88 and index.html:192. Every retired-contract warning names only the Base address 0x60749a..., so a BNB instance would have no warning at all.

Why it stays Informational under the rubric:
1. Nobody unprivileged can trigger it. Only the operator can, by running a mainnet deploy that requires ALLOW_MAINNET=yes. DEPLOY.md:63-67 also says not to do that before an independent review.
2. A hot-key admin on BNB cannot reach user funds. By the code, its powers are:
   - setClaimFee, capped at MAX_CLAIM_FEE_BPS = 100 (line 111, :742-743). Each vault snapshots its ceiling at creation, so at worst vaults created during a key compromise carry the disclosed 1% cap.
   - setFeeRecipient (:750). Redirecting it diverts operator revenue, not user principal.
   - setCreationPaused (:756), which can only deny new vault creation.
   - sweepSurplus (:774), limited to accounting surplus.
   None of these lets the admin touch a locked balance or credited payout. The finding therefore does not meet the HIGH criterion "admin able to reach user funds". The handover gap is an operational key-hygiene risk that stays inside the trust model the site already discloses.
3. The stray BNB NotifySubscription is not linked anywhere: app.js has no notify field and the site offers no purchase flow. A user would have to find the address and call subscribe() directly. The loss is voluntary, 0.001 BNB per 30 days, and withdrawable by the admin, who could refund it. This repeats F23 as a hygiene issue; it is not a theft path.
4. Nothing has happened yet. There is no deployments/bnb.json and the app.js 56 entry is empty, so this is a pre-launch fix.

On the recommendation: its direction is right, but it is incomplete and in places weaker than it should be. See better_fix.
sev.better_fix:
1. Pass the cold wallet as admin and fee recipient in the constructor. Ownable and the vault constructor already accept an arbitrary admin, so passing the hardware wallet directly makes a BNB handover unnecessary: no transfer-admin run and no hot-key window at all. That beats requiring the env vars and then transferring afterwards.
   - On any MAINNETS network, deploy.ts should throw unless ADMIN_ADDRESS and FEE_RECIPIENT are both set, and both differ from deployer.address.
   - Optionally, print getCode(admin) and require a typed confirmation of the admin address. A wrong constructor admin is permanent: Ownable2Step only protects transfers, not the constructor.
2. Remove NotifySubscription from deploy.ts. If testnet reminder rehearsals are still wanted, put it behind DEPLOY_NOTIFY=yes and refuse that flag on MAINNETS. Drop the sub checks, the subPricePerMonth record field and the CHAINS[].notify / subscription.contract "Next:" lines; DEPLOY.md:49 and :56 need the same change.
3. transfer-admin.ts:
   - Treat rec.contracts.NotifySubscription as optional: skip the sub reads and step 3/4 when it is absent.
   - Move the checks before any contract read that can throw, so the dry run always works.
   - Replace the hard-coded "on Base" and "Basescan" text with the network name and explorer.
   With fix 1 in place, this script matters only for Base and future rotations, but it must not be left unusable.
4. Source verification. Run BscScan verification as a separate, idempotent step: `hardhat verify` right after the deploy. Do not make it fatal inside deploy.ts. Otherwise an explorer outage fails a deploy that has already happened, and local rehearsals on chainId 31337 break.
5. Docs and watcher:
   - Mark notify/README.md as retired, removing the "paid product" and "audited alongside the vault" text.
   - Make watcher.js exit with an error if cfg.subscription.enforce is true. That is safer than silently deleting the code, because an old config.json with enforce: true would otherwise start sending the "renew from any wallet" email again.
   - Fix site/security.html:57, which still says the admin has not been transferred, so it matches README.md:81-83.
6. Do not add a BNB "do not pay" notice. Not deploying the contract on BNB is the fix. A warning would only be needed if one is deployed by mistake, and in that case the admin should call setPrice or withdraw as appropriate and publish the address as retired.

confirmed.title: Read-only reentrancy: surplus() and getVault() report inconsistent values while a deposit is in flight, with no view guard
confirmed.location: contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:345-356 _pull() (token call before storage writes in createVault :401-421 and topUp :446-452), :768-772 surplus(), :809-833 getVault()
confirmed.description: createVault and topUp must call the token before writing state, to measure fee-on-transfer deposits. Writes are protected by the contract-wide nonReentrant, but views are not. With a token that runs a hook after updating balances, any contract the hook calls sees surplus(token) inflated by the whole in-flight deposit, totalLocked not yet incremented, and getVault().balance still at its old value. sweepSurplus cannot act on the phantom surplus because it holds the lock, so the vault cannot be drained this way. For native and standard ERC20/ERC777 payouts the views are already consistent when the recipient runs.
confirmed.impact: Can mislead third-party integrators (proof-of-reserve, dashboards, composable wrappers) that read views inside such a callback. No funds lost in this contract.
confirmed.exploit_scenario:
1. A hook token calls an observer contract after crediting the vault's balance.
2. Alice calls createVault(hookToken, 1000, ...).
3. During the hook the observer reads surplus(hookToken) = 1000 and totalLocked = 0.
4. After the transaction surplus = 0.
confirmed.recommendation: Apply OpenZeppelin's nonReentrantView to surplus, getVault, getOpenVaults and creditOf, routing sweepSurplus through an internal _surplus() so it does not trip the guard. Otherwise, state in NatSpec that views are unreliable while the lock is held.
confirmed.poc_plan: Passing: reentrancy-payouts PoC.ts F4 (HookToken + SurplusObserver record seenSurplus = 1000 and seenLocked = 0 during createVault; surplus is 0 afterwards).
confirmed.preconditions: The deposited token calls external code during transferFrom after updating balances, and a third party trusts views read inside that callback.
confirmed.relation_to_prior_audit: Adjacent to A-01 (reentrancy), which fixed state-changing paths only.

test_names: surplus() does not report an in-flight createVault deposit as admin-sweepable surplus
surplus()/getVault() do not answer a half-applied state during an in-flight topUp
surplus() does not report a phantom while a credit payout is in flight (pre-transfer hook)
bounding: the phantom surplus cannot be swept, even by an admin reached from the hook
poc.explanation:
Reproduced. The sandbox has a new helper file, contracts/test/F33Helpers.sol, which adds two contracts:
- F33HookToken: an ERC20 that calls an observer in one of two modes. Mode 1 calls it after balances are updated on a transfer into the vault. Mode 2 calls it before balances move on a transfer out of the vault.
- F33ViewObserver: a third-party integrator. It reads surplus(), totalLocked(), totalCredited(), getVault() and balanceOf(vault) through low-level staticcalls and records whether each call succeeded and what it returned.

Tests 1-3 assert the safe property: while the contract-wide nonReentrant lock is held, surplus() either refuses to answer or returns the true surplus, which is 0 in every scenario here. Each test first checks that the hook actually fired, so a setup error cannot pass as the defect. Each also checks the value after the transaction, where surplus is 0 and totalLocked or the balance is correct.

Against the unmodified InheritanceVault.sol all three fail on the defect assertion itself:
1. createVault (InheritanceVault.sol:399, _pull at :345-356 runs before the writes at :401-421): inside the hook, surplus()=1000 (the whole deposit), totalLocked=0 and balanceOf(vault)=1000.
2. topUp (:447, before the writes at :451-452): Dave tops up Alice's 100 vault with 50. Inside the hook, surplus()=50, getVault(alice,0).balance=100 (stale) and balanceOf(vault)=150. After the transaction the balance is 150 and surplus is 0.
3. Payout path, which goes beyond the finding. withdrawCredit (:714-722) zeroes the credit and reduces totalCredited before _payout. With a token whose hook runs before its balance update, surplus() therefore shows the whole 400 payout as surplus. The finding's statement that standard ERC20/ERC777/native payouts are consistent still holds. The mirror case needs a non-standard pre-transfer hook.

Test 4 bounds the impact and passes today. The vault is deployed with the observer contract as admin, and the hook calls sweepSurplus. That call reverts with ReentrancyGuardReentrantCall, nothing leaves the vault, and surplus is 0 afterwards. The phantom surplus can mislead readers but cannot be swept.

Fix check: I made a renamed copy of the contract, F33FixedVault (a new file, contracts/test/F33FixedVault.sol; InheritanceVault.sol itself was not edited). The copy adds nonReentrantView (available in the pinned OZ 5.6.1) to surplus() and getVault(), and sweepSurplus uses a private _surplus(). With F33_VAULT=F33FixedVault set, all 4 tests pass, and every view read inside the hook reports answered=false. The default run tests the real InheritanceVault.

sev.reasoning:
The behavior is real and I confirmed it in the code. createVault (InheritanceVault.sol:399) and topUp (:447) call _pull (:345-356), which calls the token before the storage writes at :401-421 and :451-452. surplus() (:768-772), getVault() (:809-833), creditOf (:735) and the public getters for totalLocked/totalCredited (:179-180) have no guard. The call ordering is intentional: the _pull NatSpec says the contract measures what actually arrived because of fee-on-transfer tokens. The mid-flight inconsistency this creates in the views is not disclosed anywhere. The README lists only rebasing tokens and NFTs as unsupported. site/how-it-works.html:97 says only that "unusual transfer behavior can break normal accounting assumptions". OQ-1..OQ-3 do not cover it. So the finding is not refuted, but it stays INFORMATIONAL (best practice and integrator documentation) and should not be raised.

Why it stays informational under the rubric:
(1) Nobody can take funds. sweepSurplus (:774) is onlyOwner and nonReentrant, so even an admin reached from the hook reverts. PoC test 4 confirms this. Every lane is correct once the transaction ends, and the README/NatSpec T4 claim that "the admin cannot reach a wei" still holds.
(2) The inconsistency only affects the lanes of the hook token itself: surplus(T), totalLocked[T] and the vault that holds T. surplus(T) is computed from T.balanceOf(vault), and the author of a hook token controls balanceOf completely. An integrator therefore cannot trust surplus(T) for such a token at any time, and read-only reentrancy gives the attacker nothing the token did not already give them. Views for every other token are consistent.
(3) Standard tokens do not trigger it. The ERC777 tokensToSend hook runs before the balance moves. The vault registers no tokensReceived. _pull uses transferFrom, not ERC-1363/677 transferAndCall. For native and standard ERC20 payouts, withdraw, withdrawCredit and pushCredit write state before _payout (:714-732), so recipients see consistent views. The PoC's payout-side case (test 3) needs a token whose hook runs before its own balance update, which is also non-standard.
(4) Nothing consumes these views mid-transaction. Vault positions are non-transferable and there is no share token or price that another protocol would read inside a callback. The project's own frontend (site/assets/app.js:205, 216, 411) reads getVault and creditOf through eth_call, which only ever sees committed state. The values that are wrong in flight also err in the safe direction for users: balance and totalLocked read low, and only the admin-only surplus reads high.
(5) The Base contract is immutable, so a code fix can only help the BNB deployment. For Base the remedy is documentation.

The recommended fix is weaker than it looks and partly harmful. Putting nonReentrantView on creditOf, getVault and getOpenVaults turns reads that are currently harmless, and already consistent at native-payout time, into reverts. Take a recipient contract whose receive() calls creditOf or getVault to reconcile. With the fix, that call reverts, _payout fails with NativeTransferFailed, and pushCredit fails. pushCredit exists (NatSpec at :724-725) precisely for contracts that cannot originate a transaction, so for that class the fix could turn an informational note into credit stranding. Such a contract has no other route to its credit. The fix also leaves the public totalLocked and totalCredited getters answering mid-flight, as the PoC notes.
sev.better_fix:
For the live Base contract, the only remedy is documentation. Add an integrator note to README.md, security.html and how-it-works.html: surplus(), totalLocked, totalCredited and getVault() may be read from committed state only, never from inside a token or payout callback. Also say plainly that hook and callback tokens are unsupported, next to the existing ban on rebasing tokens.

For the BNB or any future deployment, do not put nonReentrantView on creditOf, getVault or getOpenVaults. A contract that receives a native payout may legitimately call those views from receive(), and the guard would make pushCredit revert for exactly the recipients it exists to serve. There are two better options:
(a) Expose the lock state and let integrators check it: `function reentrancyGuardEntered() external view returns (bool) { return _reentrancyGuardEntered(); }`. Document that every accounting view is provisional while it returns true.
(b) If a guard is wanted anyway, guard only surplus(), which only the admin uses, and have sweepSurplus call an internal _surplus(). Optionally, pre-account deposits so that mid-flight surplus errs low rather than high: add the declared amount to totalLocked before the transfer, then subtract (amount - received) after it. The global nonReentrant lock already stops the hook from reaching withdraw or close, so this does not reopen A-01.
In both cases, add a test showing that a recipient contract whose receive() reads creditOf and getVault is still paid by pushCredit.

Line 71 sets `cap = block.timestamp + MAX_PREPAID`. Line 72 reverts with `TooFarAhead(cap)` whenever `target > cap`. `paidUntil[account]` can be raised by anyone, because gifting is permissionless. Test setup:
- Price is 0.001 ETH per 30 days, matching the repo's own tests.
- CAP_VALUE = ceil(MAX_PREPAID*PRICE/MONTH) buys exactly 315,360,000 s.
- ONE_SECOND = 385,802,470 wei buys exactly 1 s. A sanity test checks both.
- Automine is off. Mallory sends `subscribe(bob, 0)` with ONE_SECOND and a 50 gwei priority fee. Bob sends `subscribe(bob, 0)` with CAP_VALUE and a 1 gwei priority fee, with an explicit gasLimit. Then one `evm_mine`.

- both transactions are in the same block;
- Mallory's transaction comes first in that block;
- Mallory's gift has status 1.

It then decodes Bob's revert data with `debug_traceTransaction` and `parseError`. The decoded error is `TooFarAhead(block.timestamp + MAX_PREPAID)`. That is the line 72 guard, not a setup error or a gas problem.

The failing assertion is the intended property: Bob's receipt status must be 1, and he should end at the cap. It fails with status 0.

A control test sends the same CAP_VALUE purchase without the gift. It succeeds and lands exactly on `block.timestamp + MAX_PREPAID`, so the purchase itself is valid and the gift is the only cause of the revert.

A bounded-impact test shows that Bob's next-block retry sized for MAX_PREPAID-1 seconds succeeds. This test passes on the current code and should still pass after a clip-and-refund fix.

poc.severity_observation:
The Informational rating is right. The PoC suggests the practical impact is slightly lower than the finding states, for four reasons.

1. The attacker pays more than the victim. Mallory's gift used 49,071 gas and Bob's early revert used 26,803 gas. Mallory also pays the 385,802,470 wei gift and a higher priority fee, and the gift gives Bob one extra second of subscription. Bob loses only the gas of the reverted call, his value is returned, and he loses no time he had already bought.

2. The gift must land in the same block, ahead of Bob. If it lands in an earlier block, the next block's timestamp is at least 1 s later, which raises the cap by at least as much as a 1-second gift adds, and Bob's purchase succeeds. To block Bob from an earlier block, the gift would have to exceed the time elapsed between the two blocks, for example about 2 s per block on Base.

3. On Base the sequencer's mempool is private, so an actual front-run needs Bob's transaction to be visible. A public mempool such as BNB Chain's makes it easier. The same revert also happens without any attacker, when a well-meaning gifter such as an heir tops up the same account earlier in the same block.

4. Only purchases within k seconds of the cap are affected, where k is the gift size. A retry that is one second shorter succeeds. The website no longer sells subscriptions (see F23).

The finding's figure of 385,802,470 wei for one second is confirmed.

I could not refute this. The code path is real and reachable, but its impact is close to zero.

- `base = max(paidUntil, block.timestamp)` (line 69) and `target = base + added` (line 70). The cap is `block.timestamp + MAX_PREPAID` (line 71) and depends only on the block, not on the account.
- A k-second gift mined earlier in the same block therefore moves `target` up by up to k seconds while the cap stays put. Any purchase within k seconds of the cap then hits `revert TooFarAhead(cap)` (line 72).
- For an account with no subscription, the 1-second gift sets paidUntil to now+1. An exact-cap purchase then computes target = now+1+MAX_PREPAID, which is greater than cap, and reverts.

- I diffed the sandbox's NotifySubscription.sol against the repo and they are identical.
- The test uses no setStorageAt, no impersonation and no time manipulation beyond turning automine off.
- It orders the two transactions by priority fee and asserts three setup conditions before the failing assertion: same block, gift first, gift status 1.
- It decodes Bob's revert as TooFarAhead(block.timestamp + MAX_PREPAID).
- The control test (same CAP_VALUE with no gift) succeeds and lands exactly on the cap, which isolates the gift as the cause.
- I re-ran it: 3 passing, 1 failing with the expected TooFarAhead. The test is not self-confirming.

Why the impact is informational at most:
1. The victim loses nothing but the gas of an early revert (about 26.8k gas). Because the whole transaction reverts, his msg.value comes back, and none of his purchased time is lost. He also keeps the attacker's gifted second.
2. The attacker pays more than the victim: the gift, about 49k gas, and a higher priority fee.
3. The grief only works inside one block, ahead of the victim. From an earlier block, the gift must be larger than the time that has passed, because the cap grows with block.timestamp. Even then it only hands the victim more free time, and a retry sized to cap minus paidUntil reaches the same end state for less money.
4. On Base, where this contract lives, the sequencer mempool is private, so a targeted front-run is not practical.
5. Only purchases within k seconds of the cap are affected. The website no longer sells subscriptions, though the contract can still be called directly.
6. The same revert happens with no attacker at all, whenever a well-meaning gifter tops up the account earlier in the same block. That makes this a UX and integrator note: a "buy max" should leave slack, or the contract should clip and refund. It is not a security defect.

The interaction between third-party gifts and exact-cap purchases is not documented anywhere I found: README, AUDIT-2026-08-09.md and the site pages have nothing on it. sev.reasoning:
The behaviour is real and I traced it. In contracts/NotifySubscription.sol, subscribe() at lines 68-72 builds `target` on `max(paidUntil[account], block.timestamp)` and reverts `TooFarAhead(cap)` when `target > block.timestamp + MAX_PREPAID`. Anyone can raise `paidUntil[account]`. So a gift of k seconds, mined earlier in the same block, makes any purchase that lands within k seconds of the cap revert. The PoC confirms this, with a control test and a decoded revert.

It is not a meaningful defect, for these reasons.

(1) It follows directly from two design choices the contract states in its own comments. Lines 13-14 say payment is "permissionless and giftable". Lines 25-27 describe the hard prepayment cap as protection for a fat-fingered payer. The revert is the fail-safe outcome: the whole msg.value comes back and no time already bought is touched. The finding's phrase "no refund of the excess" is misleading. Nothing is kept on revert; the victim loses only the gas of an early revert (about 26.8k gas in the PoC).

(2) The cost runs against the attacker. Mallory spends about 49k gas plus the gift value (385,802,470 wei per second at the test price) plus a higher priority fee. The gift itself extends Bob's subscription. Bob retries one second short and succeeds (bounded-impact test). Blocking Bob persistently means paying for time that accrues to Bob, capped at ten years in total, after which the attacker cannot gift any more.

(3) The gift must be ordered ahead of Bob in the same block. A gift in an earlier block is cancelled out, because the cap moves forward with block.timestamp (about 2 s per block on Base). Base's sequencer mempool is private, so a targeted front-run is impractical there. On a public-mempool chain it is easier but still costs more than it inflicts. The likeliest real-world trigger is not an attacker but a well-meaning concurrent gifter.

(4) It only bites exact-cap purchases. The contract is also retired, and users are told repeatedly not to call it: README.md:85-86, SECURITY.md:14-15, AUDIT_SCOPE.md:87-89, site/terms.html:44-48, site/app.html:34-35, site/about.html:67 and site/index.html:192. Relative to the documented model, where nobody should be subscribing, exposure is essentially zero.

Under the rubric this is not LOW "minor griefing", because there is no favourable cost asymmetry and no loss beyond reverted-call gas. It stays INFORMATIONAL.

I do not refute it outright, and I do not mark it by_design_and_disclosed, because the specific interaction is not written down anywhere: not in the NatSpec, the README trust table, OQ-1..OQ-3, security.html or how-it-works.html. The rejected-claims list in AUDIT-2026-08-09.md:177 covers only overflow. The two ingredients are disclosed; their combination is not. The honest disposition is an informational note for a successor contract, and no action on the deployed one.

A related, equally benign trigger the finding misses: if the admin lowers the price ahead of an exact-cap purchase, `added` grows and the purchase reverts TooFarAhead. The `minSecondsAdded` guard is a floor only, so it offers no protection here.
sev.better_fix:
The recommended fix, clipping to the cap and refunding the excess, is weaker than it looks.

- A push refund to msg.sender adds an external call inside subscribe(), which currently makes none. That opens a reentrancy surface.
- A payer that is a contract without receive() would revert anyway, so the fix does not remove the failure mode.
- Silently delivering less time than was paid for undercuts the fat-fingered-payer rationale of MAX_PREPAID. It turns a clean full-refund revert into a partial fill the payer did not ask for.

For the deployed, retired contract: take no action and keep the existing "do not call" warnings.

For a successor:
- (a) Keep the revert, because it is the safest failure: msg.value returns in full. Have the client size purchases with a small margin below the cap, for example a few minutes or several blocks.
- (b) If exact-cap buys matter, add a caller-chosen tolerance or a `maxPaidUntil` argument. If clipping is kept, credit the excess to a pull-withdrawable refund balance instead of pushing ETH back. Keep `minSecondsAdded` as the floor alongside it, since it currently guards only against receiving less time.
- (c) State in the NatSpec that a concurrent gift or a price decrease can make a purchase near the cap revert.

- Filtering VaultCreated by the indexed beneficiary topic (:192-202) returns all three vaults for Dave: Alice's real one and the two spam ones.

- Dave sends no transaction. His ETH balance, creditOf and real USDC balance all stay unchanged. There is no on-chain loss.

Site side (test 1, fails because of the defect):
- The test loads the site's own rendering code from site/assets/app.js without changes: vaultCard at :257, fmtAmount at :86-89 and meta at :77-84. It uses a minimal fake DOM and calls vaultCard the same way the heir lookup handler does (:378-398: getOpenVaults(owner) filtered by beneficiary).

- It fails because fmtAmount renders only `${formatUnits} ${symbol()}`, so Mallory's spam card and Alice's genuine card are the same apart from the owner address.
- The fixture sanity checks pass first (both lookups return the expected token), so the failing assertion is the defect itself, not a setup error.

Positive control: in a patched copy of app.js outside the repo (scratchpad/poc/F36-control/app.js), fmtAmount appends `(token ${short(token)})` for ERC20s. Pointing the test at it with F36_APP_JS makes both tests pass, so the regression test can pass once the site is fixed.

poc.severity_observation:
Informational is right for the contract.
- Nothing reaches the heir unless they claim. The spammer cannot touch the victim's own vaults, because vaults are keyed by owner.
- A spoofed or reverting symbol() on the spam token cannot break the heir's lookup of a genuine owner, because the lookup is per owner and meta() caches by token address.

The site finding is a little stronger than written:
- The site has no beneficiary-indexed discovery. The heir lookup (app.js:378-398) needs the heir to type an owner address. So a phisher cannot use the site to list vaults naming the heir. The only beneficiary-indexed surface is explorers and log indexers.
- But once the phisher gives the heir the phisher's own owner address ("your relative 0x3C44... left you funds, check on willandkey.com"), the official site shows a card that looks exactly like a real 1,000,000 USDC inheritance. Later it shows real "Initiate claim" and "Finalize inheritance" buttons. The official site therefore vouches for the lure, which suits advance-fee scams ("pay a fee to unlock your inheritance").
- A spam token can also set decimals() to inflate the amount shown.
- This could arguably be LOW as a UI defect that misleads users, but there is still no path to lose funds through the contract. The heir's worst on-chain cost is gas for claiming worthless tokens.
- Minor documentation mismatch: site/index.html:75 says "any ERC-20" and how-it-works.html:34 says "a supported asset". The contract has no allowlist.
- Fix, confirmed by the control run: show the token address, with an explorer link, next to the symbol in fmtAmount/vaultCard, and flag tokens that are not on a per-chain allowlist.

reach.reasoning:
I could not refute F36. I checked it against the code and re-ran the PoC. It holds, at informational severity.

The preconditions are reachable:
- createVault (contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:370-435) has no token allowlist. Its guards are:
  - creationPaused, which defaults to false (:184, :378)
  - amount != 0
  - beneficiary is not zero, not the contract, and not msg.sender (:380-381)
  - period, window and horizon bounds
  - the per-owner MAX_OPEN_VAULTS cap (:399). A fresh address gets around it.
- _pull (:345-356) only requires received > 0. One raw unit of a token the attacker minted is enough.
- The heir is never asked to agree. VaultCreated indexes beneficiary (:192-202), so explorers and log filters on that topic show spam vaults.

The PoC is valid:
- Its copies of InheritanceVault.sol and site/assets/app.js are byte-identical to the repo's. I checked with diff.
- The only new contract is a plain OpenZeppelin ERC20 with a chosen name, symbol and decimals, the thing any attacker can deploy. There is no setStorageAt, no impersonation and no impossible state.
- Test 1 takes vaultCard, fmtAmount and meta straight from the real app.js, with no changes, and runs them against a minimal fake DOM. Fixture sanity checks run first, and they pass: each lookup returns the expected token.
- The assertion that fails is the defect itself. fmtAmount (app.js:86-89) renders only `formatUnits + symbol()`, so the spam card and the genuine card match word for word except for the owner address.
- The reviewer can point the test at a patched copy of app.js (F36_APP_JS), so the test is not written to pass or fail no matter what.
- My re-run gave the same result: 1 failing (the heir card), 1 passing. The spam createVault cost 228,824 gas, and the beneficiary-topic filter returned all 3 vaults.

Why the severity stays informational:
- There are no per-beneficiary data structures. Storage is keyed by owner, and credits by (token, account), as the mappings at :174-180 show. Spam vaults therefore cannot deny service to, mix with, or touch the heir's genuine vaults or credits.
- A hostile token's transfer runs with the vault as msg.sender, so claiming it cannot take the heir's own funds. The heir's worst on-chain cost is gas.
- The site has no beneficiary-indexed discovery. The heir lookup (app.js:378-398) needs an owner address, so the lure only works if the phisher first gets the victim to type the phisher's owner address.
- The same lure is already possible with ordinary fake-token airdrops, so the contract adds little new risk.
- A LOW rating for the site card, as a UI that misleads users, is defensible. By the rubric, though, there is no fund-loss path.

Two corrections to the write-up:
- Step 3's "heir dashboard filtering by beneficiary" is hypothetical today. It covers only explorers and third-party indexers.
- The minor doc inconsistency is real. index.html:75 says "any ERC-20", while how-it-works.html:34 says "a supported asset", and nothing enforces a supported list.

On by_design_and_disclosed: letting anyone name any address as heir is intended (app.html:107 says "to any address you choose"). The spam and look-alike-token risk to heirs is not disclosed anywhere I searched: README, the prior audit, AUDIT_SCOPE and the site pages. So the answer is false.
reach.better_fix:
Fix the site; the immutable contract needs no change.
- In fmtAmount/vaultCard, always show the ERC-20 token address (shortened, with an explorer link) next to symbol().
- Keep a per-chain allowlist of known token addresses, and show non-listed tokens as "unverified token". Scale suspicious decimals() values or flag them.
- Add a line to the heir guide and security.html: anyone can name any wallet as heir without its consent, and only vaults from an owner address you already know and trust matter.
- Never add a "vaults naming you" discovery view without the same token labelling.

sev.reasoning:
I traced the behaviour in the code. It is real, and it is intended at the contract level, but nothing tells users about it.

**Contract (InheritanceVault.sol)**
- createVault (:370-435) accepts any token address.
- _pull (:345-356) only requires that received > 0, so a spammer can fund a vault with 1 raw unit of a self-deployed token.
- The only beneficiary checks are not zero, not the contract and not msg.sender (:380-381). There is no heir consent.
- MAX_OPEN_VAULTS (:399) is counted per owner, so a fresh address gets around it. The PoC measured 228,824 gas, which is cents on Base.
- VaultCreated indexes beneficiary (:195), so explorers and log indexers list these spam vaults under the victim's address.
- This part is inherent to the design. An heir who does not have to act until claim time cannot be asked to consent, and the deployed contract is immutable in any case.
- There is no on-chain loss path:
  - Vaults are keyed by owner, so spam cannot add vaults to a real owner's list, and it cannot touch the victim's own vaults.
  - The heir's worst on-chain cost is gas to claim a worthless token.
  - withdrawCredit sends the token from the vault to the heir, which needs no approval from the heir.

**The site is the real defect**
- There is no beneficiary-indexed view on the site. The heir tab (app.html:90-100, app.js:378-398) needs the heir to type an owner address. So the spammer must first persuade the victim to enter the spammer's owner address.
- Once the victim does, fmtAmount (app.js:86-89) shows only formatUnits plus the token's own symbol(). vaultCard (app.js:257ff) never shows the token address.
- The PoC showed that a spam card is identical to a genuine "1000000.0 USDC" card apart from the owner address. It still names the victim's wallet as heir and offers the real Initiate claim and Finalize buttons.
- In effect, the official site vouches for a lure such as "a relative left you 1M USDC; pay a processing fee to release it". decimals() is also chosen by the spammer, so the displayed amount can be inflated.

**Disclosure check: not disclosed**
- README's trust-model table (:33-43) says nothing about it. It only lists rebasing tokens and NFTs as unsupported.
- The contract header (:23-68) does not cover it.
- The prior audit's OQ-1..OQ-3 are about the check-in chain race, checkInMany skips and fee slippage. None of them is related.
- security.html and how-it-works.html carry no heir-side warning.
- Two pages say "chooses a supported asset" (how-it-works.html:34, about.html:54), which suggests the assets are curated. index.html:75 says "any ERC-20", and the create form takes a free-text token address (app.html:66-67). So the public pages disagree with each other and with the code.
- The only scam warning is a general "wallet recovery help" note in guides/crypto-inheritance-planning.html:126. It does not cover fake inheritances.

**Severity: LOW**
- Contract only: INFORMATIONAL.
- Anyone can trigger it, at near-zero cost, and the victim loses nothing on-chain. Any loss needs off-site social engineering and the victim's cooperation.
- But the project's own heir UI shows attacker-chosen metadata as though it were a real asset. That fits "misleads users/integrators" better than best practice or clarity.
- It is not MEDIUM. There is no conditional loss through the protocol, and the victim must first enter an owner address a stranger gave them.

**Better fix than the one recommended**
Do not add an on-chain allowlist or heir-acceptance step. The contract is immutable, and either one would change the trust model: an allowlist would give the admin control over which assets are usable, and heir acceptance would add a step that can be griefed. Keep the fix off-chain:
1. In fmtAmount and vaultCard, always show the full token address with a link to the chain's explorer.
2. Keep a per-chain list of known canonical token addresses (native coin, USDC, USDT, WETH and so on). For any token not on it, show a prominent "Unverified token: its name, symbol and decimals are set by whoever deployed it" banner. Consider showing no symbol at all, or labelling it "UNVERIFIED:SYM".
3. Validate decimals() against a sane range (for example 0-36), and fall back to showing the raw amount if it is out of range or if symbol() or decimals() reverts.
4. Add heir guidance to the heir tab and security.html:
   - Will & Key never charges an heir anything beyond network gas; the protocol fee is deducted on-chain at settlement.
   - Nobody can "release" an inheritance for a payment.
   - A vault from an owner address you did not get directly from the person themselves should be treated as a scam.
5. Make "supported asset" and "any ERC-20" consistent: any standard ERC-20 except rebasing and balance-adjusting tokens, and the site does not vet tokens.
sev.better_fix:
Keep the fix off-chain; an on-chain allowlist or heir-consent step would widen admin power or change the trust model. In site/assets/app.js:
- In fmtAmount and vaultCard, always show the full token address with an explorer link.
- Keep a per-chain list of known canonical token addresses. For any other token, show an "Unverified token: name, symbol and decimals are set by its deployer" banner, and do not show the bare symbol as if it were the real asset.
- Only accept decimals() in the range 0-36. If it is out of range, or if symbol() or decimals() reverts, show the raw amount.
Add a line to the heir tab and security.html: heirs never pay anything but gas; the protocol fee is deducted at settlement; a vault from an owner address you did not get from the owner personally is a scam. Make the wording consistent: how-it-works.html:34 and about.html:54 say "supported asset" while index.html:75 says "any ERC-20". Both should say that any standard ERC-20 except rebasing tokens is accepted and the site does not vet it.

confirmed.title: Chain-specific environment notes: veto inclusion depends on the Base sequencer and BNB validators, and the watcher's paging is sized for Base
confirmed.location: contracts/InheritanceVault.sol:101 MIN_CHALLENGE; notify/watcher.js LOG_PAGE and initial lookback
confirmed.description: (a) An owner's veto must be included during the window. On Base, a sequencer outage or censorship delays inclusion; the escape is OP-Stack forced inclusion via an L1 deposit, which can take up to the sequencing window (about 12 h), and nothing in the site or emails mentions it. On BNB, inclusion depends on about 21 active Parlia validators. The 7-day minimum window makes this low-probability. (b) The watcher's first-run lookback of 9,000 blocks is about 5 h on Base but under 2 h on BNB's 0.75 s blocks, and some BNB public RPCs cap or disable eth_getLogs for that range. (The BNB reflection-token point is folded into F11.)
confirmed.impact: Mostly documentation and operations. A veto delayed by sequencer issues near the end of a short window could miss.
confirmed.exploit_scenario:
1. A Base sequencer outage coincides with the last hours of a 7-day window.
2. The owner's abortClaim is not included in time, and the owner does not know about L1 forced inclusion.
3. The claim is finalized after the window.
confirmed.recommendation: Mention L1 forced inclusion for Base in the veto email and site, and recommend challenge windows of at least 14 days. Revalidate the watcher's LOG_PAGE and initial lookback per chain before a BNB launch.
confirmed.poc_plan: Not a contract test. Compute block-time coverage of the watcher's lookback per chain, and check BNB RPC eth_getLogs limits.
confirmed.preconditions: A BNB deployment, or a Base sequencer outage during a veto window.
confirmed.relation_to_prior_audit: New.

F37 -- watcher log paging vs the public RPCs of the target chains SAFE PROPERTY: against the Base RPC the shipped config names, the owner is told the claim SETTLED while reminders were down
F37 -- watcher log paging vs the public RPCs of the target chains DAMAGE: owner receives no email at all about a settled estate -- Base public RPC and BNB dataseed
poc.explanation:
Part (b) was run as a test, and it is worse than the finding says. Part (a) can only be cited.

WHAT WAS MEASURED (read-only JSON-RPC probes, 2026-09-24; the scripts measure-chains.js and probe-caps.js and their outputs are in the sandbox):
- https://mainnet.base.org is the `rpc` in notify/config.example.json. It accepts eth_getLogs only while toBlock - fromBlock <= 2000; at 2001 it returns -32614 "eth_getLogs is limited to a 2,000 range". The watcher's page (notify/watcher.js:49 `const LOG_PAGE = 9_000;`, paged at :295) has toBlock - fromBlock = 8,999, so the default Base RPC refuses it. The watcher is therefore not "sized for Base". The comment at watcher.js:45 cites the common cap as "commonly 10k blocks", but that is not what the default endpoint allows.
- BNB: bsc-dataseed.bnbchain.org (the default `bnb` RPC in hardhat.config.ts) and bsc-dataseed.binance.org return -32005 "limit exceeded" even for a 1-block range. defibit and ninicoin behave the same. 1rpc allows only 50 blocks, meowrpc does not support eth_getLogs at all, and ankr needs an API key. Only bsc-rpc.publicnode.com accepted 9,000 blocks. On Base, publicnode also accepted 9,000, 1rpc allows 50 blocks, meowrpc does not support the call, and drpc refused.
- Block times: Base 2.0000 s. BNB 0.4503 s, not the 0.75 s the finding assumes, because BNB has moved to 0.45 s blocks. The first-run lookback of 9,000 blocks is therefore 5.00 h on Base and 1.13 h on BNB. The lookback difference turns out not to matter: a settled claim's ClaimInitiated log is always at least MIN_CHALLENGE (7 days) old, so a first-run lookback of 5 h or 1.1 h can never reach it on either chain.

THE TEST: it runs the real, unmodified notify/watcher.js as a child process (read-only; its state and outbox go to a temp dir in the sandbox). The watcher talks to a local JSON-RPC proxy in front of the in-process Hardhat chain. The proxy forwards every call unchanged, except that it applies the measured eth_getLogs policy of the named endpoint. Blocks are mined at Base's real 2-second cadence, so an outage spans as many blocks as it would on mainnet (604,923). In scripts/notify-scenario.ts, by contrast, 8 days is a single block, which is why the local 14-step scenario claimed at site/security.html:63 passes.

The scenario is the case only the backfill can report, which is W-05's whole purpose:
1. The watcher runs once while alice has no vault.
2. The watcher goes down. Alice creates a 7-day inactivity / 7-day challenge vault naming bob. Bob calls initiateClaim after the deadline. Carol calls finalizeClaim after the window, and bob is credited 9.95 ETH.
3. The watcher comes back on its 6-hour cron for up to 20 runs.

Results:
- Control (no range cap): the owner gets "A claim on your vault SETTLED while reminders were down" on the second cron run. This passes, which shows the scenario itself is sound.
- Base cap: all 21 watcher runs exit with code 2, all 21 eth_getLogs calls are refused, the scan cursor is never saved, and zero emails are sent. The test FAILS.
- BNB dataseed: same result. The DAMAGE test FAILS.

terminalAlerts does not cover this case: the vault was never in `seen`, so no "vault is now closed" email goes out either. The owner hears nothing about the transfer.

The failure comes from the defect, not the setup. A copy of the watcher with LOG_PAGE = 2_000 (sandbox fixcheck/watcher.js, run with F37_WATCHER=...) makes the Base test pass; the owner is told after 7 cron runs. The BNB-dataseed half still fails, because no page size works on an RPC that refuses eth_getLogs outright. That half needs either a logs-capable BNB RPC or a fallback that doesn't use logs. The contract exposes `vaultCount(owner)` (InheritanceVault.sol:175), so the watcher could call getVault(owner, 0..n-1) to find settled vaults without logs.

PART (a), CITATION ONLY (no executable behaviour; the finding describes the chain environment):
- finalizeClaim at InheritanceVault.sol:686 is `if (block.timestamp < finalizableAt) revert ChallengeWindowOpen(finalizableAt);`. It is permissionless and has no grace period or sequencer-uptime check.
- abortClaim at :663-676 checks only STATE_CLAIM_PENDING and the horizon (:670). This means a delayed veto still works after finalizableAt as long as nobody has finalized yet. The risk is therefore an ordering race against finalizeClaim once the sequencer resumes, not a hard cutoff. The finding does not mention this nuance.
- Public claims: site/index.html:153 says "wait a challenge window of at least 7 days — during which any action from your wallet cancels the claim". The veto email at watcher.js:156-159 says "you must act before the challenge window closes at ... After that moment the transfer is final and cannot be reversed by anyone."
- A grep of site/*.html, README.md, SECURITY.md, DEPLOY.md, notify/README.md and watcher.js finds no mention of the sequencer, forced inclusion, L1 deposits or censorship.

poc.severity_observation:
Part (b) is bigger than claimed, and the reason is different from the one the finding gives. The watcher's 9,000-block page is refused by mainnet.base.org, the RPC in the shipped config.example.json, which caps ranges at 2,000 blocks. So on the chain that is live today, the claim backfill (the W-05 fix, whose only job is to report a claim that settled during a watcher outage) fails on every run. When the vault was created after the watcher's last good run, the owner gets no email at all about the estate transfer. On BNB, the dataseed endpoints refuse eth_getLogs completely, so no page size can help there.

Two things mitigate this:
- The failure is loud: every run exits with code 2 and logs "backfill failed". But a cron that is permanently red trains an operator to ignore it.
- AUDIT_SCOPE.md:87 says the production watcher is not running, and site/how-it-works.html:98 tells users not to rely on email.

There is no on-chain fund impact, so for the contracts this stays informational/low. For the watcher it is a real functional defect: a core watcher promise is broken on the default configuration, which would be MEDIUM against the watcher on its own. It should probably be split out of F37 as a separate watcher finding.

Other corrections to the finding:
- BNB's block time is now 0.45 s, not 0.75 s.
- The first-run lookback difference between chains has no impact, because a settled claim's log is always at least 7 days old.
- For part (a), abortClaim has no window-end check, so a veto delayed past finalizableAt still works unless a finalizeClaim lands first. The exposure is an ordering race after the sequencer resumes, which is somewhat less severe than "the veto misses".

Sandbox extras: measure-chains.js, probe-caps.js with their outputs (measure-output.txt, probe-caps-output.txt), fixcheck/watcher.js (the LOG_PAGE = 2_000 copy), and the run logs poc-run.txt and poc-fixcheck.txt. The repo was not modified.

reach.reasoning:
Not refuted. I checked both parts against the code, and ran one read-only probe of my own against the Base public RPC.

PART (a): veto inclusion depends on the chain. This holds, with one nuance.
- finalizeClaim (InheritanceVault.sol:686) is permissionless. Its only time check is `block.timestamp < finalizableAt`. There is no grace period and no sequencer-uptime check.
- abortClaim (:663-676) checks only STATE_CLAIM_PENDING and `block.timestamp < absoluteDeadline` (:670). It has no window-end check, so a veto that arrives after finalizableAt still succeeds as long as nobody has finalized yet.
- So a sequencer outage near the end of the window does not create a hard cutoff. It creates an ordering race between the owner's abortClaim and anyone's finalizeClaim once inclusion resumes. That is less severe than "the veto misses", and the finding does not mention this nuance.
- On OP Stack, L2 timestamps are tied to block number and L1 origin. Blocks produced during catch-up after an outage can even carry earlier timestamps. Either way, 7 days is the minimum window (:101), which keeps the scenario low-probability.
- The documentation gap is real. I grepped site/*.html, README.md, SECURITY.md, DEPLOY.md, notify/README.md, notify/watcher.js and AUDIT_SCOPE.md for sequencer, forced inclusion, L1 deposit and censor: zero hits.
- Meanwhile the veto email (watcher.js:156-159) says the transfer is final "after that moment", and site/index.html:153 promises that any action from the owner's wallet cancels the claim during the window.

PART (b): the watcher's paging is not validated per chain. This holds, and the actual defect is worse than the finding says.
- The title's claim that the paging is "sized for Base" is false.
- backfillClaims (watcher.js:287-323) starts at `latest - LOG_PAGE` when no cursor exists. Each page uses `to = from + LOG_PAGE - 1`, so toBlock - fromBlock = 8,999.
- My own probe of https://mainnet.base.org on 2026-09-24, which is the `rpc` in notify/config.example.json: a range of 2000 returns ok. Ranges of 2001 and 8999 both return -32614 "eth_getLogs is limited to a 2,000 range".
- Because the first page always fails, the throw is caught at :425-430, failures is incremented, and the cursor is never committed. Every run then exits 2 (:446) and the backfill never completes on the default configuration.

The PoC test (poc-F37.ts) is sound and not self-confirming:
- It runs the real, unmodified watcher.js as a child process against a local proxy. The proxy only rejects eth_getLogs ranges that exceed the measured cap.
- It mines at Base's 2-second cadence, and uses no storage writes or impersonation.
- An uncapped control passes, and a copy with LOG_PAGE = 2_000 (the only diff to the real watcher) passes on the Base policy. That isolates the cause to LOG_PAGE.
- The "no email at all" outcome only arises when the vault was never in `seen`. terminalAlerts (:247-277) covers vaults that were in `seen`, so the affected case is narrow.

Corrections to the finding:
- BNB block time is now about 0.45 s, not 0.75 s.
- The per-chain difference in first-run lookback has no impact. A settled claim's ClaimInitiated log is always at least MIN_CHALLENGE (7 days) old, so neither a 5-hour nor a 1.1-hour lookback can ever reach it.
- The BNB dataseed endpoint refusing all eth_getLogs calls is the Hardhat deploy default, not a configured watcher RPC. There is no BNB deployment yet, so that half is prospective.

Severity:
- For the contract audit, F37 is correctly INFORMATIONAL. There is no on-chain fund impact, and the sequencer point is an environment and documentation matter.
- The watcher paging defect should be split out as a separate off-chain finding, rated LOW rather than MEDIUM:
  - backfillClaims only reports vaults already in state 3 (SETTLED, final). The alert can never enable a veto or protect funds.
  - The case where no email arrives at all needs a vault that was never seen by a successful run.
  - The production watcher is not running (AUDIT_SCOPE.md:87-88).
  - The site tells users not to rely on email (how-it-works.html:98).
  - It does have one operational cost: a permanently exit-2 cron hides real failures, such as SMTP errors.
reach.better_fix:
(a) In the veto email and on the site:
- Say that on Base, if the sequencer is down or censoring, the owner's veto can still be forced in through an L1 deposit (OP Portal), with a delay of up to about 12 hours.
- Say that abortClaim stays valid after the window closes until someone actually calls finalizeClaim.
- Recommend challenge windows of at least 14 days.

(b) Fix the watcher's log scanning:
- Make LOG_PAGE a per-chain config value. Set it so that toBlock - fromBlock <= 1,999 on mainnet.base.org.
- On range errors (-32614, -32005, -32602) or "not supported" errors, halve the page and retry.
- Add a fallback that does not use logs: for i in 0..vaultCount(owner)-1 (public mapping at InheritanceVault.sol:175), call getVault(owner, i) and report any vault in state 3 that has not been reported yet. This covers RPCs that refuse eth_getLogs, such as BNB dataseed. It also fixes the first-run blind spot, because a settled claim's log is always at least 7 days old and falls outside any initial lookback.
- Report a backfill failure separately from delivery failures, so that one broken RPC does not leave the cron permanently red and hide SMTP errors.

sev.reasoning:
Not refuted and not disclosed. The finding bundles two unrelated things. They should be split and rated separately. Part (a) stays INFORMATIONAL. Part (b) is a real LOW defect in the off-chain watcher, and the finding gives the wrong reason for it.

PART (a): sequencer and validator dependence of the veto. This is a real property of the environment, but it is not a contract defect.
- No unprivileged party can cause it. The Base sequencer or the BNB validator set would have to fail or censor, and only in the final hours of a window that lasts at least 7 days (InheritanceVault.sol:101, :385). Historical Base outages have lasted hours, not days.
- The outage cuts both ways. While the sequencer is down, finalizeClaim (:682-686) cannot be included either.
- abortClaim (:663-676) has no check on the end of the window. It checks only STATE_CLAIM_PENDING and the horizon (:670). So a veto that arrives after finalizableAt still works until someone finalizes. The real exposure is an ordering race in the first blocks after the sequencer resumes, not a hard cutoff.
- The public wording is, if anything, conservative. watcher.js:159-161 says "you must act before the challenge window closes", and site/index.html:153 says the window is "at least 7 days". Neither understates this risk.
- Nothing mentions the sequencer, forced inclusion or censorship: not the README trust table, security.html, how-it-works.html, or OQ-1 through OQ-3. So this is undisclosed, but negligible. It is an INFORMATIONAL documentation item.
- A Base forced-inclusion hint for the veto email and site would be reasonable. Do not reword the email to say a late veto still works. The "act before" framing correctly discourages waiting until the last moment.
- The recommendation to "recommend 14-day windows" is optional guidance, not a fix.
- The BNB line is speculative, since there is no BNB watcher config or deployment yet.

PART (b): watcher paging. The defect is real but has a different cause from the one the finding gives.
- I confirmed it with my own read-only probe today against https://mainnet.base.org, the rpc in notify/config.example.json. A range of to-from=2000 is accepted. Ranges of 2001 and 8999 both return -32614 "eth_getLogs is limited to a 2,000 range".
- The watcher's page is LOG_PAGE = 9_000 (watcher.js:49), queried as [from, from+8999] (:295). So backfillClaims (:287-323) throws on every run against the shipped default RPC. The comment at :45 ("commonly 10k blocks") is wrong for that endpoint.
- The finding's lookback theory is irrelevant. A settled claim's ClaimInitiated log is always at least 7 days old, so a first-run lookback of 5 h (Base) or about 1 h (BNB, now 0.45 s blocks) could never reach it on either chain.

Why part (b) is LOW, not MEDIUM as the PoC suggests:
1. The in-scope targets are the contracts. The watcher is off-chain context, and AUDIT_SCOPE.md:87 says the production watcher is not running.
2. The only live alert affected is the after-the-fact "SETTLED while reminders were down" notice. The veto alert itself comes from getOpenVaults and ownerAlerts, which make no log calls, so it still works on mainnet.base.org. The broken email cannot prevent, reverse or enlarge any loss. The loss (a claim that settled unvetoed) would already have happened because the watcher was down for the whole challenge window.
3. The failure is loud. Every run increments failures (:427-429) and exits with code 2 (:446). Other alerts are still delivered.
4. how-it-works.html:98 tells users not to rely on email.

It does, however, break a publicly claimed feature on the default configuration, deterministically. site/security.html:63 advertises "claim backfill after an outage" on the strength of a local scenario, and on mainnet.base.org that backfill can never succeed. Two further effects: a cron that is always red trains the operator to ignore real SMTP or RPC failures, and the BNB default endpoint (hardhat.config.ts:41, bsc-dataseed) refuses eth_getLogs at any range. That is a bounded functional defect plus a code-vs-claim mismatch with no fund impact. LOW is correct.

If F37 is kept as one finding, rate it LOW, driven by (b). If it is split, rate (a) INFORMATIONAL (contracts/documentation) and the new watcher finding LOW.
sev.better_fix:
1. Stop depending on eth_getLogs for the settled-claim backfill. The contract already has everything needed: vaultCount(owner) is a public lifetime counter (InheritanceVault.sol:175, ids never reused) and getVault(owner, i) (:809). Each run, go through i = 0..vaultCount-1. For each vault with state == 3, take stamp = claimInitiatedAt and send the alert when neither `claim:${stamp}` nor `settled-unseen:${stamp}` has been sent. This matches what the log path reports today, because watcher.js:306 already filters to the settled vault's claimInitiatedAt. It works on any RPC, including BNB dataseed endpoints that refuse eth_getLogs outright, and it needs no cursor. On the first run of a watch, record the vaults that are already settled as a baseline, so a newly added watch does not fire on old history.

2. If logs are kept as a secondary source, make the page size a per-chain config value (cfg.logPage, default 2000). Shrink it automatically when the RPC returns a range error (-32614, -32005, "limit", "range"), halving and retrying, and record the working size in state. 25 pages of 2,000 blocks is about 27.8 h of Base per run, which is still enough for a 6-hour cron to catch up.

3. Correct site/security.html:63. The backfill was tested locally with 8 days mined as one block and has not been validated against a production RPC. Add a per-chain RPC capability check to the watcher's startup and to DEPLOY/notify README before a BNB launch.

4. For part (a), add one line to the veto email and security page: on Base, a veto can be forced through Ethereum L1 via the OP Stack deposit path if the sequencer is unavailable. Keep the "act before the window closes" framing, and do not advertise that a late veto can still win the race against finalizeClaim. Recommending a longer challenge window is optional guidance, not a fix.

poc.explanation:
I tested F38 by mutation testing. This is the only direct way to show a test-coverage gap. For each regression the finding names, test/poc-F38.ts writes a mutant copy of the contract into its own source tree (f38-mutants/<id>/contracts). Each copy keeps the same contract name and has exactly one edit, and every edit pattern must match exactly once, so no mutant can be a silent no-op. The harness then runs the UNMODIFIED shipped test files against each tree in a child Hardhat process, using hardhat.f38-mutant.config.ts (the shipped config pointed at the mutant tree). I never edited InheritanceVault.sol or NotifySubscription.sol.

Control (section 0, passes): on the unmutated contracts, the shipped suites pass 7/7 (NotifySubscription) and 56/56 (InheritanceVault.ts + Audit.ts). The proposed suites pass 8/8 and 3/3. So any later failure is a real kill, not a harness error. The harness also refuses to count a run unless the full expected number of tests executed.

Intended property (section 1, FAILS, 9 of 9): "the shipped suite fails when this regression is introduced". Every one of these mutants survived with all shipped tests passing:
- NotifySubscription.sol:72 `target > cap` changed to `>=` (the finding's own example)
- :66 `added < minSecondsAdded` changed to `<=`
- :65 dust guard rewritten as `msg.value < pricePerMonth / MONTH` (1 wei short, so 385,802,469 wei buys 0 seconds and is kept)
- :93 withdraw loses its address(0) check
- :98 withdraw ignores a failed send
- a receive() is added that accepts plain transfers
- Ownable2Step is replaced by one-step Ownable
- InheritanceVault.sol:364 `_payout` uses IERC20.transfer instead of safeTransfer
- :352 `_pull` uses IERC20.transferFrom instead of safeTransferFrom

Section 2 (passes): the proposed boundary and hostile-token tests (f38/NotifySubscriptionBoundary.ts, f38/VaultHostileTokens.ts, and the new mocks in contracts/test/F38HostileTokens.sol) kill all 9 mutants. Each NotifySubscription mutant is killed by exactly the boundary test aimed at it. On the real contracts these tests pass, so they can be adopted as regression tests as they are.

Section 4 (FAILS): I measured on-chain that one second at 0.001 ETH/30 days costs 385,802,470 wei. 385,802,469 wei reverts with ZeroAmount; 385,802,470 wei buys exactly +1 s. That is 0.386 gwei, against the comment's "~385 gwei" at test/NotifySubscription.ts:52, about 998x too high. The shipped dust test pays 100 wei, 3,858,024x below the boundary.

Where the finding over-claims (section 3, passes):
1. The exploit-scenario example "a v2 refactor drops the msg.value check in _pull ... all existing tests still pass" is FALSE. The shipped test "rejects bad parameters" (test/InheritanceVault.ts:152-154, `c({ token, value: 1n })` expecting UnexpectedNativeValue) kills that mutant, so "native value sent with an ERC20 call" is not untested.
2. "A rounding-direction regression would pass" is false for `added`. Rounding up is killed by the 100-wei dust assertion (test/NotifySubscription.ts:53). Only an off-by-one in the dust guard survives.
3. Plain-transfer rejection is tested for the vault (InheritanceVault.ts:610, UseTopUp), just not for NotifySubscription.

Everything else holds: the cap, slippage, withdraw(0), non-payable recipient, plain-transfer (NotifySubscription) and Ownable2Step gaps are all real, and so are the no-bool and false-returning token classes.
